Figure 3.1: The book’s project at the end of this chapter. Inputs (left) are never changed by your work; code and software (middle) say how results are made; outputs (right) are written by the script. The records along the bottom explain all of it.



The same project as text: this is what the tree command prints, run inside ~/bioinf-computing at the end of the chapter. tree comes with the book environment, so start it with pixi run, as you did seqkit in Chapter 2. Indentation shows what is inside what, -> marks a link and where it points, and the last line counts what it found.


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run tree

.
├── data
│   ├── meta
│   │   ├── reads.tsv
│   │   ├── samples.tsv
│   │   └── samplesheet_upstream.csv
│   ├── raw
│   │   ├── checksums.md5
│   │   ├── SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
│   │   └── SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
│   ├── README.md
│   └── ref -> /home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
├── logs
│   └── 01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122453_7WFs.log
├── NOTEBOOK.md
├── pixi.lock
├── pixi.toml
├── README.md
├── results
│   └── read_counts.tsv
└── src
    └── 01_count_reads.sh

7 directories, 15 files
tree sorts by name and, like ls, hides names that start with a dot, so .pixi/ is missing; tree -a shows it (and its thousands of files). tree -L 2 stops two levels down, which helps in big projects. Later chapters use tree to show a tool’s inputs and outputs; run it yourself to check your folder against the book.
The rules behind it, one sentence each:

One project, one folder. Everything an analysis needs, or points to, is inside it.
Inputs, code, and outputs apart. Raw data and metadata in data/, scripts in src/, results in results/, logs in logs/. You never write into data/raw/, and nothing in results/ is edited by hand.
Results can be rebuilt. Everything in results/ should come back if you rerun the code in src/ on the inputs in data/, with the same software. Exercise 4 tests it.
Paths inside the project are relative to its top folder (data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz, not /home/you/bioinf-computing/data/…), so scripts keep working if the folder moves (more on moving in Section 3.5).

Table 3.1 lists the parts.




Table 3.1: The folders and files of the book’s project. “Back it up?” is discussed in Section 3.6; git arrives in Chapter 21.

ImportantKey idea



Keep inputs, code, and outputs apart, so that every output can be rebuilt from preserved inputs, code, settings, and software records. That gives you the ingredients for reproducing an analysis; actually rebuilding it is the test.


This is one sensible layout, not the only one. Noble (2009) and Wilson et al. (2017) describe close relatives; pipelines add a work/ folder of their own (Chapter 25), and later books adapt the layout to their tools. What matters is that a stranger can find the raw data, the code, and the results, and tell them apart.
On a cluster the same layout goes in project storage (/project/<your-project>/ on SCINet, /work/<your-group>/ on Nova), not in your small home folder or in scratch space that is purged (Section 2.2). Large intermediate files may live in scratch while a job runs, with only the final results kept in the project (Chapter 10). Making folders and moving files is light work, fine on a login node; checksumming many large files is not.

Check yourself. You delete results/read_counts.tsv by mistake (you will make it later in this chapter). What do you need to get it back?






TipAnswer





Nothing but the project itself: rerun the script on data/raw/ with the same environment. A large published analysis is different: rebuilding it can take days of computing, or need a reference or a software version that is no longer available, which is why important final results are backed up too.

title: 3  Organizing projects and data
text:
3.3 Names that work
Start with a puzzle. In the scratch folder, make seven empty files with names like the ones on many lab drives, then list them:


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch03/names && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch03/names
1touch run1.sh run2.sh run10.sh final.txt "Final FINAL (2).txt" "9-15-25 counts.csv" "10-2-26 counts.csv"
2ls -1


1

touch makes empty files. The quotes keep each name with spaces in one piece.

2

-1 (the digit one) lists one name per line.


'10-2-26 counts.csv'
'9-15-25 counts.csv'
'Final FINAL (2).txt'
final.txt
run1.sh
run10.sh
run2.sh
(Captured on a Mac. On Linux with English language settings, run10.sh comes before run1.sh; the order depends on the system’s language settings, but the two problems below appear everywhere.) ls sorts names character by character, so run10.sh lands before run2.sh, and October 2026 (10-2-26) before September 2025 (9-15-25). ls puts quotes around names with spaces to warn you, and spaces break commands that are not quoted:


Terminal (laptop)

wc -l 10-2-26 counts.csv

wc: 10-2-26: No such file or directory
wc: counts.csv: No such file or directory
0 total
The shell split the name at the space and looked for two files. Quoting fixes it (wc -l "10-2-26 counts.csv"), and you will still learn to quote paths (Chapter 5), but names without spaces never need it. Table 3.2 gives the rules, each with a better name.




Table 3.2: Rules for file names, with the problem each one avoids.





Rule
Problem name
Why it causes trouble
Better name




Only letters, digits, _, -, .
Final FINAL (2).txt
spaces and brackets must be quoted in every command
2026-11-17_read_counts.tsv


One case, usually lowercase
Data.csv and data.csv
usually the same file on a Mac or in Windows folders, but two files on Linux, including your WSL home folder and the cluster
data.csv


Dates as YYYY-MM-DD (ISO 8601)
10-2-26 counts.csv
sorts by month, not by time; day and month order is ambiguous
2026-10-02_counts.csv


Zero-padded numbers, scripts in run order
run2.sh, run10.sh
run10 sorts before run2
02_trim.sh, 10_report.sh


Say what is inside; keep the extension true
results.txt holding tabs
.txt hides that it is a table
read_counts.tsv


Versions say what changed
final_v2.txt
no one knows what v2 changed, or which is newest
yeast_R64-1-1_test, report_2026-11-17.html; later, git (Chapter 21)







Number scripts in the order they run: 00_ for one-time setup such as downloads, then 01_, 02_, …, so ls src/ shows the analysis in order. Two exceptions to renaming. First, IDs that come from a facility or an archive (SRR6357070, WT_REP1) stay exactly as given, so they still match the records; rename only your own files. Second, a name whose meaning you do not know: is 11-3-25 counts.csv 3 November or 11 March, 2025 or 2011? Renaming cannot recover what you do not know. Ask whoever made it, then rename.

Check yourself. In what order does ls list run1.sh, run2.sh, and run10.sh, and how would you rename them?






TipAnswer





run1.sh, run10.sh, run2.sh (on Linux, possibly run10.sh first; run2.sh always comes after run10.sh). Pad the numbers and say what each step does: 01_download.sh, 02_trim.sh, 10_report.sh.

title: 3  Organizing projects and data
section: 3.4 Raw data: move it in, check it, protect it
text:
3.4 Raw data: move it in, check it, protect it
Move it in. The two FASTQ files from Chapter 1 are still in the scratch folder ~/bioinf-computing-ch01. Move them into the project:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing
1mv ~/bioinf-computing-ch01/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz ~/bioinf-computing-ch01/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz data/raw/
ls -l data/raw


1

mv moves files; the last name is where they go. Moving within one disk only changes where the file is listed, so it is instant.


total 4368
-rw-r--r-- 1 you you 2239317 Nov 17 11:22 SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
-rw-r--r-- 1 you you 2232117 Nov 17 11:22 SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
From now on the files live here: if you go back to a command in Chapters 1–2, use ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/ instead of ~/bioinf-computing-ch01/. ~/bioinf-computing-ch01 keeps fastq_summary.txt; you can delete it later.






TipMissing a file?



If mv says cannot stat … No such file or directory for a file (you skipped the read-2 exercise, or deleted ~/bioinf-computing-ch01), the other file still moved. Download each missing one straight into data/raw/:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing
curl -fL -o data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/test-datasets/9dd6d014f560e182047992834a8d267214fbccd1/testdata/GSE110004/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
curl -fL -o data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/test-datasets/9dd6d014f560e182047992834a8d267214fbccd1/testdata/GSE110004/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz

Run only the line for the file you are missing. If a file is already in data/raw/ from an earlier visit to this chapter, leave it: the check below tells you whether it is intact.


Check it. A sequencing facility, or an archive such as ENA, gives you a checksum for every file: a short value computed from every byte of it. Here are the MD5 checksums of the two files, as the book recorded them. Make a file data/raw/checksums.md5 (code data/raw/checksums.md5 opens it in VS Code; nano works too), paste the two lines, and save:


data/raw/checksums.md5

d19f3c7a8b4016fa641458257b99a1a1  SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
d126cc66ed169f69af2c07da0dd73e02  SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz

Each line is a checksum, two spaces, and a file name. Now check the files against it:


Terminal (laptop)

cd data/raw
1md5sum -c checksums.md5
cd ~/bioinf-computing


1

md5sum computes MD5 checksums; -c (check) reads a list of them, recomputes each file’s, and compares.


SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: OK
The names in checksums.md5 have no folder, so the check runs inside the folder that holds the files. Facilities ship their lists the same way. Run it from the wrong folder and every file “fails”:
md5sum: SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: FAILED open or read
md5sum: SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: FAILED open or read
md5sum: WARNING: 2 listed files could not be read
Now name the idea (Figure 3.2). A checksum is a fingerprint of a file: the same bytes always give the same value, and changing a single byte gives a completely different one. A matching checksum means your copy is byte-for-byte the file the checksum was made from.




  A checksum is a fingerprint of every byte. Three files go through md5sum. The original SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz gives d19f3c7a followed by more digits. An exact copy gives the same value, so it matches. A copy with one byte changed, out of more than two million, gives a completely different value, 78027ba8, so it does not match.
  
    
      
    
  
  
  FILE (2,239,317 BYTES)
  MD5 CHECKSUM
  
  
  md5sum
  reads every
  byte
  
  
  original
  1f 8b 08 00 …
  6a
  1c
  …
  
  
  d19f3c7a…a1a1
  the expected value
  
  
  exact copy
  1f 8b 08 00 …
  6a
  1c
  …
  
  
  d19f3c7a…a1a1
  ✓ same: OK
  
  
  copy, one byte changed
  1f 8b 08 00 …
  1c
  …
  
  6b
  
  
  78027ba8…ca55
  ✗ different: FAILED




Figure 3.2: Checksums of the real read-1 file. An exact copy gives the same MD5 value; changing one byte out of 2,239,317 (6a to 6b, halfway through) gives a completely different value.



Run md5sum -c after every download or transfer, before any analysis (Chapter 9 reuses it after copying to a cluster). Two kinds of failure mean different things:

FAILED: the bytes differ, usually an incomplete or damaged copy. Download or copy the file again and recheck. Never “fix” the list by computing a new checksum from the damaged copy.
FAILED open or read with No such file or directory: the file is missing, misnamed, or you are in the wrong folder. Check that before assuming damage.

sha256sum works the same way (sha256sum -c) with a longer, stronger value (both are documented in the GNU coreutils manual); the book’s own data/README.md records both. MD5 is still what most facilities and ENA supply, and it is fine for catching damaged copies.






CautionMisconception: “If the checksums match, my data are correct”



Reality. A match proves your copy is identical to the file the checksum was made from. It says nothing about whether that file was the right sample, or good data: if a facility mislabels a file before computing its checksum, md5sum -c happily prints OK.


Protect it, first on a toy. Raw data is never edited, so make it read-only. Try it first on a practice folder with one small file:


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch03/practice/locked && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch03/practice
echo "first line" > locked/notes.txt
1chmod a-w locked/notes.txt locked
2echo "second line" >> locked/notes.txt
3rm -f locked/notes.txt
mv locked/notes.txt notes_moved.txt
touch locked/new.txt


1

chmod changes a file’s permissions; a-w removes (-) write permission (w) for all users (a). Here it locks both the file and the folder that holds it.

2

Try to add a line, then (next lines) to delete the file, move it out, and add a new file.

3

-f deletes without asking. Without it, rm may stop to ask about a read-only file; a job running unattended cannot answer.


bash: locked/notes.txt: Permission denied
rm: cannot remove 'locked/notes.txt': Permission denied
mv: cannot move 'locked/notes.txt' to 'notes_moved.txt': Permission denied
touch: cannot touch 'locked/new.txt': Permission denied
All four were refused. Why lock the folder too? Deleting, moving, and adding files change the folder’s list of names, so the folder’s permission controls them, not the file’s. A read-only file in a writable folder can still be deleted:


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p open && echo "first line" > open/notes.txt
chmod a-w open/notes.txt
rm -f open/notes.txt
ls open

rm -f printed nothing and ls shows an empty folder: the read-only file is gone. (Without -f, rm asks before deleting a read-only file when its input is a terminal, even from a script you started there. With -f, or in a job running unattended, nothing asks.)
Now protect the real raw data, files and folder:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing
chmod a-w data/raw/* data/raw
1ls -ld data/raw
ls -l data/raw


1

-d lists the folder itself instead of its contents.


dr-xr-xr-x 2 you you 4096 Nov 17 11:22 data/raw
total 4372
-r--r--r-- 1 you you     112 Nov 17 11:22 checksums.md5
-r--r--r-- 1 you you 2239317 Nov 17 11:22 SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
-r--r--r-- 1 you you 2232117 Nov 17 11:22 SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
The w letters are gone. This guards against accidents (a script that writes to the wrong path, a slip of rm), not against you: as the owner you can always give write permission back. To add a file later, unlock the folder and the checksum list (the existing reads can stay locked), add the file and its line from the source’s checksum list, check, and lock everything again:


Terminal (laptop)

chmod u+w data/raw data/raw/checksums.md5
# add the new file and its line in checksums.md5, then:
cd data/raw && md5sum -c checksums.md5 && cd ~/bioinf-computing
chmod a-w data/raw/* data/raw

Chapter 7 explains permissions properly. Keep raw reads compressed, and never unzip them in place: every tool in this book reads .gz directly.






ImportantKey idea



Raw data is read-only: check it once with checksums, protect it, and never edit it. Every change happens in a script that writes somewhere else.



Check yourself. md5sum -c prints FAILED for a file you just copied from the cluster. What happened, and what do you do? What if it says FAILED open or read?






TipAnswer





FAILED: your copy’s bytes differ from the original, usually an incomplete transfer. Copy it again and recheck; do not analyse it. FAILED open or read: the file is missing or misnamed, or you ran the check from the wrong folder.

title: 3  Organizing projects and data
text:
3.5 Shared data: link, don’t copy
On a cluster, a lab keeps one copy of each reference genome and big shared dataset in a shared folder, something like /project/<lab>/references/, and every project points to it. No one copies a 3 GB genome into each project, and no one’s quota pays twice. You will make a stand-in for such a folder in your home folder and link it into the project.
Make the shared folder. Download the test genome (yeast chromosome I only, 71 kB) and its annotation into it:


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
cd ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
curl -fLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/test-datasets/9dd6d014f560e182047992834a8d267214fbccd1/reference/genome.fa.gz
curl -fLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/test-datasets/9dd6d014f560e182047992834a8d267214fbccd1/reference/genes.gtf.gz

Give it a checksum list, as the person who set up the folder would:


~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test/checksums.md5

4222a07bf01b12782245e0ff774459fe  genome.fa.gz
504334f6741ee771c665ae845429087f  genes.gtf.gz



Terminal (laptop)

md5sum -c checksums.md5

genome.fa.gz: OK
genes.gtf.gz: OK
And a README, so anyone who finds the folder knows what it is:


~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test/README.md

# Yeast test reference (stand-in for a lab's shared references)

- genome.fa.gz: S. cerevisiae R64-1-1, chromosome I only (one sequence, >I)
- genes.gtf.gz: matching gene annotation (test subset)
- Source: nf-core/test-datasets, rnaseq branch, folder reference/,
  commit 9dd6d014f560e182047992834a8d267214fbccd1
- Downloaded: 2026-11-17 (write your date)
- Checksums: checksums.md5 (MD5)
- License: MIT (nf-core/test-datasets)

Then protect the folder, as a lab would protect its shared references:


Terminal (laptop)

chmod a-w ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test/* ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test

Link it into the project:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing
1ln -s ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test data/ref
ls -l data/ref
ls data/ref/


1

ln -s target name makes a symbolic link called name that points to target.


lrwxrwxrwx 1 you you 53 Nov 17 11:22 data/ref -> /home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
checksums.md5  genes.gtf.gz  genome.fa.gz  README.md
ls -l shows the link itself: an l at the start, and an arrow to the path it holds (on a Mac the path starts with /Users/). ls data/ref/, with the slash, looks through the link and lists the shared folder’s files.
Now name the idea (Figure 3.3). A symbolic link (symlink) is another route to the same data, not a copy: a tiny entry that holds only a path. Programs that open data/ref/genome.fa.gz read the file in the shared folder.




  A symbolic link, in four steps. The project folder ~/bioinf-computing/data holds raw, meta, and ref; ref is a link that points to the shared folder ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test, which holds README.md, checksums.md5, genes.gtf.gz, and genome.fa.gz. Listing data/ref/ shows the shared folder's files, read through the link. Writing through the link would change the shared files themselves; because the shared folder is protected, the write is refused. unlink data/ref removes only the link; the shared folder and its files are untouched.
  data/ref is a link: a small entry that holds only the path of the shared folder. ls -l shows it with an arrow.
  Reading through the link reads the shared folder itself: ls data/ref/ lists the shared files. Nothing was copied.
  Writing through the link would change the one shared copy, which every project uses. You protected it, so the write is refused.
  unlink data/ref removes only the link. The shared folder and its files are untouched.
  
    
      
    
    
      
    
  
  
  
  ~/bioinf-computing/data/
  
  raw/
  
  meta/
  
  
    
    ref →
    holds only a path
    
  
  
    
    (link removed)
  
  
  
  ~/bioinf-shared/references/
  yeast_R64-1-1_test/
  protected
  README.md
  checksums.md5
  genes.gtf.gz
  genome.fa.gz
  one copy, used by every project
  
  
    
  
  
  
    
    
    ✗ Permission denied
  
  
  
  TERMINAL, IN ~/bioinf-computing
  
    ls -l data/ref
    data/ref -> /home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
  
  
    ls data/ref/
    checksums.md5  genes.gtf.gz  genome.fa.gz  README.md
  
  
    echo "my note" >> data/ref/README.md
    bash: data/ref/README.md: Permission denied
  
  
    unlink data/ref
    no output; ls ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test still lists all four files
  




Figure 3.3: What a symbolic link is, and what each action does to it. Use Next to step through.



See both halves of that on a toy link in the practice folder (never on the real reference). Writing through a link writes to the original, and removing the link leaves the original alone:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch03/practice
mkdir -p target && echo "original line" > target/note.txt
ln -s target toylink
echo "added through the link" >> toylink/note.txt
cat target/note.txt
1unlink toylink
ls
cat target/note.txt


1

unlink removes one link (or file) and nothing else.


original line
added through the link
locked  open  target
original line
added through the link
The line written through toylink landed in target/note.txt; after unlink, the link is gone and the target still holds both lines. (Try the same write on data/ref/README.md and you get Permission denied: the protection you added to the shared folder stops it, as step 3 of Figure 3.3 shows.) A link whose target is moved or renamed is broken: ls -l still shows the arrow (in red in many terminals), and opening a file through it says No such file or directory.






WarningPitfall: rm -r data/ref/ deletes the shared data



Remove a link with unlink data/ref or rm data/ref: no slash at the end, no -r. With a trailing slash, which TabTab completion adds for you, rm -r follows the link. On a Mac with GNU coreutils 9.11 (and with macOS’s own rm), this deleted the entire shared folder without a word, and left the link behind, now broken:
$ rm -r proj/ref/
$ echo $?
0
$ ls -l proj
total 0
lrwxr-xr-x 1 you staff 20 Nov 17 11:34 ref -> /home/you/shared/ref
$ ls -A shared/ref
ls: cannot access 'shared/ref': No such file or directory
(Captured in a test folder, with $ before each command: echo $? prints 0, the code for success, and the shared folder shared/ref is gone.) On Linux (Ubuntu 24.04, GNU coreutils 9.4) the result differs but is no better: rm deleted every file inside the shared folder, then stopped with rm: cannot remove 'proj/ref/': Not a directory, leaving the folder empty.
Do not run this. The shared folder you made survives it only because you protected it: rm then stops with Permission denied. A lab’s real shared folder may not be protected from you.


Moving the project. Relative paths in scripts let the project move, but a link is only a pointer: copy the project to another machine (say, laptop to cluster) and data/ref points at a path that does not exist there. Moving a project means three steps: copy the project’s files; reinstall the environment from pixi.toml and pixi.lock (Chapter 2); and recreate data/ref to point at that machine’s copy of the same reference, which data/README.md identifies by source, release, and checksums (Section 3.8). Transfer commands come in Chapter 9. And a link is not a backup of its target: someone (you, the lab, or the site) must look after the shared copy (Section 3.6). Which genome release to use, and why chromosome names differ between sources, is Chapter 20.

Check yourself. You run unlink data/ref. Is the reference genome gone? What must you do to use the project on a second machine?






TipAnswer





No, only the link is gone; the shared folder is untouched. On the second machine, recreate the link to that machine’s copy of the same reference, identified by its source, release, and checksums in data/README.md, and reinstall the environment from the lockfile.

title: 3  Organizing projects and data
section: 3.6 Backups: where do your files really live?
text:
3.6 Backups: where do your files really live?
Start with a question for each place you keep files: if you deleted a file there by mistake today, could you get it back? Table 3.3 answers it for a laptop and the two clusters this book uses as examples. Copy its rows for your own storage into your notebook (you will start it in Section 3.9) and fill them in from your site’s documentation.




Table 3.3: Is it backed up? Site facts from SCINet’s storage guide and ISU’s HPC file storage guide, checked 2026-11-17, and Nova’s login banner (Section 2.4); your site’s own pages are the authority, and policies change (Appendix A). “Not stated”: the site’s guide does not say.

WarningPitfall: scratch is purged and not backed up



Files in scratch space (/90daydata, /ptmp) are deleted automatically; on SCINet the deletion “is permanent and the files cannot be recovered”. Use scratch for files a job can make again, copy results you need into project storage, and find out which other areas are backed up, and for how long, before you trust them.


Then name the rule: 3-2-1. Keep three copies of anything you cannot recreate, on two kinds of storage, with one somewhere else (off site). For raw sequence data, the facility’s copy or the public archive (SRA or ENA, once you have submitted) can be one of the three, but only if you know it is kept and for how long. An archive of the original reads does not preserve a subset or a fix you made yourself.
A few points the table makes:

Cluster storage is often not a backup at all. SCINet says so for all of its cluster storage, and scratch is purged everywhere. Even storage with snapshots (Nova’s /work) should not be your only copy: Nova’s login banner says so.
A sync folder copies your mistakes too. Delete or overwrite a file and the change syncs everywhere. It is one copy in two places, unless version history is kept and you know for how long.
Git keeps the history of code (Chapter 21), but only a copy stored somewhere else, such as a remote repository (Chapter 22), protects it if your machine is lost.

What to back up: raw data, metadata, code, the notebook, logs, and the records that explain results; important final results too. A result you can rebuild in seconds, such as this chapter’s read counts, needs no backup of its own. A large or published analysis may need days of computing, a reference that is no longer online, or an old software version to rebuild, so keep it. Intermediate files that a pipeline can make again can follow a lighter rule. And test a restore once: a backup you have never restored from is a hope, not a backup.






CautionMisconception: “My Dropbox (or OneDrive) folder is my backup”



Reality. Sync copies deletions and overwrites to every device. It protects you only through version history, for as long as the service keeps it, which you need to check.



Check yourself. Your raw FASTQ files are in cluster scratch and in a OneDrive folder on your laptop. Is that a backup you can rely on? What would you check?






TipAnswer





Not as it stands: scratch is purged and not backed up, and OneDrive copies deletions. Check how long OneDrive keeps old versions, whether the facility or SRA keeps the original reads (and for how long), and put a copy in storage that is backed up.

title: 3  Organizing projects and data
text:
3.7 Sample sheets and metadata
Reads mean nothing without knowing which sample each file came from. That knowledge is metadata, and it lives in tables. Start with the sample sheet nf-core uses to test its RNA-seq pipeline, kept with the book’s reads in nf-core/test-datasets. Download it into data/meta/ and keep it exactly as it came, under a name that says so:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing
curl -fL -o data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/test-datasets/9dd6d014f560e182047992834a8d267214fbccd1/samplesheet/v3.10/samplesheet_test.csv
md5sum data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv
code data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv

fb28ab0a8cda268b2befd974804b2925  data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv
The checksum matches the one in the book’s data/README.md, so you have the same file. Its contents, with the long download addresses shortened to …/ (the real file has the full URL of each FASTQ file):


data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv (shortened)

sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness
WT_REP1,…/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz,…/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz,auto
WT_REP1,…/SRR6357071_1.fastq.gz,…/SRR6357071_2.fastq.gz,auto
WT_REP2,…/SRR6357072_1.fastq.gz,…/SRR6357072_2.fastq.gz,reverse
RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP1,…/SRR6357073_1.fastq.gz,,reverse
RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2,…/SRR6357074_1.fastq.gz,,reverse
RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2,…/SRR6357075_1.fastq.gz,,reverse
RAP1_IAA_30M_REP1,…/SRR6357076_1.fastq.gz,…/SRR6357076_2.fastq.gz,reverse

Look before reading on. There are 7 rows but only 5 sample labels: WT_REP1 and RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2 each have two rows. Three rows have an empty fastq_2, so those runs are given as single-end. And a strandedness column says how each library was made. In this sheet each row is one sequencing run, with its mate files; rows that share a label are merged into one sample by the pipeline (Chapter 26).
Now check the labels against the source. The runs are public, so the archive has a record for each. The European Nucleotide Archive’s records (ENA, for the first run) (checked 2026-11-17) tell a different story: the seven runs are seven different biological samples (GSM2879618 to GSM2879624), and all seven were sequenced paired-end (Figure 3.4). The two WT_REP1 runs are wild-type replicates 1 and 2; the sheet’s WT_REP2 is replicate 3.




  nf-core's test sample sheet compared with the archive record. The sheet has 5 sample labels over 7 runs: WT_REP1 has runs SRR6357070 and SRR6357071; WT_REP2 has SRR6357072; RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP1 has SRR6357073; RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2 has SRR6357074 and SRR6357075; RAP1_IAA_30M_REP1 has SRR6357076. The sheet lists read 1 and read 2 for four runs and read 1 only for three. Only SRR6357070's two files are in this project. ENA lists each of the 7 runs as its own biological sample, GSM2879618 to GSM2879624, all paired-end: wild type replicates 1 to 3, Rap1 degron without induction replicates 1 to 3, and Rap1 degron induced for 30 minutes replicate 1.

  The labels group runs to test the pipeline; they do not describe the experiment.




Figure 3.4: The test sample sheet beside the archive record. The sheet groups 7 runs under 5 labels and gives three as single-end; ENA lists 7 biological samples, all paired-end. Only SRR6357070’s two files are in this project.



Nothing is wrong with the sheet: it is a pipeline test fixture. Its labels group runs so the test exercises merging and single-end input; they were never meant to describe the experiment. The lesson is general. A sample label is a claim: check it against the source record, and never infer the biology from names alone. (How to design an experiment with replicates is the Transcriptomics book’s subject.)
Now the project’s own metadata, for the files actually in data/raw/. Two small tables, one per question. reads.tsv says which files belong to which run and sample; samples.tsv says what each sample is, from its archive record. These commands write them, one line at a time (printf prints its text, \t is a tab, \n ends the line; > starts the file and >> adds to it, as in Chapter 1):


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing
printf 'sample\trun\tfastq_1\tfastq_2\n' > data/meta/reads.tsv
printf 'WT_REP1\tSRR6357070\tdata/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz\tdata/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz\n' >> data/meta/reads.tsv
printf 'sample\trun\tgeo_sample\tcondition\treplicate\n' > data/meta/samples.tsv
printf 'WT_REP1\tSRR6357070\tGSM2879618\twild_type\t1\n' >> data/meta/samples.tsv
cat data/meta/reads.tsv data/meta/samples.tsv

sample  run     fastq_1 fastq_2
WT_REP1 SRR6357070      data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz  data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
sample  run     geo_sample      condition       replicate
WT_REP1 SRR6357070      GSM2879618      wild_type       1
(The columns are separated by tabs, which the terminal shows as jumps to the next multiple of 8 characters, so they do not line up. Open the files in VS Code to see them as columns.) A real project has one row per run in reads.tsv and one per sample in samples.tsv; the sample column is how the two tables join (Chapter 14).
Now name the idea. Metadata is data, not a note on the side: kept beside the reads, checked, and changed only on purpose. The rules:

One row per run (or per sample), one column per property.
Plain CSV or TSV files, not spreadsheets with merged cells, colour coding, or notes in the margins (spreadsheet pitfalls: Chapter 14).
Sample IDs are spelled the same in every table: WT_REP1 in one and WT_rep1 or WT_REP1 (with a trailing space) in another are different IDs.
File-path columns point at the right files. Sample IDs and file names need not match (WT_REP1 and SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz): the table is what connects them.
Values come from the source record, with the record’s ID (GSM2879618) kept so anyone can check them.

nf-core’s own sample-sheet format, and how it merges runs, are covered in Chapter 26.

Check yourself. The upstream sheet has two rows labelled WT_REP1. Are they two runs of one biological sample? How would you find out?






TipAnswer





Not here: ENA lists them as different biological samples, wild-type replicates 1 and 2. The test sheet groups them to test merging. Check the archive record, not the label.

title: 3  Organizing projects and data
section: 3.8 Provenance: where did this number come from?
text:
3.8 Provenance: where did this number come from?
In Chapter 1 you typed a read count into fastq_summary.txt by hand. Nothing in that file says which file was counted, with what, or when. Now make a result that records how it was made.
Add the script. Open a new file in VS Code (code src/01_count_reads.sh), paste the script below, and save. You run it in this chapter; Chapter 8 explains every line.


src/01_count_reads.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# 01_count_reads.sh: check the raw FASTQ files, then count their reads.
# Run from the project folder:  pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh
set -euo pipefail

mkdir -p results logs
log="$(mktemp "logs/01_count_reads_$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M%S)_XXXX.log")"

{
  echo "started:  $(date "+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z")"
  echo "host:     $(hostname)"
  echo "script:   $(md5sum src/01_count_reads.sh)"
  echo "seqkit:   $(seqkit version)"
  echo "checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:"
  (cd data/raw && md5sum -c checksums.md5)
  echo "command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz"
  seqkit stats --quiet -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz > results/read_counts.tsv.tmp
  mv results/read_counts.tsv.tmp results/read_counts.tsv
  echo "output:   $(md5sum results/read_counts.tsv)"
  echo "finished: $(date "+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z")"
} 2>&1 | tee "$log"

Run it from the project folder, through pixi, so it finds seqkit:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing
pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh

started:  2026-11-17 12:24:53 -0600
host:     your-laptop
script:   76fa8eb6a7b90f212042cfbe6d95cfcc  src/01_count_reads.sh
seqkit:   seqkit v2.14.0
checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: OK
command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz
output:   e1d81de77934f7ab7b44bf72b7520b32  results/read_counts.tsv
finished: 2026-11-17 12:24:53 -0600
Your date, time, host, and log name will differ. Then look at what it made:


Terminal (laptop)

cat results/read_counts.tsv
ls logs

file    format  type    num_seqs        sum_len min_len avg_len max_len
data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz  FASTQ   DNA     50000   5050000 101     101.0   101
data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz  FASTQ   DNA     50000   5050000 101     101.0   101
01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122453_7WFs.log
(Tab-separated again: -T asks seqkit for a plain table that other programs can read, without the commas and aligned columns of Chapter 2. num_seqs is 50,000 in each file.) What the script did, in plain words:

Checked the inputs against checksums.md5, and would have stopped there if any failed.
Recorded the date, the machine, the script’s own checksum, the seqkit version, and the command.
Counted the reads into a temporary file, and only then moved it into results/. A run that fails half-way cannot replace a good result with an empty one.
Recorded the output’s checksum.
Saved everything it printed, including any messages from seqkit, in a new log in logs/, named by date and time plus four random characters (_7WFs; mktemp picks a name no other file has), so every run keeps its own log, even two runs in the same second.

The log is the run’s record. A log with no finished: line means the run failed, and its last lines say where (Chapter 4 starts from exactly that). When one input was corrupted on purpose, the run stopped at FAILED, kept the old result, and left the failure in its log.
Record where the inputs came from. The log says what the script read; data/README.md says where those files came from. Make it from this template (the book keeps the same record for its own data):


data/README.md

# Data in this project

## Raw reads: data/raw/

- Files: SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz, SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz (paired-end, read 1 and read 2)
- What: S. cerevisiae RNA-seq, run SRR6357070 (GEO sample GSM2879618,
  wild type, biological replicate 1), sub-sampled to 50,000 read pairs
  by nf-core for testing
- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/test-datasets/9dd6d014f560e182047992834a8d267214fbccd1/testdata/GSE110004/
- Accessions: GEO GSE110004; SRA run SRR6357070
- Downloaded: 2026-11-13 (Chapter 1; write your own date)
- Checksums: data/raw/checksums.md5 (MD5). SHA-256:
  3f50541fa9cf2bedc87e7b682ada0fccfdfcd6d27b9bb81f17be230ff140ebe7  SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
  8590e1e01e568fba256aa7dced40519604cbb111ee44ab106a3dcb869660aaf4  SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
- License: MIT (nf-core/test-datasets); original reads public in SRA
- Cite: Wu et al. (2018), Molecular Cell 72(6), 942-954.e7,
  doi:10.1016/j.molcel.2018.10.018

## Reference: data/ref (a link)

- Points to: ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test (see its README.md)
- What: S. cerevisiae R64-1-1, chromosome I only, with gene annotation (test subset)
- Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/test-datasets/9dd6d014f560e182047992834a8d267214fbccd1/reference/
- Checksums (MD5):
  4222a07bf01b12782245e0ff774459fe  genome.fa.gz
  504334f6741ee771c665ae845429087f  genes.gtf.gz
- On another machine: link data/ref to a copy with these checksums

## Metadata: data/meta/

- samplesheet_upstream.csv: nf-core's test sheet, unchanged.
  Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/test-datasets/9dd6d014f560e182047992834a8d267214fbccd1/samplesheet/v3.10/samplesheet_test.csv
  MD5 fb28ab0a8cda268b2befd974804b2925
- reads.tsv: which local files belong to which run and sample (written by hand)
- samples.tsv: what each sample is, from its ENA record (checked 2026-11-17)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/test-datasets/9dd6d014f560e182047992834a8d267214fbccd1 is the full download address, pinned to one commit of nf-core/test-datasets, so the files at that address can never change.
Now name the idea (Figure 3.5). Provenance is the record of where something came from. For read_counts.tsv, every link in the chain is now in the project.




  Where results/read_counts.tsv came from. Four records point to it: the code (src/01_count_reads.sh, its checksum, and the command it ran); the software (pixi.lock, and the seqkit version in the log); the inputs it read (the two FASTQ files in data/raw and checksums.md5), which in turn point back to data/README.md with each file's source address, commit, accession, and date; and the log of the run (what happened, when, on which machine). The reference in data/ref and the upstream sample sheet are greyed out: they are project records, not inputs to this result.

  project records, not inputs to this result




Figure 3.5: The provenance of results/read_counts.tsv. The code, the software, the inputs it read, and the log of the run point to the result; the inputs point back to their sources. The reference and the upstream sample sheet are project records, but this result did not read them.



Table 3.4 lists what to record and where it lives.



Table 3.4: What to record for each result, and where it lives in the book’s project.










What to record
In this project
Where it lives




Source of each input

NOTEBOOK.md (next section)






Most of this costs nothing if you record it when the file is made, and is impossible to rebuild later. Later chapters add to the chain: git commits for the script (Chapter 21), parameters and random seeds (Chapter 23), and pipeline versions and reports (Chapter 26).






ImportantKey idea



Record provenance when the file is made: source, version, checksum, script, command, software, log. It costs a minute now and cannot be rebuilt later.








CautionMisconception: “I’ll remember where this file came from”



Reality. Weeks later no one does, including you. A file whose source, version, and making are not written down cannot be trusted, and often cannot be used in a paper.



Check yourself. A reviewer asks which version of seqkit made read_counts.tsv. Where in the project is the answer?






TipAnswer





In the run’s log in logs/ (the seqkit: line), and in pixi.lock.

title: 3  Organizing projects and data
section: 3.9 Writing it down: README, notebook, FAIR
text:
3.9 Writing it down: README, notebook, FAIR
The README. Open README.md from Chapter 2 and replace its two lines with an outline like this one. It answers the first questions a stranger (or you, in a year) will ask:


README.md

# Computing for Bioinformatics: book project

Worked project for the book *Computing for Bioinformatics*. Counts the
reads in one yeast RNA-seq run; later chapters add to it.

## Layout

- data/raw/   reads as received, read-only; checksums in checksums.md5
- data/meta/  sample sheets and metadata
- data/ref    link to the shared reference (see data/README.md)
- src/        scripts, numbered in run order
- results/    made by the scripts; can be rebuilt
- logs/       one log per run

## Data

Where every input came from: data/README.md.

## How to rerun

    pixi install --locked
    pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh

## Software

pixi.toml and pixi.lock (installed with pixi 0.84.2).

The notebook. A script shows what was done; it does not show why, what you tried first, or what went wrong. That goes in a notebook. Make NOTEBOOK.md in the project and give it a first dated entry:


NOTEBOOK.md

# Notebook

## 2026-11-17

- Organized the project (Chapter 3): moved the reads from ~/bioinf-computing-ch01
  into data/raw/, checked them with md5sum -c (both OK), made them read-only.
- Linked the test reference from ~/bioinf-shared/ instead of copying it.
- The nf-core test sheet groups 7 runs under 5 labels, but ENA lists
  7 biological samples, all paired-end: the labels are a test grouping.
  Used the ENA record for samples.tsv.
- Ran src/01_count_reads.sh: 50,000 reads in each file.
- Next: ...

Newest entries go at the bottom (or the top: pick one and keep to it). Write a few lines each day you work: what you did, why, what went wrong, and what is next. A plain Markdown file in the project is the book’s default; if your lab already uses an electronic lab notebook, use that. The habit matters, not the tool.






TipMarkdown in one box



README.md and NOTEBOOK.md are Markdown: plain text with a few marks. # starts a heading (## a smaller one), - starts a list item, and backticks mark code (`md5sum -c`). VS Code shows a preview with Cmd-Shift-VCmd-Shift-V (Ctrl-Shift-VCtrl-Shift-V on Windows and Linux). Quarto (Chapter 12) uses the same marks; see its Markdown basics.


FAIR, briefly. Funders and journals increasingly ask for data that is FAIR: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (Wilkinson et al. 2016). Table 3.5 shows which habits from this chapter support each principle.






NoteBackground: the FAIR principles






Table 3.5: The FAIR principles (Wilkinson et al. 2016), and habits from this chapter that support them.










Principle
What it means
Habits from this chapter that support it




Findable
Data have persistent identifiers and rich metadata, so they can be found
citing accessions (SRR6357070, GSM2879618, GSE110004) in data/README.md


Accessible
Anyone can learn how to get the data, by a standard method; access may need a login
download addresses pinned to a commit; where each input came from


Interoperable
Data use standard formats and shared vocabularies
FASTQ, FASTA, and GTF files; plain CSV/TSV metadata with clear columns


Reusable
Data come with a license, provenance, and enough description to be used again
the license and citation for each input; checksums, logs, and the README








A README and a tidy CSV do not by themselves make a project FAIR; that takes depositing data, with good metadata, in an archive that gives it identifiers (Chapter 20, Chapter 22). They make it much easier. And Accessible does not have to mean open to everyone: data behind a login are fine, as long as how to get access is clear. More on FAIR at GO FAIR.

Check yourself. Which FAIR principle does citing SRR6357070 and GSE110004 in your README support?






TipAnswer





Findable, through persistent identifiers (and Reusable, since others can trace and credit the data).

title: 3  Organizing projects and data
text:
3.10 Summary

One project, one folder, with inputs (data/), code (src/), and outputs (results/, logs/) apart, so results can be rebuilt. Names without spaces, ISO dates, zero-padded numbers, scripts numbered in run order.
Raw data is checked with md5sum -c (in the folder that holds the files) after every download or transfer, then protected with chmod a-w on the files and the folder. FAILED means damaged; FAILED open or read means missing or the wrong folder.
Shared data is linked, not copied: ln -s target data/ref. Remove a link with unlink data/ref, never rm -r data/ref/. A link does not travel with the project; data/README.md says what to link on another machine.
Each result has a record of its provenance: the inputs’ sources and checksums (data/README.md, checksums.md5), the script, the software (pixi.lock), and a log of every run. README.md and NOTEBOOK.md say what the project is and why you did what you did.
Know which of your storage is backed up, for how long, and who restores it. Scratch is purged; a sync folder copies mistakes; 3-2-1 for anything you cannot recreate.

The project now looks like this:
~/bioinf-computing/
├── README.md
├── NOTEBOOK.md
├── pixi.toml  pixi.lock  .pixi/
├── data/
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── raw/        SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz  SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz  checksums.md5
│   ├── meta/       reads.tsv  samples.tsv  samplesheet_upstream.csv
│   └── ref -> ~/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
├── src/            01_count_reads.sh
├── results/        read_counts.tsv
└── logs/           01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122453_7WFs.log

title: 3  Organizing projects and data
text:
3.11 Exercises
Practice files go in ~/bioinf-computing-ch03/, not in the project.

Exercise 1. Rename a messy folder. Make a folder of badly named files:


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch03/messy && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch03/messy
touch "SRR6357070 R1.fastq.gz" "Analysis.R" "plot 1.png" "plot 2.png" "plot 10.png" "counts final.txt" "counts final_v2.txt" "11-3-25 notes.txt"

counts final.txt and counts final_v2.txt are really tab-separated tables, and _v2 added one sample. Write down a new name for each file, then rename them with mv, quoting the old names, for example:


Terminal (laptop)

mv "plot 1.png" plot_01.png

What would you ask before renaming 11-3-25 notes.txt?






TipAnswer





One good set:








Old name
New name
Why




SRR6357070 R1.fastq.gz
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
no space; keep the archive’s ID and its _1 convention


Analysis.R
01_analysis.R
lowercase; numbered in run order (better: say what it analyses)


plot 1.png, plot 2.png, plot 10.png
plot_01.png, plot_02.png, plot_10.png
zero-padded, so they sort 1, 2, 10


counts final.txt
counts_7samples.tsv
true extension; says what it holds


counts final_v2.txt
counts_8samples.tsv
says what changed, instead of v2


11-3-25 notes.txt
ask first




Now ls -1 lists the plots in order. For the date, ask whoever wrote it: is it 3 November or 11 March, and which year? Then rename to 2025-11-03_notes.txt or 2025-03-11_notes.txt (or the right year).





Exercise 2. Catch a broken transfer. Make a truncated copy of read 1 in the practice folder, as an interrupted transfer would, copy the checksum list beside it, and check:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch03/practice
head -c 1000000 ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz > SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
cp ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/checksums.md5 .
md5sum -c checksums.md5
gzip -t SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz

(head -c 1000000 keeps the first million bytes. Read 2 is missing on purpose.) Which kind of failure does each file give? Both checks catch this copy; which one would catch a file that is complete, but the wrong sample?






TipAnswer





SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: FAILED
md5sum: SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: FAILED open or read
md5sum: WARNING: 1 listed file could not be read
md5sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match
gzip: SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: unexpected end of file
gzip: SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: uncompress failed
Read 1 is FAILED (bytes differ); read 2 is FAILED open or read (missing). gzip -t catches truncation too. Only the checksum, compared against the facility’s list, catches a wrong file that is still valid gzip. Neither tells you whether the facility’s own file was right (the misconception in Section 3.4).





Exercise 3. Labels against records. Here are the ENA records for all seven runs in the upstream sheet (captured 2026-11-17 from ENA’s file report for each run):









Run

PAIRED

PAIRED

Copy the upstream sheet into the practice folder (cp ~/bioinf-computing/data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv ~/bioinf-computing-ch03/), open the copy in VS Code, and add geo_sample and condition columns from this table. How many biological samples are there? How many runs are really paired-end? Why might a test fixture group them differently? And what goes wrong if a sample ID in one table has a trailing space?






TipAnswer





Seven biological samples, all paired-end. The fixture’s labels exist to test the pipeline: two labels with two runs each test merging, and three runs given as read 1 only test single-end input. A trailing space makes a different ID (WT_REP1 is not WT_REP1), so the two tables fail to match when joined; Chapter 14 shows how to detect it.





Exercise 4. Rebuild and compare. Save a copy of the result outside results/, delete results/, rerun the script, and compare:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing
cp results/read_counts.tsv ~/bioinf-computing-ch03/read_counts_before.tsv
rm -r results
pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh
1cmp ~/bioinf-computing-ch03/read_counts_before.tsv results/read_counts.tsv
ls logs


1

cmp compares two files byte by byte and prints nothing if they are identical.


Then add a NOTEBOOK.md entry for today.






TipAnswer





cmp prints nothing: the rebuilt result is identical. logs/ now has two logs, one per run, with different names, which is why outputs and logs are kept apart. The result could be deleted safely because the inputs, code, and software records were all kept.





Exercise 5. Your own storage. (Cluster readers.) Make the same layout in your project storage, link a reference your site or lab already provides (Appendix A) or the test reference, and fill in the rows of Table 3.3 for your site from its documentation, including who restores a deleted file. No cluster yet? Fill in the rows for your laptop and any sync folder you use.






TipAnswer





Answers depend on the site. A complete row names the path, whether it is backed up or snapshotted and for how long, whether it is purged and after how long, and whom to ask (with the link to the page you used). If the documentation does not say, write “not stated” and ask your site’s support rather than assume.

title: 4  Getting help
text:
4.1 What this chapter does
Core. Work through it, with the exercises.
Things break, for everyone, every day: a typo in a file name, a flag that does not exist, a script run from the wrong folder, a download cut short. Experienced people do not avoid errors; they get from a message to a fix quickly, and they know when and how to ask. Most fixes take the steps in this chapter, not expertise.
You will use the book’s own files and environment throughout, so every error in the chapter is one you can reproduce yourself, or read in the captured output. You will finish able to:
Asking for help is part of the job, not a sign that you are not good enough: some problems (a broken node, a full quota) only an administrator can fix, and a clear request is a skill in its own right.
Commands run on your laptop, from the book’s project folder, ~/bioinf-computing (Chapter 3). Practice files go in a scratch folder, ~/bioinf-computing-ch04, like Chapter 1’s ~/bioinf-computing-ch01, so the project stays clean. Make it now:
Cluster readers can run the same commands on a login node: they are small and quick.

title: 4  Getting help
4  Getting help
section: 4.2 Asking the tool itself: --help, man, docs
text:
4.2 Asking the tool itself: --help, man, docs
Every tool you use can tell you how to use it. Start with seqkit, from the book environment:


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit --help

SeqKit -- a cross-platform and ultrafast toolkit for FASTA/Q file manipulation

Version: 2.14.0

Author: Wei Shen <shenwei356@gmail.com>

Documents  : http://bioinf.shenwei.me/seqkit
Source code: https://github.com/shenwei356/seqkit
Please cite: https://doi.org/10.1002/imt2.191
...
Usage:
  seqkit [command]

Commands for Basic Operation:
  faidx           create the FASTA index file and extract subsequences
  ...
  stats           simple statistics of FASTA/Q files
  ...
(... marks lines left out here; the real output is longer.) The top already answers three questions you will have often: which version you have (2.14.0), where the documentation is, and what to cite. SeqKit’s authors ask you to cite the SeqKit2 paper (Shen et al. 2024). Below that comes the list of subcommands: seqkit is one program with many tools inside, and stats, which you ran in Chapter 2, is one of them. Each subcommand has its own help:

Shen, Wei, Botond Sipos, and Liuyang Zhao. 2024. “SeqKit2: A Swiss Army Knife for Sequence and Alignment Processing.” iMeta 3 (3). https://doi.org/10.1002/imt2.191.


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit stats --help

Scroll to the Flags: part. Find the flag that prints a table for other programs to read, and the one that sets how many CPUs seqkit uses:
  -T, --tabular              output in machine-friendly tabular format
  ...
  -j, --threads int                     number of CPUs. can also set with environment variable
                                        SEQKIT_THREADS) (default 4)
Now a tool that came with the system. On Linux and WSL, gzip is GNU gzip; on a Mac it is the GNU gzip you installed in Chapter 1:


Terminal (laptop)

gzip --help

Usage: gzip [OPTION]... [FILE]...
Compress or uncompress FILEs (by default, compress FILES in-place).

Mandatory arguments to long options are mandatory for short options too.

  -c, --stdout      write on standard output, keep original files unchanged
  -d, --decompress  decompress
  ...
  -t, --test        test compressed file integrity
  ...
With no FILE, or when FILE is -, read standard input.
Most command-line programs also have a manual page, a longer description that opens in a pager:


Terminal (laptop)

man gzip

Move with SpaceSpace and the arrow keys, search with / followed by a word and EnterEnter, and quit with q (these are the keys of less, Chapter 5). Now try seqkit:


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run man seqkit

No manual entry for seqkit
Many bioinformatics tools have no manual page, only --help and a website. That is normal.

4.2.1 Reading a usage line
Help text uses a compact notation, shown in Figure 4.1.




  How to read help text. Top: GNU gzip's usage line, Usage: gzip [OPTION]... [FILE]... Square brackets mark something optional, three dots mean it may repeat, and words in capitals stand for a value you supply; none of the brackets or dots are typed. Bottom: two flag lines from seqkit stats --help. The first, -T, --tabular, output in machine-friendly tabular format, shows a short form, a long form of the same flag, and its description. The second, -j, --threads int, number of CPUs, shows a flag that takes a value, typed as -j 4 or --threads 4.
  
  
  from gzip --help (GNU)
  
    Usage:
    gzip
    [OPTION]...
    [FILE]...
  
  
  
    
    
    
    
    
  
  
    the program
    optional
    may repeat
    optional
    may repeat
  
  
    Capitals (OPTION, FILE):
    something you supply.
    Never type the brackets
    or the dots.
  
  
  
  from pixi run seqkit stats --help (seqkit 2.14.0)
  
    -T,
    --tabular
    output in machine-friendly tabular format
    -j,
    --threads
    int
    number of CPUs …
  
  
    
    
    
    
  
  
    short
    long form, same flag
    what it does
    takes a value
  
  typed as -j 4 or --threads 4




Figure 4.1: How to read help text. In a usage line, square brackets mark something optional, ... means it may repeat, and capitals stand for something you supply; you never type the brackets or dots. Flag lines give a short and a long form of the same flag, a description, and, for flags that take a value, the type of value.



The conventions, from Usage: gzip [OPTION]... [FILE]...:

Square brackets mark something optional. [FILE] means you may give a file; with none, gzip reads its input from elsewhere (Chapter 6).
... means “may repeat”: any number of options, any number of files.
Capitals, or words in angle brackets such as <file>, commonly stand for a value you supply.
You never type the brackets or the dots. gzip -t reads.fastq.gz, not gzip [-t] [reads.fastq.gz]....

These are common conventions, not rules every tool follows, but most do. Flags come in a short form (-T, one dash, one letter) and a long form (--tabular, two dashes, a word); both mean the same, and the long one is easier to read later. Some flags take a value: -j 4 and --threads 4 both ask for four CPUs. Tools with subcommands, such as seqkit stats, samtools sort, or git commit, have help at each level. Not every tool answers --help: some use -h, some help, and some print their usage when run with no arguments at all.
Table 4.1 lists where to look.




Table 4.1: Where to find out how a tool works. Only the ones that come from the program you run are sure to match your installed version.





Source
What it gives
Matches your installed version?
Example




--help or -h
Usage line, flags, short descriptions
yes: the program prints it
pixi run seqkit --help


Subcommand help
The flags of one subcommand
yes
pixi run seqkit stats --help


man page
A longer manual, in a pager
usually; on a Mac, check (below)
man gzip


Official documentation site
Tutorials, examples, every option
the latest release, which may not be yours
bioinf.shenwei.me/seqkit


--version
The version you have
yes
gzip --version, pixi run seqkit version


R’s ?
The help page of an R function
yes
?read.csv (Chapter 12)


Python’s help()
The help of a Python function or module
yes
help(open) (Chapter 13)







Why the version matters. A website describes the latest release; your environment has the version in pixi.lock (pixi list shows it, Chapter 2). If a flag from the website is not in your --help, the website is probably ahead of your copy.






Tip--help always matches what you run



--help is printed by the program you actually run, so it matches your version. Online docs may describe a newer one, and on a Mac, man may show the page of a different program with the same name.


That last point is a macOS detail. After Chapter 1’s setup, ls and sed run the GNU tools, and the MANPATH lines you added there make man ls open the GNU page too. If a man page ever describes options your command rejects, trust --help.

Check yourself. In Usage: gzip [OPTION]... [FILE]..., must you give a file?






TipAnswer





No. [FILE] is in square brackets, so it is optional; with no file, gzip reads standard input, as the last line of its help says (Chapter 6).

title: 4  Getting help
text:
4.3 Reading an error message
A diagnosis round first. Below are six commands that fail, each run on the book’s files with its real output (captured with seqkit 2.14.0, R 4.4.3, and pixi 0.84.2). For each one, say what went wrong before you open the answer. Two need a file you make first, a copy of the first read file cut short:


Terminal (laptop)

(head -c 1000000 keeps the first million bytes, under half the file. It writes to the scratch folder, never into data/raw/.)
1.


Terminal (laptop)

seqkit stats data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz

bash: seqkit: command not found
2.


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit stats data/raw/SRR6357070_l.fastq.gz

[ERRO] stat data/raw/SRR6357070_l.fastq.gz: no such file or directory
3.


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit stats –T data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz

[ERRO] stat –T: no such file or directory
4.


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit stats --paired data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz

Error: unknown flag: --paired
Usage:
  seqkit stats [flags]
...
unknown flag: --paired
5.


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/broken.fastq.gz

[ERRO] /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch04/broken.fastq.gz: unexpected EOF
[ERRO]
file    format  type    num_seqs    sum_len min_len avg_len max_len
6.


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run Rscript -e 'read.csv("data/meta/samples.csv")'

Error in file(file, "rt") : cannot open the connection
Calls: read.csv -> read.table -> file
In addition: Warning message:
In file(file, "rt") :
  cannot open file 'data/meta/samples.csv': No such file or directory
Execution halted






TipAnswers






command not found, printed by the shell (bash:): no program called seqkit is on this shell’s PATH, so it never started. The fix is pixi run (Chapter 2). If another copy of seqkit were installed somewhere else, the bare command would have run that copy instead, possibly a different version (Chapter 7).
A typo. The file name has a lowercase letter l where the digit 1 belongs: _l.fastq.gz. ls data/raw/ shows the real names.
An en dash. –T starts with an en dash (–), not a hyphen (-). This happens when a command is copied from a PDF or a word processor. seqkit does not recognise it as a flag, so it treats –T as a file name and cannot find it. Retype the dash.
A flag that does not exist. seqkit stats has no --paired; it prints its usage to show what it does accept. (Section 4.8 comes back to where this flag came from.)
A file cut short. The [ERRO] line says unexpected EOF (end of file): the gzip data stops in the middle. seqkit still printed the table’s header line, with no rows.
The wrong file name. The error says only cannot open the connection; the warning below it says which file and why: there is no data/meta/samples.csv. The file in Chapter 3 is samples.tsv.





4.3.1 Who, what, and on what
You may have noticed a pattern. Figure 4.2 shows it on two of the messages.




  Reading two real error messages for who printed them, what failed, and on what. Top, from seqkit: [ERRO] stat data/raw/SRR6357070_l.fastq.gz: no such file or directory. Who: seqkit, the program you ran; [ERRO] is a severity label, not a name. What: stat, looking up the file, found no such file. On what: the file name, which has the letter l where the digit 1 belongs. Bottom, from R: Error in file(file, "rt") : cannot open the connection, followed by the call chain read.csv to read.table to file, and a warning: cannot open file 'data/meta/samples.csv': No such file or directory. Who: R's file() function, called by read.csv. What: cannot open the connection. On what: the file name, given only in the warning below the error, which holds the reason.
  
  
  you ran pixi run seqkit stats data/raw/SRR6357070_l.fastq.gz

    where the digit _1 belongs

  Not every message has all three; when one is missing, the log and the checklist carry the diagnosis.




Figure 4.2: A reading strategy for error messages: find who printed it, what failed, and on what (the file, flag, or object, often quoted). In seqkit’s message, [ERRO] is a severity label; you know seqkit printed it because you ran seqkit. In R’s, the function is named, and the file is only in the warning that follows the error.




Who printed it. A message starting bash: comes from the shell: it could not even start the program. Otherwise it usually comes from the program you ran, which you know from your command. [ERRO], Error, and WARNING are severity labels, not names. R’s Error in file(...) names the function that failed.
What failed: stat (looking a file up), cannot open, unknown flag, unexpected EOF.
On what: the file, flag, or object, often in quotes. Read it character by character; that is where _l and –T were hiding.

Not every message has all three. A program that runs out of memory may print only Killed; a crash may print almost nothing. Then the log and the checklist (Section 4.4) carry the diagnosis.
Read all of it. Long messages are common, and the last line is not always the one that matters. Look for the earliest relevant failure in this run: later lines are often consequences of the first one. But the useful detail can sit further down, as in R’s message, where the reason is in the warning after the error. And a log you append to may still hold errors from earlier runs; check the times.






ImportantKey idea



Look for who printed the message, what failed, and on what. Read all of it, and find the earliest relevant failure in this run. An exit status of 0 means “reported success”, not “right answer”.




4.3.2 Errors and warnings
An error reports that something failed. Whether the program or your script then stops depends on the program and the script (Chapter 8). A warning asks you to look: sometimes the result is still what you wanted, sometimes not. In R:


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run Rscript -e 'as.integer(c("12","7","n/a"))'

[1] 12  7 NA
Warning message:
NAs introduced by coercion
R turned "n/a" into NA (missing) and carried on. That is right if n/a really means “missing” in that column, and wrong if it was a typo for a number. Only you know which.


4.3.3 Exit status
Every command, when it finishes, reports a number to the shell: its exit status. 0 means the program reports success; anything else means it reports a failure. echo $? prints the status of the command just before it, so run it immediately after: any other command in between replaces the number.


Terminal (laptop)

seqkit version
echo $?

bash: seqkit: command not found
127
127 is the shell’s code for “command not found”. Now the truncated file from round 5:


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/broken.fastq.gz
echo $?

[ERRO] /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch04/broken.fastq.gz: unexpected EOF
[ERRO]
file    format  type    num_seqs    sum_len min_len avg_len max_len
0
seqkit 2.14.0 printed an error and reported success. (SeqKit’s current documentation says read errors give a nonzero status, so a later version may behave differently.) That is the lesson, whatever the version: the exit status says what the program reported. It does not prove the output answers your question. Read the messages, and check the result against something you know: here, a table with no rows instead of 50,000 reads. Given an intact file and this broken one in the same command, seqkit 2.14.0 printed only the header line: the intact file’s row was lost too, and the status was still 0. How scripts and pipelines use exit status is Chapter 8.






CautionMisconception: “If no error appears, the result is right”



Reality. Warnings let runs continue, and some tool versions report success after printing an error (seqkit 2.14.0 on a truncated file). Check outputs against something you know: a read count, a file size, a number from the paper.


Table 4.2 collects the messages you are most likely to meet in the first part of this book.




Table 4.2: Common messages in Part I, and what to check first.

Other languages have their own common messages (R’s could not find function, Python’s ModuleNotFoundError); they come with Chapter 12 and Chapter 13.

Check yourself. A message starts bash: samtools: command not found. Did samtools run?






TipAnswer





No. The message comes from the shell (bash:), which could not find a program called samtools, so it never started. Check whether you need pixi run (or, on a cluster, module load).

title: 4  Getting help
section: 4.4 Before you ask: a troubleshooting checklist
text:
4.4 Before you ask: a troubleshooting checklist
Two cases first.
Case 1: the wrong folder. Go to your home folder and run Chapter 3’s script, the way you ran it there:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~
pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh

Error:   × could not find pixi.toml or pyproject.toml with tool.pixi at directory /home/you
pixi looks for pixi.toml in the folder you are in (and the folders above it) and finds none. (If some folder above yours held a pixi.toml, the message would differ: pixi would use that one, and the error would come later.) The fix is the folder, not the command:


Terminal (laptop)

pwd
cd ~/bioinf-computing

Case 2: a pattern that matches nothing.


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fq.gz

[ERRO] stat data/raw/*.fq.gz: no such file or directory
The clue is the * inside the message. bash replaces a pattern such as *.fq.gz with the matching file names, but when nothing matches it passes the pattern on unchanged, and seqkit looks for a file literally called *.fq.gz. ls data/raw/ shows the files end in .fastq.gz, not .fq.gz. Why bash does this is Chapter 5.
Both cases are solved by a question you can ask of almost any problem. Figure 4.3 puts those questions in order.




  A troubleshooting checklist in seven steps, each with an exit when the problem is solved. 1, read the message, all of it. 2, find the log. 3, where am I, with what: pwd, hostname, ls, pixi run or not. 4, do the inputs exist and look right: ls -l, head, gzip -t, md5sum -c. 5, are resources short: disk space, quota, time limit, Killed. 6, what changed since it last worked. 7, make it small: 100 reads, one sample. The wrong-folder case stops at step 3 and the unmatched *.fq.gz case at step 4. If the problem is still not solved after step 7, leave the checklist and ask for help.
  Step 1. Read the whole message: who printed it, what failed, and on what. Often that is enough, and you stop.
  Step 2. Not solved? Find the log. The terminal may show only the last lines; a log can hold the first error.
  Step 3. Check where you are and with which software. The wrong-folder case stops here: pwd shows you are not in the project.
  Step 4. Check that the inputs exist and look right. The *.fq.gz case stops here: ls shows the files end in .fastq.gz.
  Step 5. Check resources: disk space, quota, time, memory.
  Step 6. Ask what changed since it last worked: data, versions, folders, machines.
  Step 7. Make it small. Still stuck after that? Leave the checklist and ask, with what you checked.

Figure 4.3: A troubleshooting checklist. Each step has an exit: stop as soon as the problem is solved. The wrong-folder case stops at step 3, the *.fq.gz case at step 4. Still stuck after step 7? Leave the checklist and ask.




Read the message, all of it (Section 4.3).
Find the log. The terminal may show only the last lines; a log can hold the first error. More below.
Where am I, with what? pwd, hostname, ls; did you use pixi run? On a cluster, which modules are loaded?
Do the inputs exist and look right? ls -l, head, gzip -t, md5sum -c (Chapter 3); do the names in your sample sheet match the file names?
Are resources short? No space left on device, Disk quota exceeded, a time limit, Killed (Table 1.4).
What changed since it last worked? New data, a new version, a new folder, a new machine?
Make it small. Does it still fail on 100 reads, on one sample? (Section 4.7 shows how.)

Not every step is needed every time; stop when it is solved. If it is still not solved after step 7, the way out is to ask (Section 4.6, Section 4.7), with what you checked.






ImportantKey idea



Most problems are found by the same few questions: where am I, with which software, on which inputs, with enough resources, and what changed. Stop when it is solved.


Finding the log. Chapter 3’s script writes a log in logs/ every time it runs, one file per run, with everything it printed. Here is the log of a run that failed because a raw file had been moved out of data/raw/ (captured; the host name is replaced):


logs/01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122821_jlSC.log

started:  2026-11-17 12:28:21 -0600
host:     <laptop>
script:   76fa8eb6a7b90f212042cfbe6d95cfcc  src/01_count_reads.sh
seqkit:   seqkit v2.14.0
checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
md5sum: SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: FAILED open or read
md5sum: WARNING: 1 listed file could not be read

No finished: line, so the run stopped early. The earliest relevant failure is the line naming SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: who (md5sum), what (could not open it), on what (the R2 file). The run never reached seqkit stats, so results/ still holds the previous run’s counts: another reason to check the log, not only whether a results file exists. The log keeps all this after the terminal is closed, with the date, the machine, and the versions.
Not every program writes a log, and a log does not always name the cause. Later chapters add more places to look: a cluster job’s output file, slurm-<jobid>.out (Chapter 10), and a pipeline’s .nextflow.log and each task’s .command.err (Chapter 26). On a cluster, steps 3 and 5 matter more: which node you are on, which modules are loaded, and which quota is full.
When to ask. If you have made no progress for about an hour, that is a good point to stop and ask; your lab’s habits come first, and it is not a limit you must reach. Ask at once for anything about accounts, passwords, or keys; when a fix could damage data or affect other users; and when something that worked stops working in a way your own changes do not explain (a slow or missing filesystem, a module that will not load, a quota). You do not need to know whether the system is at fault: report what you saw and what you checked.






WarningPitfall: changing many things at once



Change one thing, rerun, and look. Three changes at once leave you not knowing which one fixed the problem, or which one broke something else.


Table 4.3 is the same checklist as a table, with the chapter that goes deeper on each step.

2

Check yourself. A script worked yesterday and fails today with No such file or directory. Name two checklist questions to ask first.






TipAnswer





Where am I (pwd)? Do the inputs exist (ls -l)? And what changed: a moved folder, a renamed file?

title: 4  Getting help
text:
4.5 Reading a methods section
When you want to repeat or build on an analysis, the paper’s methods section is where you find out which tools, versions, and parameters were used. The book’s running dataset comes from Wu et al. (2018), which is openly licensed (CC BY), so it can be quoted here. Open it in PubMed Central and find two places: the Software and Algorithms rows of the Key Resources Table, and the paragraph Differential Expression Analysis in the methods.
Four words you will meet there, one line each (the Transcriptomics book explains them):

Adapter trimming: cutting the sequencing adapters off the ends of reads.
Alignment: finding where in the genome each read comes from.
Counting: how many reads fall in each gene.
Differential expression: which genes change between conditions.

Your turn. Fill in Table 4.4 for the RNA-seq analysis from those two places, before you open the answer. The last two columns matter: what the paper prints, and what you would type.

Trim adapters

1.9.1
–minimum-length=25–quality-cutoff=20 -a AGATCGGAAGAGC -A AGATCGGAAGAGC
--minimum-length=25 --quality-cutoff=20 -a AGATCGGAAGAGC -A AGATCGGAAGAGC
—
