Three things to notice.
The dashes and the spaces. The paper prints –minimum-length and –forward-prob with a single en dash: typesetting turned the two hyphens of -- into one –. Copied as printed, they fail exactly like round 3 of Section 4.3. Look again at the spacing, too: –minimum-length=25–quality-cutoff=20 and –star-output-genome-bam–forward-prob have no space between the two options, so a program would read each pair as one long, unknown word. Both faults need repairing before the command can run.






WarningPitfall: commands copied from PDFs and web pages



Typesetting turns -- into – and straight quotes (", ') into curly ones (“, ’). The command looks right and fails, or worse, does something else. Retype dashes and quotes when you copy from a paper.


The strandedness setting. --forward-prob 0 says how the library was made: which strand of the gene each read comes from (Chapter 26 and the Transcriptomics book explain strandedness). The nf-core test sheet the book uses (Chapter 3) says auto for our sample, WT_REP1. auto asks the pipeline to work out the strandedness from the reads; it does not state it, so it is not a second source for the paper’s value.
What this excerpt does not report. The STAR and RSEM index settings, DESeq2’s design and thresholds, and any code. Before saying the paper omits them, check its supplements and any deposited code. A complete methods section names the tool, the version, the parameters, the reference release, and where the code and data are: the same chain you recorded for your own project in Chapter 3.
Two cautions. First, the book later runs these reads through nf-core/rnaseq (Chapter 26). That is a different, newer analysis, not a reconstruction of the paper’s. Second, a methods section can describe several kinds of library: this paper also has single-end TSS-seq reads of 76 bases. Which paragraph describes our reads? Exercise 4 checks it against the run’s public record.

Check yourself. The excerpt says “STAR (version 2.5.2a)” but not the index options. Can you reproduce the alignment exactly from the excerpt?






TipAnswer





Not for certain: index settings can change the results. Check the supplements and any deposited code; then either assume the defaults (and say so) or ask the authors.

title: 4  Getting help
section: 4.6 Searching, and choosing where to ask
text:
4.6 Searching, and choosing where to ask
Most errors have been seen before. Searching well means turning your message into one that matches other people’s. Take this one, from a truncated file on a cluster:
[ERRO] /home/<user>/proj/sample_17_R1.fq.gz: unexpected EOF
Remove what is yours (the path, the sample name), keep the distinctive part in quotes, and add the tool’s name:
seqkit "unexpected EOF"
Search the tool’s own GitHub issues too, for example seqkit’s, including closed ones: a closed issue often holds the answer. Reading issues is all you need here; filing one is 1.






TipSearch tip



Search the distinctive part of the message in quotes, without your paths and sample names, plus the tool’s name.


Where to ask depends on the kind of problem (Table 4.5). If your lab has local experts and asks them first, do that.




Table 4.5: Where to ask, by kind of problem.





Kind of problem

An nf-core pipeline

the tool’s authors

Judging an answer. How old is it, and which version does it assume? Is it from the tool’s authors or documentation? Does it explain why? And does it work on your small example? A 2015 answer may name flags that no longer exist.

Check yourself. Your job on the cluster cannot write to /project, and the quota command shows you at your limit. Where do you ask?






TipAnswer





Your cluster’s help desk, or your PI if the project’s quota is theirs to raise. Not Biostars: nobody there can change your quota.

title: 4  Getting help
text:
4.7 Asking for help
Here is a request that is hard to answer:

seqkit doesn’t work on the cluster, help!!
[a screenshot of the last few lines of a terminal]

A helper cannot tell which command, which files, which version, or even which error: the screenshot cuts off the first line. They have to ask four questions before they can start. Figure 4.4 shows the same problem written so that someone can answer at once.




  A help request built from the book's Something doesn't run form plus four added fields, with why each field matters. Title: seqkit stats, unknown flag --paired when counting read pairs. Where it ran: laptop, macOS 15, no cluster. What I wanted and expected: count read pairs in the two mate files, one number for the sample. Exact command, copied. Complete message as text: Error: unknown flag: --paired. What I tried: seqkit stats --help shows no --paired flag. Versions: seqkit v2.14.0 from pixi run seqkit version, and pixi info with the home folder replaced by the placeholder <home>. Small example: the error appears with no input file at all, pixi run seqkit stats --paired, rerun to check. Before posting: replace home paths and user names with placeholders, never include passwords, keys, or tokens, and keep the fault itself visible.
  
  seqkit stats: unknown flag: --paired
  why it is there
  Where it ran
  laptop · macOS 15 (Intel) · no cluster
  laptop, login node, and compute
  node can behave differently
  
  What I wanted, and expected
  count read pairs in the two mate files;
  expected one number for the sample
  helpers can spot a wrong
  approach, not just a wrong flag
  
  Exact command (copied)
  pixi run seqkit stats --paired \
    data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz \
    data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
  copied, not retyped: the fault
  may be a single character
  
  Complete message (as text)
  Error: unknown flag: --paired
  Usage: … (full output attached)
  text can be searched, quoted,
  and read by screen readers
  
  What I tried
  seqkit stats --help: no --paired flag
  saves helpers repeating it
  
  Versions
  seqkit v2.14.0  (pixi run seqkit version)
  pixi info: Platform osx-64,
    Manifest file: <home>/bioinf-computing/pixi.toml
  the tool's own version, and
  where and how it was installed
  
  Small example
  fails with no input file at all:
  pixi run seqkit stats --paired (rerun: same error)
  someone else can reproduce it
  in seconds
  
  
  Before posting: home paths and user names become placeholders (<home>); no passwords,
  keys, or tokens. Keep the fault visible: the l in _l.fastq.gz, an en dash, the wrong flag.




Figure 4.4: A help request someone can answer. It starts from the book’s Something doesn’t run form (where it ran, the exact command, the complete message as text, pixi info) and adds what a question about a tool needs: what you wanted and expected, what you tried, the tool’s version, and a small example. Private details become placeholders that keep the fault visible.



The book’s own Something doesn’t run form is a good starting model: where it ran (laptop, login node, or compute node; operating system; cluster), the exact command, copied, the complete message as text, and pixi info. A question about a tool also needs:

what you were trying to do, and what you expected;
what you tried already;
the failing tool’s version;
a small example that still fails.

Versions, each for its own question.

pixi info describes where and how: the platform, pixi’s version, the environment, and its folders. It does not list package versions.
pixi run seqkit version gives the version of the tool that failed. With pixi run, it reports the copy that actually ran.
pixi list shows every package’s version, when several might matter.
In R, pixi run Rscript -e 'sessionInfo()' (Chapter 12).

Do not paste the whole pixi.lock; it is thousands of lines.

4.7.1 A minimal reproducible example
A minimal reproducible example is the smallest input and the shortest command that still show the problem. Shrink until it still fails, and rerun after every cut, to check that it still fails the same way. Fewer files, one sample, the first 100 reads:


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit head -n 100 data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz \
  -o ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/small_R1.fastq.gz

That writes the first 100 reads (10,100 bases) to the scratch folder, never to data/raw/. Now the catch. Do the same with the truncated file, and check the small copy:


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit head -n 100 ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/broken.fastq.gz \
  -o ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/small_broken.fastq.gz
pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/small_broken.fastq.gz

file    format  type    num_seqs    sum_len min_len avg_len max_len
/home/you/bioinf-computing-ch04/small_broken.fastq.gz   FASTQ   DNA 100 10100   101 101.0   101
No error. The first 100 reads of the broken file are intact; the damage is at its end. Shrinking removed the bug: this example is too small. That is why you rerun after every cut. Some failures need no real data at all (a wrong file name fails on any file), and often the shrinking finds the bug for you. In R, the reprex package builds such examples (reprex.tidyverse.org, Chapter 12).


4.7.2 Text, not screenshots
Paste commands and messages as text. Text can be searched, copied, quoted, and read by screen readers; a screenshot can do none of these, and it usually cuts off the first error. Put it in a Markdown code block, between lines of three backticks (Markdown, Chapter 3):
```
Error: unknown flag: --paired
```
A screenshot can add to the text when the problem is something on screen, such as a VS Code panel or a dialog. For a long log, post the relevant part with a few lines around it, and keep the full log to share if the venue asks for it.


4.7.3 Privacy and etiquette
Before you post, replace user names, paths, and host names you would rather not share with placeholders, and do it consistently (always <home>, always <user>). Keep the fault visible while you do: the relative layout, the extension, upper and lower case, the l vs 1, the en dash. pixi info, for example, prints paths in your home folder.






WarningPitfall: secrets in public



Never post passwords, SSH private keys, tokens, unpublished data, or data under a use agreement (ask your PI if unsure). Forums and issue trackers are public, and what you post is copied and indexed: deleting it later does not take it back.


Two habits of good askers: if you post the same question in two places, say so in each; and when it is solved, post the answer and mark it solved, for the next person who searches.

Check yourself. Why paste the error as text rather than a screenshot?






TipAnswer





Text can be searched, copied into a search engine, quoted in a reply, and read by screen readers. Screenshots often cut off the first error, and they hide the command.




Table 4.6 sums up what goes into a request.




Table 4.6: What a help request includes, and what it never includes.











Include
Example

Never include

title: 4  Getting help
text:
4.8 AI coding assistants
AI coding assistants can explain an error, suggest a command, or draft a help request. They can also be confidently wrong. Here is an answer to “count read pairs in my paired FASTQ files with seqkit”. It was written for this book to show a typical mistake, not captured from a particular assistant:

Use seqkit’s stats command with the --paired flag:
seqkit stats --paired data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz

Check it, in three steps:

Is the flag real? pixi run seqkit stats --help lists no --paired.
Run it. You did, in round 4 of Section 4.3: Error: unknown flag: --paired.
Fix it, then check what the answer means. Without the invented flag, the command runs:


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit stats data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz

It prints one row per file, each with 50,000 reads. The two files are the two mates of the same fragments (Chapter 1), so the run has 50,000 read pairs, not 100,000. A command that runs is not yet an answer to the question.

Rules for using an assistant:

Treat its suggestions as coming from a fast, confident colleague who is sometimes wrong.
Check every flag against --help for your version.
Test on small data with a known answer before real data.
Understand any command before you run it, above all ones that delete or overwrite (rm, >, mv). Never run those unread on raw data or on shared systems.
Paste error text and small toy examples. Never paste credentials, private or unpublished data, or anything your institution’s or your data agreement’s current policy restricts.
Follow your journal’s and your university’s rules on disclosing AI use.

Used this way, assistants are good at the two skills this chapter teaches: explaining an error message, and drafting a help request. As long as you check the result.






WarningPitfall: trusting an AI-suggested flag



Check every flag against --help, and test on data with a known answer, before you run an AI-suggested command on real data.








CautionMisconception: “Code from an AI assistant works; I can assume it has been tested”



Reality. It is generated text. Flags can be invented or belong to another version, and even code described as tested may have been tested on other inputs or another system. Check flags in --help and reproduce a known result.


Table 4.7 lists the checks.



Table 4.7: Checks for an AI-suggested command.










Check
How
What it catches




The flag exists
--help for your version
invented flags, flags from other tools


The version matches
pixi run <tool> version, pixi list
flags from a newer or older release


It works on toy data
100 reads with a known answer
wrong output that looks plausible


The output means what you asked
compare with what you know (reads vs pairs)
an answer to a different question


Nothing is destroyed
read every rm, >, mv before running
lost or overwritten data


Nothing private is sent
paste only the question and toy examples
leaked data and credentials







Check yourself. An assistant suggests pixi run seqkit stats --count-pairs data/raw/*.fastq.gz. What do you check before trusting it?






TipAnswer





That --count-pairs appears in pixi run seqkit stats --help for your version. It does not in seqkit 2.14.0: running it gives Error: unknown flag: --count-pairs.

title: 4  Getting help
text:
4.9 Summary

--help comes from the program you run, so it matches your version; man pages and websites may not. In a usage line, brackets mean optional, ... means repeatable, and you type neither.
Read the whole message for who printed it, what failed, and on what, and find the earliest relevant failure. An exit status of 0 means the program reported success, not that the result is right.
Before asking, work through the checklist: message, log, where and with what, inputs, resources, what changed, a small example. Stop as soon as it is solved.
A methods section should give tool, version, parameters, and reference; retype its dashes, and say “not reported in this excerpt” until you have checked the supplements.
A good help request has the exact command, the complete message as text, versions, and a small example that still fails, with nothing private in it. Check every AI-suggested flag in --help and test on data with a known answer.

title: 4  Getting help
text:
4.10 Exercises

Exercise 1. Fix a broken script. Make the script below in the scratch folder (in VS Code: code ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/count.sh, paste, save). Copy it from this page exactly, faults and all:


~/bioinf-computing-ch04/count.sh

# count.sh: count reads in both raw files (has three faults)
# Run from ~/bioinf-computing:  pixi run bash ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/count.sh
seqkit stats –T --paired data/raw/SRR6357070_l.fastq.gz data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz

From ~/bioinf-computing, run it with pixi run bash ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/count.sh. It fails three times. Fix one fault at a time, using only the message and --help, and rerun after each fix. Note in NOTEBOOK.md (Chapter 3) what each message said and what you changed.






TipAnswer





seqkit checks its flags before it looks at files, so the faults appear in this order (exit status in brackets):

Error: unknown flag: --paired, followed by the usage [255]. Delete --paired.
[ERRO] stat –T: no such file or directory [255]. The en dash made –T a file name; retype it as -T.
[ERRO] stat data/raw/SRR6357070_l.fastq.gz: no such file or directory [255]. Change the letter l to the digit 1.

The fixed line is seqkit stats -T data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz, and it prints [0]:
file    format  type    num_seqs    sum_len min_len avg_len max_len
data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz  FASTQ   DNA 50000   5050000 101 101.0   101
data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz  FASTQ   DNA 50000   5050000 101 101.0   101
With several files, seqkit may also show a processed files: 2 / 2 progress line; it is not an error.





Exercise 2. Read the help. From pixi run seqkit stats --help, find the flag that adds quartiles and N50. Run pixi run seqkit stats with that flag and -T on both raw files. Which columns appear that were not there before? Do the two files differ in any of them?






TipAnswer





-a, --all. The command is pixi run seqkit stats -a -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz. The new columns are Q1, Q2, Q3 (quartiles of read length), sum_gap, N50, N50_num, Q20(%), Q30(%), AvgQual, GC(%), and sum_n. With every read 101 bases long, the length columns are all 101. The quality columns differ: R1 has Q30(%) 92 and AvgQual 26.89, R2 90 and 23.28; R2 also has far more N bases (sum_n 18,842 vs 280). Read 2 being a little worse is common in Illumina data (Chapter 15).





Exercise 3. Write a help request. Pretend that exercise 1’s first error is one you cannot solve. Write the request in ~/bioinf-computing-ch04/help_request.md, following Figure 4.4: the Something doesn’t run fields (where it ran, the exact command, the complete message as text, pixi info with your home path replaced by <home>), plus what you expected, what you tried, the output of pixi run seqkit version, and a small example. For the example, make a 100-read file with the seqkit head command from Section 4.7, and check that the same error still appears with it. Then shrink once more: does the error need an input file at all? Do not submit the request. Then test it: could someone reproduce the failure from the request alone, without access to your home folder?






TipAnswer





The 100-read file gives the same unknown flag error, so the example works. But one more cut shows it is not needed: the error appears with no input file at all, because seqkit rejects the flag before it looks for files:


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit stats --paired
echo $?

Error: unknown flag: --paired
Usage:
  seqkit stats [flags]
...
unknown flag: --paired
255
So the smallest example is the command alone. A model request:
**seqkit stats: `unknown flag: --paired` when counting read pairs**

Where it ran: laptop, macOS 15 (Intel); no cluster.

Trying to: count read pairs in two mate files; expected one number.

Command (copied, run from the book's project folder):
```
pixi run seqkit stats --paired
```
No input file is needed: the same error appears with or without one.

Message (abbreviated here; the full output, with the usage and
flag list, is attached as error.txt):
```
Error: unknown flag: --paired
Usage:
  seqkit stats [flags]
...
unknown flag: --paired
```
Exit status: 255.

Tried: `pixi run seqkit stats --help` lists no `--paired`.

Versions: seqkit v2.14.0 (`pixi run seqkit version`), installed from
the book environment (pixi.toml and pixi.lock from Chapter 2 of
Computing for Bioinformatics). `pixi info`: Platform osx-64.
The test: yes, someone could reproduce it, because it needs only seqkit 2.14.0 and one command, with no data, and the request says where the environment comes from. Two things made the first draft fail the test: a message cut with ... but called complete, and a file name (small_R1.fastq.gz) that a helper does not have. The fact most often left out is the tool’s version (pixi info does not show it); a helper’s first reply would be to ask for it.





Exercise 4. Match the paper to the data. Open the ENA record for the book’s run, SRR6357070. Find the library layout, the instrument, and the read count, and say what unit the read count is in. Which methods paragraph of Wu et al. (2018) describes this run: the RNA-seq one, or the TSS-seq one?

Wu, Andrew C. K., Harshil Patel, Minghao Chia, et al. 2018. “Repression of Divergent Noncoding Transcription by a Sequence-Specific Transcription Factor.” Molecular Cell 72 (6): 942–954.e7. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molcel.2018.10.018.






TipAnswer





Recorded 2026-11-17, in case the page changes: sample GSM2879618, “Wild-type total RNA-Seq biological replicate 1”; layout PAIRED; Illumina HiSeq 2500; read_count 47,629,288; base_count 9,621,116,176. For a paired run, ENA’s read count is in read pairs: 9,621,116,176 bases ÷ 47,629,288 = 202 bases per pair, which is 101 + 101.
It is the RNA-seq paragraph: about 45 million 101-base, strand-specific, paired-end reads on a HiSeq 2500 or 4000. The TSS-seq reads were 76 bases, single-end, on a HiSeq 4000. Our files are a 50,000-pair subset made by nf-core, so ENA’s checksums are for the full files, not ours (Chapter 20).





Exercise 5. Check an AI answer. Take the assistant’s answer from Section 4.8, or, if you already use an AI assistant, ask it for a seqkit command that counts read pairs in data/raw/. Check every flag in --help, run the command, and say whether the output answers the question: pairs, not reads. Record in NOTEBOOK.md what you checked. If you use an assistant, paste only the question, no files.






TipAnswer





The book’s answer fails at the first check (--paired is not in --help) and at the second (unknown flag). Without the flag, seqkit prints one row per mate file, 50,000 reads each, so the run has 50,000 pairs. An answer that adds the two num_seqs and reports 100,000 pairs has run correctly and still answered the wrong question. Another assistant may suggest something else; the checks are the same.

title: 4  Getting help
text:
4.11 Further reading

Dall’Olio et al. (2011) — written by people from Biostars and other bioinformatics forums: how to ask so that strangers want to answer.
Haller (2022) — what makes a bug report fixable, from a tool developer’s side; useful now, and again when you file issues in



Auslander (2026) — rules for using AI assistants in computational biology, among them owning every line of generated code and using chatbots to recall syntax, not scientific reasoning.
Stack Overflow (2026), How to create a Minimal, Reproducible Example — one short page on shrinking a problem until someone else can run it.




Dall’Olio, Giovanni M., Jacopo Marino, Michael Schubert, et al. 2011. “Ten Simple Rules for Getting Help from Online Scientific Communities.” PLoS Computational Biology 7 (9): e1002202. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1002202.

Haller, Benjamin C. 2022. “Ten Simple Rules for Reporting a Bug.” PLOS Computational Biology 18 (10): e1010540. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1010540.

title: 5  Shell basics
text:
5.1 Why the command line
Core. Work through it, with the exercises.
This chapter opens Part II, six chapters on the Linux command line. That is a large share of a bioinformatics book to spend on typing commands, so first, the reason.
Real work runs on Linux machines that you reach through a terminal. A university cluster such as Nova or SCINet’s Ceres runs Linux. You log in with ssh, and what you get is a prompt, not a desktop. Companies, and labs without a cluster, rent Linux servers in the cloud (Chapter 38) and reach them the same way. Your laptop is for editing, small tests, and writing up. The data and the long jobs live on those machines (Section 1.7). Section 1.6 explained why they run Linux; this part teaches you to work on them.
The command line also suits the work itself, not only the machines it runs on (Table 5.1).
Why bash. The shell is the program that reads what you type (Section 5.3). There are several shells. Bash is the default on nearly every Linux system and cluster, cluster job scripts are usually bash scripts, and tools’ install instructions assume it. So the book uses bash everywhere, including on a Mac, where you made it your shell in Chapter 1. Learn it once, and the same commands work on your laptop, the cluster, and a cloud server.
Part II builds up to running a real job on a cluster, one chapter at a time (Table 5.2).

title: 5  Shell basics
text:
Table 5.1: Why bioinformatics is done at the command line.









Reason

title: 5  Shell basics
text:
5.2 What this chapter does
You have already run about thirty shell commands in Part I, mostly by copying them: mkdir -p … && cd …, ls -lh, cat, head, mv, cp, ln -s, chmod, touch. Each time the book said “explained in Part II”. This is that explanation. Once you know what each part of a command does, you can change it, predict what it will do, and spot the one character that is wrong.
The chapter covers what the shell does with a line before any program runs; how to move around the filesystem; how to copy, move, link, and delete without losing files; wildcards and quoting; find; looking inside files of any size; and recalling earlier commands instead of retyping them. Pipes and redirection (|, >) are Chapter 6; permissions, PATH, and your shell’s settings are Chapter 7; variables and scripts are Chapter 8. A few supplied commands here contain a |; copy those as they are.
Commands run on your laptop. In the book’s project, ~/bioinf-computing, you only look at files in this chapter; the one thing you write there is your own notes in NOTEBOOK.md, as in Chapter 3 and Chapter 4. Everything that creates, moves, or deletes happens in a scratch folder, ~/bioinf-computing-ch05, so a mistake cannot touch the project.
Build the practice folder. Paste the block below into your terminal in one go. It makes ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/, a stand-in for the kind of folder a former lab member leaves behind: reads in three run folders, one with spaces in its name; plots and a counts file; two sample tables; a stray temporary file; and a link that points nowhere. Chapter 6, Chapter 7, and Chapter 8 reuse this folder, so keep it.


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch05
mkdir ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share && {
mkdir run1 run2 "Run 3 final" analysis meta
printf '@A.%s\nACGTACGTAC\n+\nIIIIIIIIII\n' 1 2 | gzip > run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
printf '@A.%s\nGTACGTACGT\n+\nIIIIIIIIII\n' 1 2 | gzip > run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
printf '@B.%s\nACGTACGTAC\n+\nIIIIIIIIII\n' 1 2 3 | gzip > run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
printf '@B.%s\nGTACGTACGT\n+\nIIIIIIIIII\n' 1 2 3 | gzip > run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
cp run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp
printf '@C.%s\nACGTACGTAC\n+\nIIIIIIIIII\n' 1 2 3 4 | gzip > "Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz"
printf '@C.%s\nGTACGTACGT\n+\nIIIIIIIIII\n' 1 2 3 4 | gzip > "Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz"
touch "analysis/plot 1.png" "analysis/plot 2.png"
seq 1 1000 > "analysis/counts FINAL.txt"
rows=(sample run_folder condition reads
  sample_C "Run 3 final" treated 12
  sample_A run1 control 9
  sample_B run2 control 30
  sample_E run5 treated 105
  sample_B run2 control 30
  sample_D run4 control 8)
printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "${rows[@]}" > meta/samples.tsv
printf '%s,%s,%s,%s\r\n' "${rows[@]}" > meta/samples_from_excel.csv
printf 'Reads from runs 1-3. Ask Sam about run 3.\n' > notes.txt
printf 'colour=on\n' > .old_settings
touch -d 2025-03-01 notes.txt .old_settings
ln -s /no/such/genome ref
printf 'pwd\nls data/raw\n' > ../where.sh
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05 && ls -A share
}

 .old_settings   analysis   meta   notes.txt   ref  'Run 3 final'   run1   run2
It is safe to paste without understanding it yet. This chapter explains mkdir, cd, cp, touch, and ln -s; printf, gzip, and the | come in Chapter 6, and the rows=(…) list in Chapter 8. The read files are real, tiny gzipped FASTQ files (2, 3, and 4 reads for samples A, B, and C), so the tools you use on them behave as on real data. On a Mac, touch -d needs the GNU tools from Chapter 1’s setup.
Pasting the block a second time is safe: mkdir stops with File exists and nothing else runs, so it cannot undo changes you made. To rebuild the folder on purpose, rename the old one first and paste again: mv ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share_old. The book never deletes a scratch folder for you.

title: 5  Shell basics
text:
5.3 What a shell is
Type these, one at a time:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~
ls
lss
type cd
type mkdir

bioinf-computing       bioinf-computing-ch03  bioinf-computing-ch05
bioinf-computing-ch01  bioinf-computing-ch04  bioinf-shared
bash: lss: command not found
cd is a shell builtin
mkdir is /usr/bin/mkdir
Your home folder will hold other things too. lss gives the message from Table 4.2: no program has that name. (Ubuntu may add a suggestion: Command 'lss' not found, did you mean ….) type asks bash what a name is: cd is part of bash itself, while mkdir is a program stored in a file. On a Mac after Chapter 1’s setup, type mkdir shows the GNU copy, /usr/local/opt/coreutils/libexec/gnubin/mkdir or a path under /opt/homebrew. (Try type ls too: on many systems it says ls is aliased to …. Aliases are Chapter 7.)
Now name the parts. The terminal is the window. The shell is the program inside it that reads what you type and starts other programs; this book’s shell is bash. A command is either a program (ls, mkdir, seqkit) or a builtin, part of bash itself (cd, pwd, echo, type, history). cd has to be a builtin: a separate program runs as its own process, and changing its folder would leave your shell where it was.
Every line follows the shape you met in Chapter 4’s usage lines: the command first, then its options (-l, --help), then its arguments, usually names of files or folders. Whatever the command, bash first does the same work on the line (Figure 5.1):

It reads the line into words, at spaces, but respecting quotes and backslashes: "Run 3 final" stays one word.
It expands ~, wildcards such as *, and $… where quoting allows.
It removes the quote characters themselves.
It finds the command and starts it with the resulting arguments.





  What bash does with the line ls -l "Run 3 final" run1/*.fastq.gz, typed in ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share, where run1/ holds sample_A_R1.fastq.gz and sample_A_R2.fastq.gz. Step 1: bash reads the line into four words at the spaces, ls, -l, "Run 3 final", and run1/*.fastq.gz; the quoted part stays one word. Step 2: the unquoted pattern run1/*.fastq.gz is replaced by the two matching file names, each one word; the quoted word is left alone. Step 3: the quote characters are removed, so "Run 3 final" becomes Run 3 final, still one word with its spaces. Step 4: bash starts the program ls with four arguments: -l, Run 3 final, run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz, and run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz. ls never sees the quotes or the star.
  Read: bash reads the line into words at the spaces, but the quoted part stays one word, so there are four words.
  Expand: the unquoted pattern run1/*.fastq.gz is replaced by the file names that match it, each one word; the quoted word is left alone.
  Unquote: bash removes the quote characters, so "Run 3 final" becomes Run 3 final, still one word with its spaces.
  Run: bash finds the program ls and starts it with four arguments; ls never sees the quotes or the *.
  
  
  TERMINAL, IN ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
  ls -l "Run 3 final" run1/*.fastq.gz
  
  
  run1/
  holds
  
  sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
  
  sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
  
  
    1 · Read into words: 4 words
    2 · Expand the pattern: 5 words
    3 · Remove the quotes: still 5 words
    4 · Run: start ls with 4 arguments
  
  
  
    
    ls
    
    -l
    
    "Run 3 final"
    Run 3 final
    
      
      run1/*.fastq.gz
    
    
      
      run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
      
      run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
    
  
  
  
    
      
      
    
    
      quoted: one word,
      spaces and all
      unquoted pattern
    
  
  
  
    
      
      
    
    
      quoted: left alone
      run1/*.fastq.gz replaced by the 2 matching names,
      one word each
    
  
  
  
    
    
      quote marks removed,
      still one word

      program
      its 4 arguments
    
  
  
  
  
    Spaces separate words; the quotes keep "Run 3 final" together.
    Only the unquoted pattern is expanded: 4 words became 5.
    The quotes were instructions for bash, not part of the name.
    ls never sees the quotes or the *.
  




Figure 5.1: What bash does with a line before ls starts. The quoted name stays one word, the unquoted pattern is replaced by the matching names, the quotes are removed, and ls receives four arguments. Use Next to step through.



Quoting decides what happens in steps 1 and 2. A file name produced by a wildcard is one argument even if it contains spaces, as Section 5.8 shows. (Bash calls something else “word splitting”: splitting the result of a $… expansion, which is Chapter 8. Step 1 is just reading the line.) This is the frame for the whole chapter: quoting and wildcards are steps 1–3, and how bash finds a program in step 4 (PATH) is Chapter 7. The Bash manual gives the full order of expansions, for later.






ImportantKey idea



Before any program starts, bash reads your line into words (respecting quotes), expands ~, wildcards, and $… where quoting allows, and removes the quotes. The program gets only the resulting arguments. Most surprises in this chapter come from that step.


Bash, not zsh. A new Mac’s default shell is zsh, which is similar but not the same. Chapter 1 made bash your shell on every system, because clusters use it. Check:


Terminal (laptop)

echo "$BASH_VERSION"

5.3.15(1)-release
Any version from 4 up is fine; Ubuntu 24.04 has 5.2 and 26.04 has 5.3 (what WSL installed in November 2026), and a cluster may have an older one (Nova had 5.1 in November 2026). If nothing prints, you are not in bash: go back to Chapter 1.
The prompt. A prompt such as you@laptop:~/bioinf-computing$ tells you who you are (you), which machine you are on (laptop), and which folder you are in (~/bioinf-computing), then $: ready. Clusters set theirs up for you; the host name tells you whether you are on a login node (Chapter 10). Yours may look different; Chapter 7 shows how to change it.

Check yourself. Why can’t cd be a separate program, like mkdir?






TipAnswer





A program runs as its own process. If it changed folder, only its own folder would change, and your shell would stay where it was. type cd says cd is a shell builtin.

Figure 5.2 shows the same moves on the folder tree.




  Moving around with cd, in six steps, in a tree where your home folder you (written ~, /home/you) holds bioinf-computing and bioinf-computing-ch05, bioinf-computing holds data, src, and logs, and data holds raw and meta. A terminal strip shows each command and the path pwd prints.
  A new terminal opens in your home folder, ~. cd ~/bioinf-computing moves into the project, and pwd prints where you are as an absolute path.

Figure 5.2: The cd sequence above, one step per command. The outlined folder is the current working directory; the terminal strip shows what pwd prints there.



Now name the parts (Figure 5.3). Every file on the machine sits in one tree that starts at /, the root. Your home folder is one branch of it, /home/you, and ~ is short for it. A path names a place in the tree:

An absolute path starts at the root, with /: /home/you/bioinf-computing/data/meta. It means the same thing from anywhere. A path starting with ~ is absolute too, since bash turns ~ into /home/you (step 2 above).
A relative path starts from where you are, the current working directory that pwd prints. From data/raw, ../meta means “up one folder, then into meta”.
. is the current folder and .. the one above it.





  The file system as one tree that starts at the root, /. Under / are home and usr; on a cluster there are also project and scratch (Chapter 10). usr holds bin, where programs such as ls and mkdir live. home holds you, your home folder, written ~ (on macOS /Users/you). Your home holds the project folder bioinf-computing and the practice folder bioinf-computing-ch05. The project holds data, src, results, and logs; data holds raw, meta, and ref, which is a link to the shared reference. Two routes reach meta. The absolute path /home/you/bioinf-computing/data/meta starts at the root and walks down. The relative path ../meta starts where you are, in raw: up one to data, then down to meta.

Names are case-sensitive, as Chapter 3 said: Data and data are different folders on Linux and on clusters.
Relative to what? A relative path always means “from where I am now”, even inside a script. The setup block made a two-line script, ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/where.sh, that prints the current folder and lists data/raw:


Terminal (laptop)

cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/where.sh
cd ~/bioinf-computing

cd ~
bash ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/where.sh

pwd

/home/you/bioinf-computing
checksums.md5  SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz  SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
/home/you
ls: cannot access 'data/raw': No such file or directory
The same script, run by the same absolute path, gives two results, because data/raw is looked up from the folder you ran it in. From ~ it looked for ~/data/raw, which does not exist. Chapter 4’s wrong-folder case was related but failed earlier: pixi run itself looks for pixi.toml in the current folder and the folders above it, and found none.






CautionMisconception: “A relative path is relative to the script that contains it”



Reality. It is relative to the current working directory of the shell that runs the command, wherever the script is stored. Run project scripts from the project folder, as the book does, or cd there first.


Errors you will meet:


Terminal (laptop)

cd nowhere
cd ~/bioinf-computing/README.md

bash: cd: nowhere: No such file or directory
bash: cd: /home/you/bioinf-computing/README.md: Not a directory
Note that the second message shows ~ already expanded: cd never saw the ~.






TipPress Tab



Type cd ~/bioi and press TabTab. Bash completes as far as the name is certain, here ~/bioinf-, because several folders start that way (bioinf-computing…, bioinf-shared). Press TabTab twice to list the choices, type a few more letters, and press it again. Tab saves typing and catches typos: more in Section 5.8.


On a cluster. The same commands work on a login node. Log in as in Chapter 1 and run:


Terminal (login node)

pwd
echo "$HOME"
type ls

On Nova and on SCINet’s Ceres (both captured November 2026; <user> is your user name):
/home/<user>
/home/<user>
ls is aliased to `ls --color=auto'
pwd prints your cluster home: a different machine with a different home folder, which holds none of your laptop’s files (ls there shows only what you have put on the cluster). type ls shows the alias from Section 5.3, which makes ls colour its output. ~ always means the home of the machine you are on. Project and scratch areas are Chapter 10 and Appendix A; moving files between machines is Chapter 9.

Check yourself. You are in ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw. Give a relative and an absolute path to samples.tsv in data/meta.






TipAnswer





Relative: ../meta/samples.tsv. Absolute: ~/bioinf-computing/data/meta/samples.tsv, or /home/you/bioinf-computing/data/meta/samples.tsv written out.

Your dates, sizes of logs, and log names will differ, and you may have more logs. What each option did:

-a (all) shows names starting with a dot. .pixi is the hidden folder where Chapter 2’s environment lives: do not edit it by hand; pixi install rebuilds it. . and .. are the current and the parent folder. A leading dot hides a name by convention; it does not protect it. (-A shows hidden names without . and ...)
-F adds / after folders (and @ after links, * after programs).
-l (long) gives one line per file, and -h prints sizes in human units (2.2M instead of 2239317). Options combine: -lh is -l -h, as in Chapter 4.
-d lists a folder itself instead of its contents (Chapter 3 used it to check data/raw was locked).
-t sorts by time, newest first: the quickest way to find the latest log.

With names as arguments, ls lists only those. Most systems colour names by type in the terminal (folders blue, links cyan); the book shows output without colour. When a name contains a space, GNU ls puts it in quotes, as in 'Run 3 final' in the setup block’s output: the quotes show where the name starts and ends and are not part of it.

title: 5  Shell basics
text:
5.6 Creating, copying, moving, and deleting
Work in a new practice folder inside the scratch folder:


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/practice
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/practice
mkdir notes
mkdir p/q
1mkdir -p p/q
2touch notes/todo.txt
cp notes/todo.txt notes/todo_copy.txt
cp notes backup
3cp -r notes backup
4mv backup/todo_copy.txt backup/done.txt
mv backup old_notes
ls


1

-p makes every missing folder on the way, and is quiet if the folder exists.

2

touch makes an empty file (or updates the time of an existing one).

3

-r (recursive) copies a folder and everything inside it.

4

mv renames a file here, and renames a folder on the next line: one command, two jobs, moving and renaming.


mkdir: cannot create directory ‘p/q’: No such file or directory
cp: -r not specified; omitting directory 'notes'
notes  old_notes  p
mkdir p/q failed because p did not exist; -p makes both. cp without -r refuses a folder. mv old new moves a file or folder to a new name, or into a folder if new is an existing folder: mv backup/done.txt notes/ would move the file into notes.
Now the ways to delete:


Terminal (laptop)

rmdir p
rm p
1rm -r p
ls


1

rm -r removes a folder and everything in it.


rmdir: failed to remove 'p': Directory not empty
rm: cannot remove 'p': Is a directory
notes  old_notes
rmdir removes only empty folders, which makes it the safe choice when you think a folder is empty. rm removes files, and with -r, folders and everything in them.

5.6.1 Three surprises
cp and mv overwrite without asking. Make two small files and copy one over the other (> writes a command’s output into a file, as in Chapter 1; Chapter 6 explains it):


Terminal (laptop)

echo "version 1" > old.txt
echo "version 2" > new.txt
cp new.txt old.txt
cat old.txt
echo "version 3" > newer.txt
mv newer.txt old.txt
cat old.txt
ls

version 2
version 3
new.txt  notes  old_notes  old.txt
No question, no warning: version 1 is gone, then version 2. -i (interactive) asks first, and -n (no-clobber) never overwrites:


Terminal (laptop)

echo "version 4" > new.txt
cp -n new.txt old.txt
cat old.txt
cp -i new.txt old.txt

version 3
cp: overwrite 'old.txt'? n
cp -n skipped the copy without a message; cp -i asked, and n kept the old file. (On Ubuntu 24.04 and later, cp -n also prints cp: warning: behavior of -n is non-portable and may change in future; use --update=none instead. The copy is still skipped, so ignore it: --update=none does not exist on older systems such as many clusters.)
rm has no trash folder and no undo. A file removed with rm is gone at once; nothing on the command line puts it back. rm -i asks before each file. rm -r on the wrong folder is the classic disaster.
A trailing slash matters for links. Chapter 3 showed that rm -r data/ref/ follows the link and deletes the shared files. Remove a link with unlink name or rm name: no slash, no -r.






WarningPitfall: no undo



rm deletes for good, and cp and mv overwrite silently. Before you delete, list exactly the names the command will get, with ls -d -- <the same names>. Keep raw data read-only and backed up (Chapter 3): those are the only undo.




5.6.2 The safe habit: preview, then delete
Go to the practice tree and list what a wildcard would hand to rm (wildcards are explained in Section 5.8; run* means “names starting with run”):


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
ls run*
ls -d -- run*

run1:
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz  sample_A_R2.fastq.gz

run2:
sample_B_R1.fastq.gz  sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp  sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
run1  run2
Plain ls run* showed what is inside the two folders. But rm -r run* would get the folders themselves, run1 and run2, and ls -d -- run* lists exactly those. So the habit is:

Run ls -d -- with the names or pattern you mean to delete.
If the list is right, press UpUp, change ls -d to rm -i (Section 5.11 shows the editing keys), and run it.

-- means “no more options after this”. Quotes keep a name with spaces as one argument, but they do not stop a name that starts with - from being read as an option. Try it on a throw-away file named -n:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/practice
touch -- -n
rm -n
rm -i -- -n

rm: invalid option -- 'n'
Try 'rm ./-n' to remove the file '-n'.
Try 'rm --help' for more information.
rm: remove regular empty file '-n'? y
rm itself suggests the other way out: ./-n starts with ., so it cannot be an option. That was your first real deletion, of a file you made a minute ago, with -i asking first.






CautionMisconception: “Deleted files go to a trash folder I can restore from”



Reality. rm removes the name at once. There is no trash on the command line; only backups, or snapshots that some sites keep of some storage (Appendix A), can bring a file back. Ask before you count on snapshots.


More habits, one line each:

Never run rm -rf on a path built from a variable or a wildcard you have not previewed (variables are Chapter 8).
Keep raw data read-only: in Chapter 3, chmod a-w turned a slip into Permission denied.
The book does not suggest making rm always ask (an alias for rm -i): the habit stops protecting you the day you work on a machine without it.

title: 5  Shell basics
text:
5.7 Symbolic links, revisited
Chapter 3 made data/ref, a link to the shared reference folder. Here are four ways to ask where a link points:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing
ls -l data/ref
readlink data/ref
readlink -f data/ref
realpath data/raw/../ref

lrwxrwxrwx 1 you you 53 Nov 17 11:22 data/ref -> /home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
/home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
/home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
/home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
readlink prints the path the link stores; readlink -f and realpath print where it finally leads, after following every link and every ... Here they agree because the link stores an absolute path. (For reference: you will rarely need readlink -f and realpath, but they are the tools for “where does this really go?”)
A broken link. The practice folder’s ref points to a path that does not exist:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
ls -l ref
cat ref
find . -xtype l

lrwxrwxrwx 1 you you 15 Nov 17 11:40 ref -> /no/such/genome
cat: ref: No such file or directory
./ref
ls -l still shows the link and its arrow (often in red), but anything that opens it fails with No such file or directory, although ref is right there in the listing. find . -xtype l lists broken links; it comes back in Section 5.9.
Relative targets. A link can store an absolute path or a relative one, and a relative one is read from the link’s own folder, not from the folder where you ran ln -s. This is the most common way to make a broken link (Figure 5.5). Try it from share, making links in a new folder tidy next to it:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
mkdir -p ../tidy
ln -s run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz ../tidy/wrong.fastq.gz
ln -s ../share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz ../tidy/right.fastq.gz
file -h ../tidy/wrong.fastq.gz ../tidy/right.fastq.gz

../tidy/wrong.fastq.gz: broken symbolic link to run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
../tidy/right.fastq.gz: symbolic link to ../share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
wrong.fastq.gz stores run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz, which is read from tidy/, where there is no run1. right.fastq.gz stores a path that goes up from tidy/ and into share/. (file names the kind of thing a path is, more in Section 5.10; -h makes it describe the link itself instead of following it, which Linux does by default but a Mac does not.) Remove both with unlink, which removes only the links:


Terminal (laptop)

unlink ../tidy/wrong.fastq.gz
unlink ../tidy/right.fastq.gz





  A relative link target is read from the link's own folder, not from where you ran ln -s. The folder ~/bioinf-computing-ch05 holds share, with run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz inside, and tidy. You are in share. Panel A, broken: ln -s run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz ../tidy/wrong.fastq.gz. The link tidy/wrong.fastq.gz stores the text run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz; read from tidy, that means tidy/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz, which does not exist, and file reports a broken symbolic link. Panel B, works: ln -s ../share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz ../tidy/right.fastq.gz. Read from tidy, ../ goes up to ch05, then down into share/run1 to the real file. Below: an absolute target, starting with /, works from any folder but breaks if the target moves.

  but breaks if the target file moves.
  ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz ../tidy/abs.fastq.gz




Figure 5.5: A relative link target is read from the folder the link is in. Both commands were run in share/, but both links live in tidy/, so run1/… leads nowhere, while ../share/run1/… reaches the file.









WarningPitfall: a relative target is read from the link’s folder



ln -s run1/x.fastq.gz ../tidy/x.fastq.gz stores run1/x.fastq.gz, which is looked up from tidy/, not from where you ran the command. Use an absolute target, or write the path as seen from the link’s folder.


When to use which (Table 5.6): absolute targets for shared lab data and references, as in Chapter 3; relative targets inside one project that you might move or copy as a whole. In ln -s target name, the target comes first, as the source does in cp source destination. Hard links (ln without -s) also exist; this book does not use them.

Check yourself. In ~/proj/data/ you run ln -s raw/x.fq.gz ~/proj/results/x.fq.gz. Does the link work?






TipAnswer





No. The link is in ~/proj/results/, so its target raw/x.fq.gz is looked up there, and there is no results/raw/. Use ../data/raw/x.fq.gz or an absolute path.

title: 5  Shell basics
text:
5.8 Wildcards, quoting, and tab completion
A prediction round first. Go to run1 in the practice folder. ls shows two files, sample_A_R1.fastq.gz and sample_A_R2.fastq.gz. For each line, write down what echo will print (it prints its arguments), then run it:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1
echo *
echo *.fastq.gz
echo *_R1*
echo sample_?_R1.fastq.gz
echo *.fq.gz

Then one level up, in share:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ..
echo *
echo .*







TipOutput





sample_A_R1.fastq.gz sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
*.fq.gz
analysis meta notes.txt ref Run 3 final run1 run2
.old_settings
* matches any characters, including none; ? matches exactly one. *.fq.gz matched nothing, so it came out unchanged. * skipped .old_settings, and .* found only it. (Bash before 5.2, such as Nova’s 5.1, also lists . and .. for .*.)



Now name it. echo did not do any matching. Bash replaces an unquoted pattern with the matching names before the command starts (called globbing, or filename expansion). The program receives a list of names and never sees the *. When nothing matches, bash’s default is to pass the pattern on unchanged (changing that default is Chapter 8). That explains Chapter 4’s case 2, [ERRO] stat data/raw/*.fq.gz: no such file or directory: seqkit was handed the literal data/raw/*.fq.gz and looked for a file with that name. ls does the same:


Terminal (laptop)

ls *.fq.gz

ls: cannot access '*.fq.gz': No such file or directory
Figure 5.6 shows all three cases.




  How bash expands a file-name pattern, in ~/bioinf-computing, where data/raw/ holds checksums.md5, SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz, and SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz. Step 1: the line pixi run seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz contains an unquoted pattern, so before seqkit starts, bash looks for matching file names. Step 2: the two .fastq.gz files match and checksums.md5 does not; seqkit receives stats, -T, data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz, and data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz, and never sees the star. Step 3: with data/raw/*.fq.gz nothing matches, so bash passes the pattern on unchanged; seqkit receives the literal data/raw/*.fq.gz and prints the error [ERRO] stat data/raw/*.fq.gz: no such file or directory. Step 4: in find data/raw -name "*.fastq.gz" the quotes stop bash, so find receives the literal *.fastq.gz, does its own matching, and prints the two .fastq.gz paths.
  Pattern: before seqkit starts, bash looks for file names that match the unquoted pattern data/raw/*.fastq.gz.
  Match: two names match, so seqkit gets two file names and never sees the *.
  No match: nothing ends in .fq.gz, so bash passes the pattern on unchanged and seqkit looks for a file literally named *.fq.gz.
  Quoted: the quotes stop bash, so find receives *.fastq.gz itself and does its own matching as it searches data/raw.
  
  
  TERMINAL, IN ~/bioinf-computing
  
    pixi run seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz
    pixi run seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fq.gz
    find data/raw -name "*.fastq.gz"
  
  
  
  data/raw/
  
    
    
    
  
  
  
    
    
  
  
    
    
  
  
    checksums.md5
    SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
    SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
  
  
    
      ✗
      ✓
      ✓
    
    
      ✗
      ✗
      ✗
    
    
      ✗
      ✓
      ✓
    
  
  
    which names match?
    2 of 3 names match (✓)
    no name ends in .fq.gz
    find matches the same 2 (✓)
  
  
  
  
    
      
    
  
  
  
    Before seqkit starts, bash reads:
    
    data/raw/*.fastq.gz
    
    
      An unquoted pattern, so bash looks in
      data/raw/ for names that end in
      .fastq.gz (* matches any characters).
    
  
  
  
    seqkit receives:
    
      
      
    
    
      stats
      -T
    
  
  
    
      
      
    
    
      data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
      data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
    
    
      2 file names,
      no *
    
  
  
    
    data/raw/*.fq.gz
    
      the pattern itself
      Nothing matched, so bash passed the
      pattern on exactly as typed.
    
  
  
  
    find receives:
    
      
      
      
    
    
      data/raw
      -name
      *.fastq.gz
    
    
      The quotes stopped bash and were removed,
      so the * reaches find, which compares
      it with each name as it searches.
    
  
  
  
  OUTPUT
  
    (nothing yet: seqkit has not started)
    a table: a header line, then one row for each of the 2 files
    
      
      [ERRO] stat data/raw/*.fq.gz: no such file or directory
    
    
      data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
      data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
    
  




Figure 5.6: Who matches a pattern. Unquoted, bash matches it against the files and the program gets the names; with no match, the program gets the pattern itself. Quoted, the pattern reaches the program unchanged, which is what find -name wants.









CautionMisconception: “The program reads the * and finds the matching files itself”



Reality. For an unquoted pattern, bash does the matching first, and the program gets names, or the unchanged pattern when nothing matches. Only a quoted pattern reaches the program, which some programs, such as find -name, want.


One argument per name, spaces included. echo joins its arguments with spaces, so it cannot show where one ends and the next begins. In share/analysis, plot 1.png is one name, but echo makes it look like two. printf '<%s>\n' prints each argument on its own line, between < and >:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
echo analysis/*
printf '<%s>\n' analysis/*

analysis/counts FINAL.txt analysis/plot 1.png analysis/plot 2.png
<analysis/counts FINAL.txt>
<analysis/plot 1.png>
<analysis/plot 2.png>
Three arguments, spaces kept: a name that comes from a wildcard is not split again. That is why ls analysis/* handles these names fine, and why echo is only a quick preview for simple names like the ones in run1. To see the exact list a command would get, use ls -d -- or printf '<%s>\n'.
Patterns. Table 5.7 lists the ones you need. Brace expansion looks similar but is different: it makes words, whether or not files exist.




Table 5.7: Wildcard patterns, tried in ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share (before Exercise 3 tidies it).











Pattern
Matches
Example
Result




*
any characters, including none (not a leading .)
echo run1/*
run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz


?
exactly one character
echo run?
run1 run2


[12]
one of the listed characters
echo run[12]/*_R1*
run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp


[!1]
one character not listed
echo run[!1]
run2


{A,B}
brace expansion: makes each word, files or not
echo sample_{A,B}_R1.fastq.gz
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz sample_B_R1.fastq.gz


{01..03}
brace expansion: a range
echo sample_{01..03}
sample_01 sample_02 sample_03







Note the [12] row: *_R1* also matched the .tmp copy, because * at the end matches .fastq.gz.tmp too. Patterns match file names, not what is inside files (that is grep, Chapter 6), and they are not regular expressions, which Chapter 6 also covers. Brace ranges are for reference; you will meet them again in loops (Chapter 8).
Programs that match patterns themselves. Compare these two in share:


Terminal (laptop)

ls *.fastq.gz
find . -name '*.fastq.gz'

ls: cannot access '*.fastq.gz': No such file or directory
./run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
./run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
./run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
./run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
share itself holds no .fastq.gz file, so bash passed *.fastq.gz to ls unchanged. In the find line the quotes stop bash, so find receives the * on purpose and matches it against every name in every folder below. Your order may differ from this one.

5.8.1 Quoting
Step 1 of Figure 5.1 reads a line into words at spaces. So a name with a space, typed plainly, becomes two arguments:


Terminal (laptop)

ls analysis/plot 1.png

ls: cannot access 'analysis/plot': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access '1.png': No such file or directory
Three ways to keep it one word, all of which work:


Terminal (laptop)

ls "analysis/plot 1.png"
ls 'analysis/plot 1.png'
ls analysis/plot\ 1.png

The backslash form is what TabTab inserts for you. Double and single quotes differ in one way that matters later: inside double quotes bash still expands $… (variables, Chapter 8), and inside single quotes it expands nothing. Quoting also turns off wildcards and ~ (Table 5.8):


Terminal (laptop)

ls "run1/*.fastq.gz"
ls "~/bioinf-computing"

ls: cannot access 'run1/*.fastq.gz': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access '~/bioinf-computing': No such file or directory
The first looked for a file literally named *.fastq.gz. In the second, ~ was not expanded, so the path is relative: a folder literally named ~ inside the current folder, then bioinf-computing inside that (the / still separates folders). Leave ~ outside the quotes, or use $HOME, which double quotes do expand:


Terminal (laptop)

ls ~/"bioinf-computing-ch05/share/Run 3 final"
ls "$HOME/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/Run 3 final"

sample_C_R1.fq.gz  sample_C_R2.fq.gz
sample_C_R1.fq.gz  sample_C_R2.fq.gz






WarningPitfall: ~ and wildcards inside quotes



"~/data" is a relative path: a folder literally named ~, then data inside it. Write ~/"My Data" or "$HOME/My Data". And "*.fastq.gz" is the name *.fastq.gz, not a pattern.





Table 5.8: What each kind of quoting keeps and expands.













Form
Example
Spaces kept in one word?
* expanded?
~ expanded?
$… expanded?




none
ls plot 1.png
no
yes
yes, at the start of a word
yes


double quotes
ls "plot 1.png"
yes
no
no
yes


single quotes
ls 'plot 1.png'
yes
no
no
no


backslash
ls plot\ 1.png
yes, for that character
not for an escaped \*
not for an escaped \~
not for an escaped \$






Curly quotes copied from a PDF or a word processor (“…”, ‘…’) are not quotes to bash: they become part of the name, the same trap as Chapter 4’s en dash.


5.8.2 Tab completion
TabTab completes as far as the name is unique; a second TabTab lists the choices. It completes command names and paths, and with the bash-completion package (installed on most Linux systems) often options too. It is also a typo detector: if Tab will not complete a name you are sure of, check with ls. It would have flagged Chapter 4’s SRR6357070_l at once. Treat it as a clue, not proof: a prefix may match several names, permissions can get in the way, and completion differs between commands.






ImportantKey idea



Bash expands an unquoted wildcard; the program sees the matching names, each as one argument. No match means the pattern is passed on as it is. Quote a pattern when the program should match it itself (find -name).



Check yourself. In a folder with no .bam files you run ls *.bam. What does ls receive, and what does it print?






TipAnswer





The literal word *.bam, because nothing matched. It prints ls: cannot access '*.bam': No such file or directory.






5.8.3 Why careful names pay off
Experienced users name files 2026-11-17_read_counts.tsv rather than Read Counts (final).txt. This is not a matter of taste. On the command line, names are typed, matched by wildcards, and split into words, not clicked. The practice tree is messy on purpose: Run 3 final breaks three of the naming rules in Table 3.2 at once (a space, a capital letter, and the vague word “final”). This chapter has made you pay for each one. Table 5.9 gathers the costs in one place.



Table 5.9: What each naming rule from Chapter 3 saved you in this chapter.









Rule
What breaking it cost here




No spaces
Run 3 final needed quotes in every cd, ls, and ln -s; echo could not show where the name ended; ls printed it inside quotes


One case, lowercase
run? and run* missed Run 3 final; Tab completion is case-sensitive, so cd ru then TabTab never offers it


Only letters, digits, _, -, .
*, ?, and [ ] match names; $ expands; ( ), ;, &, \|, <, and > split or redirect commands. ls Final FINAL (2).txt stops with syntax error near unexpected token `('


Never start a name with -
rm -n read the file name as an option, so you needed -- or ./-n


Start with . only for hidden files
ls and * skip .old_settings; you see it only with ls -a






What about CamelCase or MyData? Capital letters work, and nothing breaks the first time you use them. The cost comes later. You have to remember which letters were capitals every time you type a name or press Tab. On Linux and the cluster, MyData and mydata can sit side by side as two folders. On a Mac or in a Windows folder they are the same name, so copying a project between them can overwrite one with the other. All lowercase removes the question. Join words with _ (read_counts.tsv), and use - inside a single part, such as a date or a version (2026-11-17, R64-1-1), as Table 3.2 does. For code, prefer _: Python cannot import a file named with a hyphen, such as count-reads.py (Chapter 13).
Two kinds of names keep their capitals. IDs from an archive or a sample sheet stay exactly as given (SRR6357070, WT_REP1), so they still match the records. A few files are capitalized by long convention so that people and tools find them first: README.md, LICENSE, Makefile, and your NOTEBOOK.md.

title: 5  Shell basics
text:
5.9 Finding files with find
find walks down a folder tree and prints every name that passes its tests. Start with no tests:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05
find share

share
share/ref
share/analysis
share/analysis/plot 1.png
share/analysis/plot 2.png
share/analysis/counts FINAL.txt
share/notes.txt
share/meta
share/meta/samples.tsv
share/meta/samples_from_excel.csv
share/run2
share/run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
share/run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
share/run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp
share/.old_settings
share/run1
share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
share/run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
share/Run 3 final
share/Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
share/Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz
Everything, hidden files included, in the order find meets it (yours may differ). Now add tests:


Terminal (laptop)

find share -name "*.fastq.gz"
find share -type l
find share -iname "*final*"
find share -maxdepth 1 -type f

share/run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
share/run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
share/run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
share/ref
share/analysis/counts FINAL.txt
share/Run 3 final
share/notes.txt
share/.old_settings
-name matched the pattern against each name (not the folders above it), and missed the .fq.gz files in Run 3 final. -type l found the link; -type f means ordinary files and -type d folders. -iname ignores upper and lower case, so *final* matched FINAL and final. -maxdepth 1 stopped find from going into subfolders. To find all six read files, accept either ending:


Terminal (laptop)

find share -type f \( -name "*.fastq.gz" -o -name "*.fq.gz" \)

share/run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
share/run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
share/run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
share/Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
share/Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz
The structure is find <where> <tests> [action]:

Tests written next to each other must all be true (an implicit AND): -type f -name "*.tmp" means “an ordinary file and named *.tmp”.
-o means OR, and \( … \) groups. The backslashes stop bash from reading the parentheses itself; the spaces around them are needed. Without the group, -type f -name A -o -name B means “(file and A) or B”.
The default action is to print each name.

Two tests for reference, useful on real data:


Terminal (laptop)

find share -type f -size +1k
find share -mtime +30

share/analysis/counts FINAL.txt
share/notes.txt
share/.old_settings
-size +1k means larger than 1 kilobyte: only the counts file, since the toy FASTQ files are under 50 bytes each. -type f keeps it to files: on Linux every folder takes 4 KB, so without it share and its folders would be listed too (a Mac’s folders are smaller). On a .gz file, -size measures the compressed file. -mtime +30 means last changed more than 30 days ago: the two files the setup block back-dated to 2025-03-01. -mtime -1 would find files changed in the last day.






WarningPitfall: quote the pattern after find -name



Unquoted, bash expands the pattern first (Section 5.8), and find gets file names instead of the pattern. It can fail, or worse, run and miss files.


Both cases, on throw-away files:


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/practice/findtest/deep
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/practice/findtest
touch a_1.fastq.gz a_2.fastq.gz deep/b_1.fastq.gz
find . -name *.fastq.gz
rm -i -- a_2.fastq.gz
find . -name *.fastq.gz
find . -name "*.fastq.gz"

find: paths must precede expression: `a_2.fastq.gz'
find: possible unquoted pattern after predicate `-name'?
rm: remove regular empty file 'a_2.fastq.gz'? y
./a_1.fastq.gz
./deep/b_1.fastq.gz
./a_1.fastq.gz
With two matches in the current folder, bash turned the command into find . -name a_1.fastq.gz a_2.fastq.gz, and find objected (helpfully guessing why). With one match, it became find . -name a_1.fastq.gz: no error, and deep/b_1.fastq.gz silently missed. That is the worse case, Chapter 4’s lesson that no error does not mean a correct result. Quoted, the last line found both.
Table 5.10 sums up the parts.




Table 5.10: The parts of a find command used in this book.










Part
Meaning
Example




-name "pat"
the name matches a quoted pattern
-name "*.fastq.gz"


-iname "pat"
the same, ignoring case
-iname "*final*"


-type f / d / l
ordinary file / folder / link
-type f


-xtype l
a broken link (GNU find)
find . -xtype l


-maxdepth N
go at most N levels down
-maxdepth 1


-size +N (reference)
larger than N (k, M, G)
-size +1G


-mtime +N / -N (reference)
changed more / less than N days ago
-mtime -1


next to each other
AND: all must be true
-type f -name "*.tmp"


-o
OR
-name "*.fq.gz" -o -name "*.fastq.gz"


\( … \)
group
-type f \( … -o … \)


(no action)
print each name (the default)



-exec, -delete
actions: run a command on each, delete each
not used here (below)







Where you will use it. Finding where a pipeline wrote its outputs (Chapter 26); counting your files when a cluster limits how many you may have, with find … -type f | wc -l (Chapter 10; the | is Chapter 6); and finding broken links, as in Exercise 3.
-exec and -delete are actions, not tests, and this chapter does not use them. -delete in particular is unforgiving: what it deletes depends on where it sits in the expression (placed before the tests, it deletes everything find reaches), it turns off printing, and it changes the order of the search (GNU findutils manual). Clean-up here uses unlink and rm -i.
On a Mac, -xtype and -printf (used in Exercise 3) need GNU find, which Chapter 1’s setup installed; GNU and BSD tools are compared in Chapter 7. You may also meet locate, which searches a prebuilt index: fast, but missing on most clusters and often out of date.

Check yourself. Why is find . -name *.fastq.gz wrong even when it seems to work?






TipAnswer





Bash may expand the pattern first. With exactly one match in the current folder, find looks only for that one name and misses the rest, with no error.

title: 5  Shell basics
text:
5.10 Looking inside files
In the project, start with a short file, then the start and end of longer ones:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing
cat data/meta/samples.tsv
head -n 3 logs/01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122453_7WFs.log
tail -n 3 logs/01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122453_7WFs.log

Use your own log’s name: ls -t logs lists them newest first, and TabTab completes the name.
sample  run geo_sample  condition   replicate
WT_REP1 SRR6357070  GSM2879618  wild_type   1
started:  2026-11-17 12:24:53 -0600
host:     your-laptop
script:   76fa8eb6a7b90f212042cfbe6d95cfcc  src/01_count_reads.sh
command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz
output:   e1d81de77934f7ab7b44bf72b7520b32  results/read_counts.tsv
finished: 2026-11-17 12:24:53 -0600
cat prints the whole file: fine for two lines. head -n 3 prints the first 3 lines and tail -n 3 the last 3 (10 if you leave out -n). head reads only the start of a file, so it is instant even on 100 GB.
less lets you move around a file of any length:


Terminal (laptop)

less logs/01_count_reads_2026-11-17T122453_7WFs.log
less data/ref/README.md

Move with SpaceSpace and b, search with /finished and EnterEnter, and quit with q (Table 5.11). These are the keys you used in man in Chapter 4, because man shows its pages with less.



Table 5.11: Keys in less (and in man).









Key
Action




SpaceSpace / b
one page forward / back


DownDown / UpUp
one line forward / back


g / G
start / end of the file


/word then EnterEnter
search forward for word


n / N
next / previous match


-S then EnterEnter
chop long lines instead of wrapping them (also less -S file)


-N then EnterEnter
show line numbers (also less -N file)


q
quit






less -S keeps each line of a wide table on one screen line; scroll sideways with the arrow keys. You will want it for wide tables and SAM files (Chapter 16).
What kind of file is it? Before you cat something, file tells you:


Terminal (laptop)

file data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz data/meta/samples.tsv data/raw data/ref

data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: gzip compressed data, last modified: Mon Apr 12 16:55:05 2021, from Unix, original size modulo 2^32 12776642
data/meta/samples.tsv:          ASCII text
data/raw:                       directory
data/ref:                       symbolic link to /home/you/bioinf-shared/references/yeast_R64-1-1_test
file looks at the content, not the name: a .txt that is really compressed would show as gzip. (On a Mac, file follows the link and says directory for data/ref.) The FASTQ file is compressed, about 12.8 MB of text in 2.2 MB: cat on it prints binary noise, which can garble the terminal (type reset and press EnterEnter, or close the tab). Read compressed text with zless, which comes with gzip, or with gunzip -c … | head, as in Chapter 1:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 4
zless data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz

@SRR6357070.25017281 25017281/1 kraken:taxid|4932
CCTGAATCGAGAAGGAGGTGTCCAGGGAGTTCATCATCAGAATGATTAGTATGATTTACTGTAGATTCAGTAAGTTTCTGGCCTAAGATGAAGGTCGTGCT
+
BBBBBFFFFFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFBFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFBFFBFFFFFFF
One read, four lines (Chapter 15 explains them). zless opens the same file in less; quit with q. On some Linux systems plain less also opens .gz files, because of a helper set up for it (Ubuntu, WSL, Nova, and Ceres have one); on others, including a Mac, it shows noise. Do not rely on it.






WarningPitfall: cat on a compressed or binary file



It floods the terminal with noise and can leave it garbled. Check with file first; read compressed text with zless or gunzip -c … | head.


Two more. tail -f follows a file as it grows, printing new lines as they arrive, until you press Ctrl-CCtrl-C: you will watch cluster job logs this way (Chapter 10). wc -l counts lines, as in Chapter 1, and head -c cuts by bytes, as in Chapter 4’s truncated copy.
Editor or viewer? Open a file in VS Code (code file, Chapter 2) when you want to edit it. To look, use head or less: an editor may try to load the whole file at the start, and a 5 GB file can freeze it. head reads only the start; less loads more as you move, though searching or jumping to the end (G) can still read most of the file, and paging through a decompressed stream is slower than through a plain file.



Table 5.12: Ways to look inside a file.











Command
Best for
Reads the whole file?
Works on .gz?




cat f

yes, and prints it all
no: noise


head -n 5 f

no
no; use gunzip -c f \| head


tail -n 5 f

no
no


tail -f f

follows new lines
no

as far as you move
on some systems


zless f
browsing compressed text
as far as you move
yes
