  kill and kill -9 work on any job; Ctrl-C reaches only the foreground.




Figure 7.6: The life of a process started from your shell. & and bg run it in the background, fg brings it back; Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z stops it, still holding its memory, until fg, bg, or kill. Ctrl-CCtrl-C and kill ask it to end; kill -9 forces it.



A program in the foreground has your keyboard; one in the background runs while you type other commands. To stop a program, the shell sends it a signal (Table 7.9).



Table 7.9: Ways to stop a process, and what the program can do about each.











Key or command
Signal
The program can
Use it




Ctrl-CCtrl-C
SIGINT (interrupt)
clean up first, or ignore it
to stop the foreground command


kill PID or kill %1
SIGTERM (terminate), the default
clean up first, or ignore it
to end a background or stuck process


kill -9 PID
SIGKILL
nothing: ended at once
last resort, when kill alone did not work


Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z
SIGTSTP (stop)
(it pauses)
rarely on purpose; see the pitfall






Ctrl-CCtrl-C and kill ask: a well-written tool deletes its half-written files and exits. kill -9 cannot be caught, so the program gets no chance to clean up: look for and delete partial output files afterwards. You can signal only your own processes.
Stopped is not ended. Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z pauses the foreground program and gives you the prompt back. It looks like a way out, but the program is still there:


Terminal (laptop)

sleep 600

Press Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z, then:


Terminal (laptop)

jobs
1ps -o pid,stat,rss,command
exit


1

-o chooses columns: stat the state (T stopped, S sleeping, R running), rss the memory it holds, in kB, command the command line. Linux also accepts cmd, but the Mac’s ps does not.


^Z
[1]+  Stopped                 sleep 600
[1]+  Stopped                 sleep 600
    PID STAT   RSS COMMAND
   3217 S     4776 bash
   3221 T     1952 sleep 600
   3222 R+    4152 ps -o pid,stat,rss,command
exit
There are stopped jobs.
Bash refuses the first exit to warn you. (In a login shell, such as a WSL window or a Mac Terminal, exit prints logout first.) Resume the job with fg (foreground) or bg (background), or end it with kill %1. A large analysis stopped with Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z keeps all its memory until then.






WarningPitfall: Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z does not stop a program for good



It pauses it, still holding its memory. Use Ctrl-CCtrl-C to stop a command; if you pressed Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z, finish with fg or kill %1.


Some clusters switch Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z off (SCINet’s Ceres and Atlas leave it on). On Nova, a site startup file (/etc/profile.d/disable-control-z.sh) runs stty susp undef, so the key does nothing and the command keeps running: no paused jobs are left holding memory on a shared login node. stty -a shows susp = <undef> when the key is off, and susp = ^Z when it works. Press Ctrl-CCtrl-C instead, which still works there.
Watching the machine: top. top shows the busiest processes, updated every few seconds; q quits. Here two busy test processes run alongside everything else (Linux top, sorted by CPU):
top - 14:25:42 up  9:05,  1 user,  load average: 0.38, 0.28, 0.19
Tasks:   9 total,   3 running,   5 sleeping,   0 stopped,   0 zombie
%Cpu(s):  6.7 us,  5.5 sy,  0.0 ni, 87.7 id,  0.0 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.0 si,  0.0 st
MiB Mem :   7837.4 total,   3956.1 free,   1369.3 used,   2810.8 buff/cache
MiB Swap:   1024.0 total,   1024.0 free,      0.0 used.   6468.1 avail Mem

    PID USER      PR  NI    VIRT    RES    SHR S  %CPU  %MEM     TIME+ COMMAND
   3233 you       20   0    5688   1820   1820 R 100.0   0.0   0:02.21 yes
   3232 you       20   0    5688   1836   1836 R 100.0   0.0   0:02.20 yes
The columns to read first:

%CPU: in Linux top’s usual display, 100% is one logical CPU (Chapter 1’s cores and threads). A tool running on four threads can show about 400%.
RES: the memory it really holds, in kB unless marked (m, g).
USER and COMMAND: whose it is and what it is.

On Linux, press M to sort by memory and P by CPU. macOS top looks different and sorts with top -o cpu or top -o mem (Section 7.9). htop, where installed, is a friendlier version with the same information; this book uses top, which every system has.
On a cluster. Do not rely on a command started in an ordinary SSH terminal surviving when the connection drops, and do not rely on closing the window to stop everything you started either: what happens depends on how the program was started and how it handles signals (the Bash manual’s Signals has the rules). For work that must keep running, use the site’s persistent sessions (tmux, Chapter 9), or submit it to the scheduler as a job, whose life does not depend on your window at all (Chapter 10). On a login node, ps -u "$USER" or top -u "$USER" lists only your own processes, so you can find and end leftovers. You need the -u: on Nova, top’s header showed 41 users and 1,714 processes on one login node, and on Ceres 62 users and 1,165. (top cuts long user names to eight characters, so first.last shows as first.+; -u still takes the full name.) Heavy work belongs in a job, not on the login node (Chapter 1).






CautionMisconception: “Closing the window decides whether my command keeps running”



Reality. Neither “it keeps going” nor “it always stops” is safe to assume. Run long work in tmux (Chapter 9) or as a scheduler job (Chapter 10), and check with ps -u "$USER".



Check yourself. top shows your python at 400% CPU. How many CPUs is it using? And what is the difference between Ctrl-CCtrl-C and Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z?






TipAnswer





About four logical CPUs, in Linux top’s usual display (100% is one). Ctrl-CCtrl-C asks the program to end; Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z only pauses it, and it keeps its memory until fg, bg, or kill.

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.8 Disk usage: df and du
Two questions come up all the time: how much space is left, and what is using it. Chapter 1 used df -h ~ for the first:


Terminal (laptop)

df -h ~

Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sdd       1007G  2.0G  954G   1% /
df reports a whole filesystem: one disk or storage area, named in the first column and reached through the folder in the last. (Your first column will differ: /dev/nvme0n1p2 on a Linux laptop, /dev/disk3s1 on a Mac.) df -h ~ /tmp shows whether two folders sit on the same filesystem. For the second question, du adds up what is inside folders. Ask it about the project, including the hidden .pixi folder:


Terminal (laptop)

1du -sh ~/bioinf-computing/* ~/bioinf-computing/.pixi | sort -h


1

-s one total per name, -h human units. sort -h is like Chapter 6’s sort -n, but understands sizes such as 512K and 1.2G (with -n, 1.2G would sort before 512K).


4.0K    /home/you/bioinf-computing/NOTEBOOK.md
4.0K    /home/you/bioinf-computing/pixi.toml
4.0K    /home/you/bioinf-computing/README.md
8.0K    /home/you/bioinf-computing/logs
8.0K    /home/you/bioinf-computing/results
8.0K    /home/you/bioinf-computing/src
160K    /home/you/bioinf-computing/pixi.lock
4.3M    /home/you/bioinf-computing/data
1.3G    /home/you/bioinf-computing/.pixi
The book’s software is three hundred times bigger than its data. Real projects reverse that, but environments are never small, which is why they belong on storage with room for them (1).
Now name it. df answers “how full is this disk?”; du answers “how much is in these folders?”. Three details make du less obvious than it looks:

ls -l on a folder shows the size of its list of names (4096), not of its contents (Chapter 5); du measures the contents.
du reports space used on disk, rounded up to whole blocks, so a folder of small files uses more than the file sizes add up to: du -sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1 says 12K for files totalling 86 bytes (du -sh --apparent-size gives the sum of sizes).
Files can share space. pixi keeps downloaded packages in a cache (~/.cache/rattler on Linux) and links the environment’s files to it, so the same 1.3 GB shows up once: du -sh ~/.cache/rattler ~/bioinf-computing/.pixi counts it under whichever comes first (here 1.3G for the cache, then 97M for .pixi). PIXI_CACHE_DIR

moves the cache; it does not move an environment that already exists.


Table 7.10 gathers the questions.



Table 7.10: Disk questions and the commands that answer them.











Question
Command
Read
On a cluster




How full is the disk this folder is on?
df -h folder
Avail, Use%
often the whole shared system, not your share


What is big in here?
du -sh * .[!.]* \| sort -h
the last lines
run it on the folder you suspect, not on /


How big is one folder?
du -sh folder
the one total
slow on huge trees


What is my limit?
the site’s quota command or usage file
used vs limit
Chapter 10, Appendix A






(In the second row, .[!.]* matches hidden names such as .pixi without matching .., Chapter 5.)
On a cluster df on shared storage often shows the whole system, many terabytes or petabytes, not your share. On Nova, df -h ~ gives <server>:/<path>/home  14T  7.5T  5.9T  56% /home (server address replaced): the home folders of everyone, on another machine (the address:/path form means network storage). Your real limit is a quota for your user or project, which each site reports its own way (Chapter 10, Appendix A). Table 7.11 compares two clusters.



Table 7.11: Checking storage limits on two clusters (captured November 2026).











Nova (ISU)
Ceres (SCINet; Atlas the same)




Quota command
none (quota -s prints nothing)
my_quotas: home and every project you belong to, usage vs quota in GB


Home limit
10 GB; check with du -sh ~
about 30 GB; my_quotas or quota -s


Group storage
/work/<group>; usage and quota in the file /work/<group>/group_storage_usage, updated hourly
/project/<name>; in my_quotas


df -h on group storage
shows the group’s share
shows the project’s quota as the size






So df can mislead in both directions: on one folder it shows the disk everyone shares, on another just your group’s allowance. Trust the site’s own command or file (ISU file storage, SCINet project management).
Quotas can also count files, not just bytes; df -i shows a whole filesystem’s file slots (inodes), which is likewise not your file-count quota. And du on a huge tree is slow and loads storage that everyone shares, so point it at the folder you suspect. ncdu, where installed, lets you browse sizes interactively.






TipFind what fills a folder



du -sh * .[!.]* | sort -h | tail -n 5 lists the five largest items in the current folder, hidden ones included. (If there are no hidden names, du says it cannot access .[!.]*: the pattern matched nothing and was passed on as it is, Chapter 5.)



Check yourself. df -h on a shared folder says 2.1P available, but your job fails with Disk quota exceeded. Why?






TipAnswer





There df describes the whole shared filesystem. Your group’s quota is a separate, much smaller limit; check it the way your site says, with a quota command or a usage file (Appendix A). It may also be a limit on the number of files.

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.9 GNU (Linux) and BSD (macOS) tools
Chapter 1 promised this section. Each command below works on Linux and on a Mac after Chapter 1’s setup, but fails with a Mac’s own tools. Read each message and guess why before opening the answer:
$ ls --version
ls: unrecognized option `--version'
usage: ls [-@ABCFGHILOPRSTUWXabcdefghiklmnopqrstuvwxy1%,] [--color=when] [-D format] [file ...]
$ cat -A samples.csv
cat: illegal option -- A
usage: cat [-belnstuv] [file ...]
$ stat -c '%a' samples.csv
stat: illegal option -- c
usage: stat [-FLnq] [-f format | -l | -r | -s | -x] [-t timefmt] [file ...]
$ sed -i 's/x/y/' samples.csv
sed: 1: "samples.csv": unterminated substitute pattern






TipAnswer





These are the BSD versions of ls, cat, stat, and sed that come with macOS (captured on macOS 15 with /bin/bash 3.2 and the system’s own tools). They do not know --version, -A, or -c. BSD sed -i expects a suffix for a backup copy right after -i, so it took s/x/y/ as that suffix and the file name as the script: a confusing message about something you did not mean. With GNU tools first on PATH, the same commands work (ls --version prints ls (GNU coreutils) 9.11).



Now name it. The Linux systems you will use come with the GNU versions of the core tools this book uses: ls, cp, stat, sed, grep, find, awk, sort. (Not every Linux tool is GNU: ps and top usually come from a package called procps.) macOS comes with BSD versions: same names, mostly the same basic use, different options and messages. Chapter 1’s gnubin lines put GNU first on your Mac’s PATH, so the book’s commands work as written. To see which you have, use type -a (Section 7.4) or --version: GNU tools print a version, BSD tools usually reject the option.
A third family on new Ubuntu. From Ubuntu 25.10, and in 26.04 LTS (what WSL installs in late 2026), ls --version prints ls (uutils coreutils) 0.8.0. uutils is a rewrite of GNU’s core tools in the Rust language that aims to accept the same options; Ubuntu keeps GNU’s cp, mv, rm, and df, and grep and sed are still GNU (release notes). The book’s commands work there; a few messages read differently, as noted where they appear. Clusters still run GNU.
It still matters in three places:

Scripts from a colleague’s Mac, written for BSD tools (sed -i '', date -v), fail on Linux, and the book’s GNU commands fail on a Mac without the setup. The installed manual page (man sed) is the authority for what a Mac’s own tool does.
#!/bin/bash on a Mac means Apple’s bash 3.2, which lacks features from 2009 on that Chapter 8 may use. This book’s #!/usr/bin/env bash avoids it.
Minimal containers (Chapter 24) often have a third set, BusyBox, with fewer options still.




Table 7.12: Options you may meet that differ between GNU and BSD (overview).











Task
GNU (Linux)
BSD (macOS)
GNU form on a Mac’s own tools




Edit a file in place
sed -i 's/a/b/' f
sed -i '' 's/a/b/' f
a confusing sed: 1: … error


Show invisible characters
cat -A f
cat -et f
cat: illegal option -- A


Permissions as a number
stat -c '%a' f
stat -f '%Lp' f
stat: illegal option -- c


A date from text
date -d 2026-01-01
date -j -f %Y-%m-%d 2026-01-01
date: illegal option -- d


Perl-style regular expressions
grep -P
(none)
grep: invalid option -- P


Sizes as file lengths
du --apparent-size
du -A
du: unrecognized option






(Captured on macOS 15. Some older differences are gone: recent macOS has readlink -f, sort -h, and sort -V.)






Tip--version is a quick test



GNU tools answer --version; BSD tools usually refuse it. If a command’s options behave oddly on a Mac, check type -a first.



Check yourself. A colleague’s script runs sed -i 's/chr//' genes.bed and fails on a Mac without Chapter 1’s setup, with sed: 1: "genes.bed": …. Why?






TipAnswer





The Mac’s own sed is BSD sed, whose -i takes a backup suffix, so it read s/chr// as the suffix and the file name as the script. Use GNU sed (after the setup), or write sed -i '' 's/chr//' genes.bed for BSD only.

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.10 Line endings: LF and CRLF
The practice folder from Chapter 5 has the same table twice: meta/samples.tsv (tab-separated) and meta/samples_from_excel.csv (comma-separated, as if saved from Excel). Ask both the same question: how many rows have 30 reads?


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
1grep -c $'\t30$' meta/samples.tsv
grep -c ',30$' meta/samples_from_excel.csv


1

$'\t' is bash’s way to write a tab; $ in the pattern is the end of the line (Chapter 6).


2
0
No error, and the CSV gives the wrong answer. cat shows nothing odd:


Terminal (laptop)

cat meta/samples_from_excel.csv
cat -A meta/samples_from_excel.csv | head -n 3
cat -A meta/samples.tsv | head -n 3

sample,run_folder,condition,reads
sample_C,Run 3 final,treated,12
sample_A,run1,control,9
sample_B,run2,control,30
sample_E,run5,treated,105
sample_B,run2,control,30
sample_D,run4,control,8
sample,run_folder,condition,reads^M$
sample_C,Run 3 final,treated,12^M$
sample_A,run1,control,9^M$
sample^Irun_folder^Icondition^Ireads$
sample_C^IRun 3 final^Itreated^I12$
sample_A^Irun1^Icontrol^I9$
cat -A (Chapter 6 used it to show tabs as ^I) marks each line end with $. In the CSV every line ends in ^M$: an invisible carriage return character (\r) before the newline. So the line ends in 30\r, not 30, and ,30$ does not match (Figure 7.7).




  Line endings, and why a Windows-saved CSV breaks a pattern match. Top, the same last line of a table, ending in the bytes 3 and 0: as TSV with Unix endings, sample_B, tab, run2, tab, control, tab, 30 ends in one byte, \n (line feed); as CSV saved on Windows, sample_B,run2,control,30 ends in two bytes, \r\n, where \r (carriage return) is the extra one. Middle, cat shows both lines clean, because \r is invisible; cat -A shows tabs as ^I, \r as ^M, and each line end as $, giving sample_B^Irun2^Icontrol^I30$ and sample_B,run2,control,30^M$. Bottom, how a command splits the CSV line into fields: field 2, run2, is clean, but the last field is 30\r, not 30, so grep ',30$' finds 0 lines.
  
  
  1 · The same last line, with the bytes at its end
  
  TSV
  Linux, macOS
  sample_B⇥run2⇥control⇥
  
    
    
  
  
  
    3
    0
    \n
  
  \n = LF, line feed:
  one byte ends the line
  
  CSV
  saved on Windows
  sample_B,run2,control,
  
    
    
  
  
  
  
    3
    0
    \r
    \n
  
  \r\n = CRLF: \r, carriage return,
  is an extra, invisible byte
  
  
  2 · What you see
  CAT FILE
  CAT -A FILE
  TSV
  sample_B        run2    control 30
  sample_B^Irun2^Icontrol^I30$
  CSV
  sample_B,run2,control,30
  sample_B,run2,control,30^M$
  both look clean: \r prints nothing
  ^I tab · ^M \r · $ end of line
  
  
  3 · What a command reads from the CSV line
  
    field 1
    field 2
    field 3
    field 4 (last)
  
  
  
  
  
  
    sample_B
    run2
    control
    30\r
  
  
    ,
    ,
    ,
  
  ✓ clean
  ✗ 30\r, not 30
  grep ',30$' finds 0 lines: $ wants the line to end right after 30, but \r comes first




Figure 7.7: The same row in the two files. cat shows them alike; cat -A shows the CSV’s extra carriage return (^M), which sticks to the last field, so a pattern anchored at the line end finds nothing.



The damage sticks to the last field. Fields in the middle are clean; the last one carries the \r:


Terminal (laptop)

cut -d, -f2 meta/samples_from_excel.csv | head -n 3 | cat -A
1f=$(sed -n 3p meta/samples_from_excel.csv | cut -d, -f4)
2printf '%q\n' "$f"
[ "$f" = 9 ] && echo same || echo different


1

Store the reads field of line 3 in f. $( ) and variables are Chapter 8; copy this as it is.

2

%q prints a value with invisible characters spelled out.


run_folder$
Run 3 final$
run1$
$'9\r'
different
The value is 9\r, so a comparison with 9 is silently false. When the last column holds file names, the result is a “missing” file that is plainly there. A two-line sheet in scratch shows it:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch07
printf 'sample,fastq_1\r\nWT_REP1,SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz\r\n' > sheet.csv
ls ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/$(tail -n 1 sheet.csv | cut -d, -f2)

ls: cannot access '/home/you/bioinf-computing/data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz'$'\r': No such file or directory
GNU ls spells out the $'\r'; many tools print a name that looks exactly right. And a script saved with CRLF fails on its first line, because the shebang now names a program called bash\r:


Terminal (laptop)

printf '%s\r\n' '#!/usr/bin/env bash' 'echo "hello"' > crlf.sh
chmod u+x crlf.sh
./crlf.sh

/usr/bin/env: ‘bash\r’: No such file or directory
/usr/bin/env: use -[v]S to pass options in shebang lines
(The second line is env guessing at a different problem; ignore it. Older env, such as Nova’s, prints only the first line. Ubuntu 26.04’s env writes it as env: $'bash\r': No such file or directory; on a Mac it is env: bash\r: No such file or directory. With #!/bin/bash instead, bash 5.1 (Nova) and 5.3 say /bin/bash^M: bad interpreter: No such file or directory, with status 126 instead of 127: the ^M is the carriage return. Bash 5.2 says only cannot execute: required file not found, which is even less helpful.)
How to detect it. Look with cat -A (for ^M), and count with grep -c $'\r' file, which prints how many lines contain a carriage return: 7 for the CSV, 0 for the TSV. Do not rely on file: it reports with CRLF line terminators for some text (file crlf.sh does), but once it recognises a CSV it says only CSV ASCII text, with or without carriage returns (Ubuntu’s file 5.45; macOS’s and Nova’s 5.39 say CSV text). On a two-line CSV saved by Excel, file did mention CRLF; on the seven-line sheet it did not, so its answer depends on the file.
Now name it. Linux and macOS end each line with one character, a line feed (LF, \n). Windows ends lines with two, carriage return + line feed (CRLF, \r\n). CRLF is normal in CSV files, and proper CSV readers in R and Python handle it (Chapter 14); what breaks is a shell tool or simple script that keeps the \r as part of the last field. Files get CRLF endings from Windows editors, Excel’s “Save as CSV”, and email attachments. In WSL, files under /mnt/c (Chapter 1’s pitfall) are often edited with Windows programs, which is where the CRLF comes from; the folder itself does not change the bytes. Excel’s CSV UTF-8 format also puts three invisible bytes, a byte order mark, before the first column name: cat -A shows M-oM-;M-?sample,reads^M$, and a shell tool then sees a first column called something other than sample. sed '1s/^\xEF\xBB\xBF//' removes it; R’s and Python’s CSV readers handle it.
Fix it by deleting the \r at each line end. Write a fixed copy first and check it:


Terminal (laptop)

sed 's/\r$//' ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/meta/samples_from_excel.csv > samples_lf.csv
grep -c $'\r' samples_lf.csv
echo $?
grep -c ',30$' samples_lf.csv

0
1
2
No carriage returns left, and the count is right. The 1 from echo $? is not a failure: grep exits with 1 when it finds no matching lines, which is what you wanted here (Chapter 8 returns to this). Once you trust the command, GNU sed -i 's/\r$//' file fixes a file in place: on your own copy, never on data/raw/ (Chapter 6). Two other tools you will see: tr -d '\r' < in > out deletes every carriage return, not only those at line ends (fine for a sample sheet), and dos2unix file, where installed, does the same job as sed. Line-ending fixes are for text files only, never for compressed or binary data.



Table 7.13: Line endings by system.












System
Line ending
Bytes
cat -A shows
Convert with




Linux, macOS
LF
\n
$
(already right)


Windows
CRLF
\r\n
^M$
sed 's/\r$//' in > out


Classic Mac OS (before 2001)
CR
\r
one long line with ^M
tr '\r' '\n' < in > out






Prevent it where you can. VS Code shows LF or CRLF in the status bar at the bottom of the window; click it to change a file, and set "files.eol": "\n" in your settings to make LF the default (VS Code docs). Git can convert line endings for you (Chapter 21). Before a pipeline run, check sample sheets with grep -c $'\r' (Chapter 26). One more invisible character from Excel, the byte-order mark at the start of a file, is Chapter 36.






WarningPitfall: CRLF from Windows or Excel



Files from Windows or Excel can end lines in CRLF. Shell tools then see a \r stuck to the last field, and matches and comparisons fail silently. Check with cat -A (look for ^M) or grep -c $'\r' before a script reads them.








CautionMisconception: “A CSV file is a CSV file; where it was saved doesn’t matter”



Reality. The program and system that saved it decide its line endings (and whether it starts with an invisible byte-order mark). A \r at each line end sticks to the last field, so matches and comparisons on it fail without an error.



Check yourself. cat -A samples.csv shows ^M$ at every line end. Name one way it got that way and one fix.






TipAnswer





It was saved by Excel or a Windows editor. Fix: sed 's/\r$//' samples.csv > samples_lf.csv, check with grep -c $'\r' samples_lf.csv (prints 0), then use the new file.

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.11 Summary

A permission string is a type letter and three triplets (user, group, other) of r, w, x; each triplet is also one octal digit (4 + 2 + 1). On a folder, r lists names, x reaches the entries, and w with x adds or removes them, so deleting a file depends on its folder. chmod changes permissions; read the string and change one letter, never 777.
A script runs as a command with a shebang line (#!/usr/bin/env bash) and the x bit. Permission denied (126) means found but not runnable; command not found (127) means not on PATH.
Bash checks aliases, functions, and builtins, then searches the PATH folders in order and runs the first match; type -a shows them all. pixi run and module load work by putting a folder first on PATH.
export passes a variable to the programs a shell starts; a line in ~/.bashrc sets it for every new terminal. Login shells read the first of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.profile; in the book’s setup that file reads ~/.bashrc. Back up before editing, and keep it silent.
A process has a PID and a parent. Ctrl-CCtrl-C and kill ask it to end, kill -9 forces it, Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z only pauses it. df shows how full a disk is, du what is in folders; on a cluster your limit is a quota. GNU and BSD tools share names but not options. Windows line endings leave a \r on the last field: find it with cat -A or grep -c $'\r', remove it with sed 's/\r$//'.




Table 7.14: The chapter’s commands on one page.









Task
Command




Who am I, which groups
whoami, id


Read permissions
ls -l, ls -ld folder, stat -c '%A %a %n' f


Change permissions
chmod u+x f, chmod a-w f, chmod 644 f, chmod 700 d, chmod -R g+rX d


Make a script run
#!/usr/bin/env bash on line 1, chmod u+x script.sh, ./script.sh


What runs, from where
type -a name, echo "$PATH" \| tr ':' '\n', hash -r


Add a folder to PATH
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"


Variables
NAME=value cmd, export NAME=value, env, locale


Startup files
~/.bashrc; cp -n ~/.bashrc ~/.bashrc.bak-ch07; source ~/.bashrc


Processes
cmd &, jobs, fg, bg, ps, ps -u "$USER", top, kill %1, kill PID, kill -9 PID


Disk
df -h folder, du -sh * .[!.]* \| sort -h


Which tools
type -a ls, ls --version


Line endings
cat -A f, grep -c $'\r' f, sed 's/\r$//' in > out

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.12 Exercises
Do these in ~/bioinf-computing-ch07. Exercise 4 is the only one that changes a file outside it (your ~/.bashrc, after a backup).

Exercise 1. Make a broken tool run. A labmate’s script, count_lines.sh, prints a file’s name and its number of lines. It arrived from a Windows laptop with a sample sheet. Set up the copy (the printf writes the script with Windows line endings, and chmod 644 makes sure it starts out not executable):


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/bin && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch07
printf '%s\r\n' '#!/usr/bin/env bash' \
  '# count_lines.sh: print a file name and its number of lines' \
  'printf "%s: %s lines\n" "$(basename "$1")" "$(wc -l < "$1")"' \
  > bin/count_lines.sh
chmod 644 bin/count_lines.sh
cp ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/meta/samples_from_excel.csv samples.csv

The goal: from any folder, count_lines.sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv prints samples.csv: 7 lines. Fix one fault at a time, using only the message, and run the script by its path until the last step:

Run ./bin/count_lines.sh samples.csv. Fix what the message says.
Run the same command again. Fix what the new message says.
Run it once more: it should work.
cd ~ and run it by name: count_lines.sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv. Make that work for this terminal.

Then the sample sheet: count its rows with 30 reads (grep -c ',30$') and its carriage returns (grep -c $'\r'), fix it in place with GNU sed -i, and count again. Record each message and fix in NOTEBOOK.md. (The script’s $1, $( ), and basename are Chapter 8; you only need to make it run.)






TipAnswer





$ ./bin/count_lines.sh samples.csv
bash: ./bin/count_lines.sh: Permission denied
$ chmod u+x bin/count_lines.sh
$ ./bin/count_lines.sh samples.csv
/usr/bin/env: ‘bash\r’: No such file or directory
/usr/bin/env: use -[v]S to pass options in shebang lines
$ sed -i 's/\r$//' bin/count_lines.sh
$ ./bin/count_lines.sh samples.csv
samples.csv: 7 lines
$ cd ~
$ count_lines.sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
bash: count_lines.sh: command not found
$ export PATH="$HOME/bioinf-computing-ch07/bin:$PATH"
$ count_lines.sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
samples.csv: 7 lines

No x bit (126): chmod u+x. 2. Windows line endings in the shebang, so env looked for bash\r (127): remove the \r. 4. The folder is not on PATH (127): add it, for this terminal only.

The sheet:
$ grep -c ',30$' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
0
$ grep -c $'\r' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
7
$ sed -i 's/\r$//' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
$ grep -c ',30$' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
2
$ grep -c $'\r' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
0
The line count was 7 before and after: wc -l counts line ends, and a carriage return does not change how many there are. Only the \r count shows that the fix worked. (echo $? after the last grep gives 1, “no lines matched”, which is the result you wanted.)





Exercise 2. Read and set permissions. In ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/perm2/, make notes.txt, run.sh, and a folder private/. Set them to -rw-r--r--, -rwxr-xr-x, and drwx------: once with symbolic chmod, then again from the start with octal. Check with ls -l and stat -c '%A %a %n'. Then explain, from ls -ld ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw, why rm on a raw file fails.






TipAnswer







Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/perm2 && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/perm2
touch notes.txt run.sh && mkdir private
chmod u+x,go+rx run.sh              # from -rw-r--r--: add x for all, r for group and other
chmod go-rx private                 # from drwxr-xr-x
stat -c '%A %a %n' notes.txt run.sh private
chmod 644 notes.txt && chmod 755 run.sh && chmod 700 private

-rw-r--r-- 644 notes.txt
-rwxr-xr-x 755 run.sh
drwx------ 700 private
notes.txt already had 644 from the umask. data/raw is dr-xr-xr-x: nobody has w on the folder, and removing a file changes the folder, so rm is refused even with -f.





Exercise 3. Which copy runs? Make a fake seqkit that only prints a version, put its folder first on PATH in this terminal, and see which copy each command finds:


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin
printf '%s\n' '#!/usr/bin/env bash' 'echo "seqkit v0.0.1 (fake)"' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin/seqkit
chmod u+x ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin/seqkit
export PATH="$HOME/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin:$PATH"
type -a seqkit
seqkit version
cd ~/bioinf-computing
pixi run bash -c 'type -a seqkit; seqkit version'

Which copy runs in each case, and why? Close the terminal afterwards to undo the PATH change. (Do not put this in ~/.bashrc.)






TipAnswer





seqkit is /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin/seqkit
seqkit v0.0.1 (fake)
seqkit is /home/you/bioinf-computing/.pixi/envs/default/bin/seqkit
seqkit is /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin/seqkit
seqkit v2.14.0
In the plain terminal, fakebin is first on PATH, so bare seqkit is the fake. (If another seqkit is installed on your machine, type -a lists it below.) Under pixi run, the environment’s folder goes in front of everything, so the real seqkit wins, and type -a shows the fake one second. This is why the book always writes pixi run seqkit.





Exercise 4. Make a setting permanent. Back up ~/.bashrc with cp -n, then add export EDITOR=nano (and, on a cluster where 1 told you to, the PIXI_CACHE_DIR line) if it is not there yet. Prove it works in a new terminal and, if you have a cluster account, in a new SSH login. Record in NOTEBOOK.md which of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.profile, and ~/.bashrc exist on each machine, and which one reads ~/.bashrc.






TipAnswer







Terminal (laptop)

cp -n ~/.bashrc ~/.bashrc.bak-ch07
1grep -n 'EDITOR=' ~/.bashrc
grep -qxF 'export EDITOR=nano' ~/.bashrc ||
2  echo 'export EDITOR=nano' >> ~/.bashrc
ls -a ~ | grep -E '^\.(bash|profile)'
grep -n bashrc ~/.bash_profile ~/.bash_login ~/.profile 2>/dev/null


1

Look first. If an active line (not starting with #) already sets EDITOR to something else, change that line in nano rather than adding a second one.

2

-x matches whole lines only, -F treats the text as plain text, not a pattern, and -q prints nothing. The || adds the line only if that exact line is missing, so running it twice does not add it twice. A commented-out # export EDITOR=vim does not count.


A later line wins over an earlier one, so the real check is a new terminal, where echo "$EDITOR" prints nano. On Ubuntu and WSL you will usually find ~/.profile reading ~/.bashrc; on a Mac, ~/.bash_profile from Chapter 1. If the SSH login does not see the setting, the cluster’s login file does not read ~/.bashrc (see the check in Section 7.6).





Exercise 5. Find and end a process; find the space. Start sleep 600 &, find its PID with ps and in top, end it with kill, and confirm with jobs. Then list the five largest items in ~/bioinf-computing, hidden ones included. Which is the environment, and why is it so large compared with the data?






TipAnswer







Terminal (laptop)

sleep 600 &
ps
kill %1          # or: kill <the PID from ps>
jobs
cd ~/bioinf-computing
du -sh * .[!.]* | sort -h | tail -n 5

In top, look for sleep in the COMMAND column (press q to quit). The largest item is .pixi (about 1.3 GB on Linux): Python, R, and seqkit with every library they need, for one operating system. The data are a few megabytes. Real projects have far more data, but environments are always this kind of size, which is why pixi’s cache and environments go on project storage on a cluster (1).

Shotts (2025), The Linux Command Line, chapters on permissions, processes, the environment, and customising the prompt — the same ground as this chapter, with more examples; free online.
Ramey and Fox (2025), the Bash Reference Manual, sections Bash Startup Files, Environment, and Job Control — the exact rules behind Table 7.8 and Figure 7.6, short and authoritative.

title: 8  Shell scripts
text:
8.1 What this chapter does
Core. Work through it, with the exercises.
In Chapters 1 to 7 you typed commands one at a time and pasted the occasional block. A script is those commands saved in a file. Saved, they run the same way every time, they record exactly what was done, and you can share them, keep their history, and, in Chapter 10, hand them to a cluster to run as a job. You have already run one: Chapter 3 asked you to paste src/01_count_reads.sh into your project and run it on trust. By Section 8.9 you will be able to explain every line of it.
Several earlier chapters left loose ends here. Chapter 1’s read count $(( $(gunzip -c … | wc -l) / 4 )) was copied without explanation, and so was its warning that the shell does not stop on errors unless told to. Chapter 4 said that whether a script stops after a failing command “depends on the program and the script”. Chapter 6 promised set -o pipefail and said that grep’s exit status 1 matters “in scripts that stop on any nonzero status”. Chapter 7 gave you the shebang line and the x bit. This chapter ties them together.
It is the longest chapter in Part II, so it comes in two sittings, marked in the text:
Practice happens in a scratch folder, ~/bioinf-computing-ch08. Make it now, with a bin/ folder inside for the exercise scripts:
Most examples in sitting A read the practice folder ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/ from Chapter 5: the run folders, the one with spaces in its name, the stray .tmp file, and the two sample tables. Nothing in this chapter changes, renames, or deletes anything there, so later chapters still find it as they expect. Scripts that write files write them in ~/bioinf-computing-ch08. If you do not have the practice folder, paste the setup block from Section 5.2 first.
The project, ~/bioinf-computing, is touched only in sitting B: you read src/01_count_reads.sh, add two scripts beside it, and turn the project into a git repository.
The outputs shown were captured on a Mac (macOS 15, Homebrew bash 5.3.15 with the GNU tools first on PATH, as set up in Chapter 1) and on Ubuntu 24.04 (bash 5.2.21), with GNU gzip. A Mac’s own gunzip words its errors differently (gunzip: can't stat: … where GNU says gzip: …: No such file or directory), and so do other versions; the meaning is the same. Paths start with /home/you on Linux and /Users/you on a Mac.

title: 8  Shell scripts
text:
A. Writing scripts (Section 8.2 to Section 8.6): saving commands in a file, variables and quoting, loops, tests, and arguments. Exercise 1, part A, fits at the end.
B. Making them dependable (Section 8.7 to Section 8.12): stopping on errors, logging, reading Chapter 3’s script line by line, chaining scripts into a small pipeline, finding bugs, and saving scripts with git.




Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08

title: 8  Shell scripts
section: 8.2 From the command line to a script
text:
8.2 From the command line to a script
Start with a command you already know. Chapter 6 counted the feature types in the book’s annotation file with one pipeline:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c ~/bioinf-computing/data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr

    129 exon
    124 transcript
    118 CDS
    115 start_codon
    114 stop_codon
Typing that again next month means remembering it exactly. Save it instead. Open a new file in VS Code (or nano if you prefer, as in Chapter 2):


Terminal (laptop)

code ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/gtf_types.sh

Paste these lines and save:


~/bioinf-computing-ch08/gtf_types.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# gtf_types.sh: count the feature types (column 3) in the book's GTF file.
# Run:     bash gtf_types.sh   (from ~/bioinf-computing-ch08)
# Input:   ~/bioinf-computing/data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
# Output:  counts on the screen, most common first
gunzip -c ~/bioinf-computing/data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr

The first line is the shebang from Section 7.3. The lines starting with # are comments: bash skips them, and they are for the next person to read the file, who is usually you. A short header saying what the script does, how to run it, what it reads, and what it writes is worth the four lines in every script you keep.
Run it, first with bash, then as a command of its own:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08
bash gtf_types.sh
./gtf_types.sh
chmod u+x gtf_types.sh
./gtf_types.sh

bash gtf_types.sh prints the same five lines as before. ./gtf_types.sh then fails with bash: ./gtf_types.sh: Permission denied (exit status 126) until chmod u+x gives the file its x bit, exactly as hello.sh did in Section 7.3. After that, it prints the five lines again.
What a script is. A script is a text file of commands that a new bash process reads and runs from top to bottom. Because it is a new process, it starts fresh: it does not see the aliases you typed or the variables you set without export in your terminal (Table 7.6). It also cannot change your terminal: a cd or a variable set inside the script is gone when the script ends.
Relative paths are read from where you run it. A script does not run “from its own folder”. Every relative path in it is read from the folder you are in when you start it. Chapter 5 left a two-line script for exactly this, ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/where.sh, which runs pwd and then ls data/raw. Run it from your home folder:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~
bash ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/where.sh

/home/you
ls: cannot access 'data/raw': No such file or directory
The script is stored in ~/bioinf-computing-ch05, but pwd says it runs in ~, and data/raw is looked up there. gtf_types.sh does not have this problem because its one path starts with ~, which is absolute. Project scripts use relative paths on purpose, so a project folder can be moved or copied as a whole. The book’s rule is simple: project scripts live in src/ and are run from the project folder, as pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh, and each says so in its header. Section 8.9 adds one line that checks it.
The parts of a script. Longer scripts follow the same order as the header lines above, and Figure 8.1 shows it on Chapter 3’s script: the shebang; a header comment; settings that change how bash behaves; the inputs and checks on them; the work; and the outputs. You will meet each part in this chapter and read that script line by line in Section 8.9.




  Chapter 3's script src/01_count_reads.sh, shortened, with its parts named in the margin. Line 1, the shebang #!/usr/bin/env bash, names the program that runs the file. Lines 2 and 3, comments, say what the script does and how to run it. Line 4, set -euo pipefail, is the settings line. Lines 6 and 7 set up: mkdir -p results logs, and a unique log file name made with mktemp and date. Inside a group that starts with an opening brace, echo lines record provenance: start time, the script's checksum, host and seqkit version. The line (cd data/raw && md5sum -c checksums.md5) checks the inputs against their checksums. seqkit stats does the work and writes to a .tmp file, and mv then gives the output its real name. Two more echo lines record the output's checksum and the end time. The last line, closing brace 2>&1 | tee "$log", sends everything the group prints both to the screen and to the log file.
  src/01_count_reads.sh
  (shortened)
  
  
  
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    # 01_count_reads.sh: check the raw FASTQ files, then count their reads.
    # Run from the project folder:  pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh
    set -euo pipefail
    mkdir -p results logs
    log="$(mktemp "logs/01_count_reads_$(date …)_XXXX.log")"
    {
    echo "started:  $(date …)"
    echo "script:   $(md5sum src/01_count_reads.sh)"
    …  (host, seqkit version)
    (cd data/raw && md5sum -c checksums.md5)
    seqkit stats --quiet -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz > results/….tmp
    mv results/read_counts.tsv.tmp results/read_counts.tsv
    echo "output:   $(md5sum results/read_counts.tsv)"
    echo "finished: $(date …)"
    } 2>&1 | tee "$log"
  
  
  
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
    
  
  
    shebang
    header: what, how
    to run it
    settings
    set-up: folders,
    log file name
    record: start time,
    script, tools
    inputs: check
    work
    outputs: .tmp, mv
    record: output,
    end time
    log: { … } to the
    screen and log file
  




Figure 8.1: The parts of a script, shown on src/01_count_reads.sh from Chapter 3 (shortened): the shebang line, a header comment saying what it does and how to run it, a settings line (set -euo pipefail, Section 8.7), inputs and checks, the work, and the outputs, written to a temporary name and then moved into place, with a log of the run. Section 8.9 uses this map to read every line.




Check yourself. You run bash ~/bioinf-computing/src/01_count_reads.sh from your home folder instead of from the project folder. What goes wrong, and why?






TipAnswer





The script’s paths are relative, so they are read from ~. Its mkdir -p results logs makes those two folders in your home folder, then md5sum cannot find src/01_count_reads.sh and cd data/raw fails with No such file or directory. Run project scripts from the project folder; Section 8.9 adds a guard that stops the script straight away when you do not.

title: 8  Shell scripts
text:
8.3 Variables, quoting, and expansions
Go to the practice folder and store a folder name in a variable, then list that folder twice, once without quotes and once with them:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
d="Run 3 final"
ls $d
ls "$d"

ls: cannot access 'Run': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access '3': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access 'final': No such file or directory
sample_C_R1.fq.gz
sample_C_R2.fq.gz
The first ls exits with status 2 after three errors; the second lists the two files.
What happened. d="Run 3 final" stores the text Run 3 final under the name d (no spaces around =, Section 7.5). When bash meets $d, it replaces it with that value. Without quotes, bash then does two more things to the value, the steps that Figure 5.1 in Chapter 5 set aside:

Word splitting. The value is cut at spaces, tabs, and newlines (the default contents of a setting called IFS) into separate words. Run 3 final becomes three words, so ls received three names.
Wildcard matching. Each piece that holds *, ?, or [ is matched against file names, as if you had typed it (Section 5.8).

Inside double quotes neither happens: "$d" is replaced by its value and stays one word, spaces and all (Figure 8.2). That gives the rule this chapter follows everywhere:






ImportantKey idea



Put double quotes around every $…: write "$d", "$f", "$1". An unquoted value is split at spaces and matched as a wildcard, so a file name with a space becomes several arguments.






  What bash does with gunzip -c $f when f holds Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz, a path with spaces. Step 1: the line as typed is three words: gunzip, -c, and $f. Step 2: $f is replaced by its value, Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz. Step 3: because $f was not in double quotes, the value is split at its spaces into three words, Run, 3, and final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz, so the command now has five words. Step 4: gunzip receives three file names, none of which exists, and fails on each: gzip: Run.gz: No such file or directory, gzip: 3.gz: No such file or directory, gzip: final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz: No such file or directory. Step 5: typed as gunzip -c "$f", the value stays one word, gunzip receives the one real file, and prints its FASTQ records.
  Typed: the line is three words, gunzip, -c, and $f.
  Expand: bash replaces $f with its value, a path that contains spaces.
  Split: $f was not in double quotes, so bash splits the value at its spaces into three words.
  Run: gunzip receives three file names, none of which exists, and fails on each.
  Quoted: with "$f" the value stays one word, so gunzip receives the one real file and reads it.
  
  
  TERMINAL, IN ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
  f="Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz"
  gunzip -c $f
  gunzip -c "$f"
  
  
    1 · As typed: 3 words
    2 · Expand: $f is replaced by its value
    3 · Split: unquoted, the value breaks at its spaces: 5 words
    4 · Run: gunzip receives 3 file names
    5 · Quoted: "$f" stays one word, one real file
  
  
  
    
    gunzip
    
    -c
    
    
      
      $f
    
    
    
      
      Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
    
    
    
      
      Run
      
      3
      
      final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
    
    
    
      
      Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
    
  
  
  
    one value, with spaces inside
    three arguments: three file names
    one argument: the whole path
  
  
  
  WHAT GUNZIP DOES
  (nothing yet: bash is still building the command)
  
    gzip: Run.gz: No such file or directory
    gzip: 3.gz: No such file or directory
    gzip: final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz: No such file or directory
    exit status 1
  
  
    @C.1
    ACGTACGTAC
    +
    IIIIIIIIII… four reads in all
  




Figure 8.2: What bash does with gunzip -c $f when f holds Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz. The variable is replaced by its value, the unquoted value is split at its spaces into three words, and gunzip receives three file names that do not exist. The last step shows "$f", which arrives as one word. Use Next to step through.



Two places do not split, and you will see unquoted variables in them in other people’s scripts: a plain assignment (x=$y copies the value whole) and the inside of [[ … ]] (Section 8.5). Quoting there does no harm, and quoting everywhere is the simpler habit. Single quotes stop all expansion, as in Chapter 5: '$d' is the two characters $d. Use double quotes when you want the value, single quotes when you want the text exactly as typed.
A misspelled variable is empty, not an error. Set a variable and then use it with a typo, through echo so nothing happens:


Terminal (laptop)

outdir=~/bioinf-computing-ch08/out
echo "would delete: $outdri/"

would delete: /
outdri was never set, so bash replaced it with nothing, silently. Inside a real command such as rm -rf "$outdri/", the quotes would faithfully hand rm the one argument /: the wrong path, built by a typo. What rm then does depends on its safeguards and your permissions; the point is that the command was built wrong and nothing warned you. Never run that line. Section 8.7 shows the setting, set -u, that turns an unset variable into an error.






WarningPitfall: a misspelled variable is empty



rm -rf "$outdri/" with outdri unset is handed the argument /. Quotes keep an argument whole, but they do not check that it is the path you meant. Preview any command built from variables by putting echo in front of it, and use set -u in scripts (Section 8.7).


Two naming habits avoid trouble. Use lower-case names for your own variables (d, outdir, sample): upper-case names such as PATH, HOME, and USER belong to the system (Section 7.5), and overwriting PATH inside a script stops it finding any command. And use names that say what the value is: fastq tells the next reader more than x.

8.3.1 The expansions you have already met
Several pieces of syntax from earlier chapters are expansions too, and the quoting rule applies to all of them.
Command substitution, $( ), runs a command and puts its output in its place. Chapter 3’s script names its log with $(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M%S), and Chapter 7 stored a field with f=$(…). Quote it like a variable: "$(date +%Y-%m-%d)".
Arithmetic, $(( )), does whole-number arithmetic. Now Chapter 1’s read count can be taken apart. Run the inner part first, then the whole line:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | wc -l
echo $(( $(gunzip -c ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))

200000
50000
The inner $( ) runs the pipeline and becomes 200000, the number of lines; $(( 200000 / 4 )) becomes 50000, one read per four lines. Bash arithmetic is integers only: $(( 7 / 2 )) is 3. Anything with decimals belongs in R or Python (Chapter 12, Chapter 13) or awk (Chapter 6).
Braces, ${name}, mark where a variable’s name ends. Compare:


Terminal (laptop)

sample=WT_REP1
echo "$sample_R1.fastq.gz"
echo "${sample}_R1.fastq.gz"

.fastq.gz
WT_REP1_R1.fastq.gz
In the first line, bash read the longest name it could, sample_R1, which is unset and so empty. Braces end the name where you mean it to: use "${sample}_R1.fastq.gz" whenever a name is followed by a letter, digit, or _.
Trimming a value. Inside braces, #, %, and / cut or replace part of a value without starting another program. On a path from the practice folder:


Terminal (laptop)

f="Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz"
echo "${f##*/}"
echo "${f%.gz}"
echo "${f/_R1/_R2}"
basename "$f"

sample_C_R1.fq.gz
Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq
Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz
sample_C_R1.fq.gz
${f##*/} removes everything up to the last /, which leaves the file name, the same as the basename command. ${f%.gz} removes .gz from the end. ${f/_R1/_R2} replaces the first _R1 with _R2, which Section 8.4 uses to find the partner of each R1 file. Table 8.1 collects these forms.



Table 8.1: Expansions, with examples on f="Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz" and the rows list below. Quote every one of them.











Form
Gives
Example
Output




"$f"
the value, as one word
echo "$f"
Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz


"${f}"
the same; braces mark where the name ends
"${sample}_R1.fastq.gz"
WT_REP1_R1.fastq.gz


"$(cmd)"
the output of a command
"$(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
today’s date


$(( expr ))
whole-number arithmetic
$(( 200000 / 4 ))
50000


"${f##*/}"
remove up to the last /
"${f##*/}"
sample_C_R1.fq.gz


"${f%.gz}"
remove an ending
"${f%.gz}"
Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq


"${f/_R1/_R2}"
replace the first match
"${f/_R1/_R2}"
Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz


"${rows[@]}"
every item of a list, each as its own word
printf '[%s] ' "${rows[@]}"
[sample] [run_folder] …


${#rows[@]}
the number of items in a list
echo "${#rows[@]}"
28








8.3.2 Lists
Chapter 5 and Chapter 6 built the sample table from a list, rows=(…), and promised an explanation. A list (bash calls it an array) holds several values under one name. Paste the same list again:


Terminal (laptop)

rows=(sample run_folder condition reads
  sample_C "Run 3 final" treated 12
  sample_A run1 control 9
  sample_B run2 control 30
  sample_E run5 treated 105
  sample_B run2 control 30
  sample_D run4 control 8)
echo "${#rows[@]} items"
echo "${rows[5]}"

28 items
Run 3 final
The quotes around "Run 3 final" in the list made it one item, so the list has 28 items, not 30. Items are numbered from 0: ${rows[5]} is the sixth, Run 3 final. "${rows[@]}", in double quotes, gives every item as its own word, spaces kept. The table itself came from one printf:


Terminal (laptop)

printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "${rows[@]}"

printf takes a format and fills each %s with the next item. When it has more items than %s slots, it reuses the format until the items run out: four slots, 28 items, so seven lines of four tab-separated columns. A small case shows the rule:


Terminal (laptop)

printf '%s-%s\n' a b c d e

a-b
c-d
e-
Prefer printf to echo for anything with tabs, backslashes, or a format: printf treats \t and \n the same way everywhere, while echo’s handling of them differs between shells and systems. echo is fine for a plain message.

Check yourself. (a) sample=WT_REP1; echo "$sample_R1.fastq.gz". What prints? (b) f="Run 3 final/a.fq.gz"; ls $f: how many names does ls receive?






TipAnswer






.fastq.gz. Bash read a variable called sample_R1, which is unset, so it became nothing. Write "${sample}_R1.fastq.gz". (b) Three: Run, 3, and final/a.fq.gz, because the unquoted value is split at its spaces. ls "$f" receives one.

title: 8  Shell scripts
text:
8.4 Loops
Count the reads in every R1 file of the practice folder. Here is the version most people write first. It has two bugs; run it and look for them in the output:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
for f in */*_R1*; do n=$(gunzip -c $f | wc -l); echo "$f $((n/4))"; done

gzip: Run.gz: No such file or directory
gzip: 3.gz: No such file or directory
gzip: final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz: No such file or directory
Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz 0
run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz 2
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz 3
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp 3
The exit status is 0. Sample C really has 4 reads, and the last line is the stray temporary copy from Chapter 5, counted as if it were a sample. Neither bug stopped the loop or changed its exit status; the three error lines are the only hint, and in a long run they scroll past. (GNU gunzip tries adding .gz to a name it cannot find, which is why it reports Run.gz; a Mac’s gunzip prints gunzip: can't stat: Run and so on.)
Fix one bug at a time. First quote "$f":


Terminal (laptop)

for f in */*_R1*; do n=$(gunzip -c "$f" | wc -l); echo "$f $((n/4))"; done

Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz 4
run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz 2
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz 3
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp 3
Sample C now arrives as one name and gives 4. Then tighten the pattern so it only matches names that end the way FASTQ files end, .fastq.gz or .fq.gz:


Terminal (laptop)

for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz; do n=$(gunzip -c "$f" | wc -l); echo "$f $((n/4))"; done

Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz 4
run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz 2
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz 3
Three samples, three correct counts. (The lines may come out in a different order on your system: the order of a wildcard’s matches depends on the language settings. On these machines Run 3 final sorted first; on several Linux clusters it sorts last. The counts are what matter.)
What a for loop does. The general form is:


the form of a for loop

for name in list; do
  commands that use "$name"
done

Bash expands the list once, before the loop starts: here the wildcard became the list of matching file names. Then it runs the commands once per item, with f set to each in turn. The one-line version above just puts ; where the line breaks would be. In a script, write it on several lines and indent the body, as in the box.
Loop over a wildcard, never over the output of ls: for f in $(ls) splits the names at their spaces, exactly like an unquoted variable.
Preview first. A loop repeats a command many times, so a mistake is repeated too. Before a loop that changes files, put echo in front of the command and read what it would do:


Terminal (laptop)

for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz; do echo cp "$f" ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/; done

cp Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch08/
cp run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch08/
cp run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch08/
This is Chapter 5’s habit with rm, now for loops. The list is right, so the real loop would copy three files. (echo joins its arguments with spaces, so it cannot show that Run 3 final/… is one argument; the quotes in the loop make sure it is.) When the list looks right, remove echo and run it.

8.4.1 When nothing matches
Try a pattern that matches nothing in the practice folder:


Terminal (laptop)

for f in */*.bam; do echo "got: $f"; done

got: */*.bam
When a wildcard matches nothing, bash passes the pattern unchanged (Section 5.8), so the loop ran once with f set to the literal text */*.bam. The next command would fail with a confusing No such file or directory for a file called */*.bam. Bash can be told to drop a pattern that matches nothing instead:


Terminal (laptop)

shopt -s nullglob
for f in */*.bam; do echo "got: $f"; done
shopt -u nullglob

With nullglob set the loop runs zero times and prints nothing; shopt -u unsets it again in your terminal. In a script that loops over a wildcard, put shopt -s nullglob near the top. But zero passes is not a success either: a script that “processes” no files and exits 0 looks exactly like one that worked. So store the matches in a list and stop if it is empty:


in a script

shopt -s nullglob
files=(*/*_R1.f*q.gz)
if (( ${#files[@]} == 0 )); then echo "no R1 files found" >&2; exit 1; fi
for f in "${files[@]}"; do
  echo "would count $f"
done

These are script lines: typed into a terminal, the exit would close it. if is explained in Section 8.5 and >&2 in Section 8.6; here they read “if the list has zero items, print a message and stop”.
Numbered ranges. Brace ranges from Chapter 5 work as a loop list: for i in {01..03}; do echo "sample_$i"; done prints sample_01, sample_02, sample_03.


8.4.2 Paired files
Paired-end reads come as R1 and R2 files with matching names. From each R1 name, build the R2 name with the replacement from Table 8.1 and check that the file exists (-e, “exists”, is one of the tests in Section 8.5):


Terminal (laptop)

for r1 in */*_R1.f*q.gz; do
  r2="${r1/_R1/_R2}"
  if [[ -e "$r2" ]]; then echo "pair: $r1 + $r2"; else echo "no R2 for $r1"; fi
done

pair: Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz + Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz
pair: run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz + run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
pair: run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz + run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
${r1/_R1/_R2} replaces the first _R1 in the whole path. A folder called run_R1_old/ would break it, which is one more reason for Chapter 3’s naming rules: _R1 and _R2 appear only once, just before the file ending.


8.4.3 Rows of a table
A sample table and the files on disk can disagree, as Chapter 6 warned. Check each row of the practice table against the folders:


Terminal (laptop)

1tail -n +2 meta/samples.tsv | while IFS=$'\t' read -r sample folder cond reads; do
  if [[ -d "$folder" ]]; then echo "$sample: folder '$folder' found"
  else echo "$sample: folder '$folder' MISSING"; fi
done


1

tail -n +2 skips the header line; read takes one line at a time from the pipe.


sample_C: folder 'Run 3 final' found
sample_A: folder 'run1' found
sample_B: folder 'run2' found
sample_E: folder 'run5' MISSING
sample_B: folder 'run2' found
sample_D: folder 'run4' MISSING
Two rows point at folders that do not exist. Three details make this loop work:

while … read …; do … done runs once per line of its input, and stops when there are no more lines.
IFS=$'\t' sets, for this read only, the characters it splits a line at: tabs only. So Run 3 final arrives whole in folder, spaces and all. ($'\t' is bash’s way to write a tab character.)
read -r keeps backslashes as they are, instead of treating them as escapes. Always use -r.

read puts the first field in sample, the second in folder, and so on; the last name gets whatever is left.
The tempting alternative loops over the table’s words:


Terminal (laptop)

for line in $(tail -n +2 meta/samples.tsv | head -n 2); do printf '[%s] ' "$line"; done; echo

[sample_C] [Run] [3] [final] [treated] [12] [sample_A] [run1] [control] [9]
$( ) unquoted is split at spaces, tabs, and newlines alike, so the “lines” arrive one word at a time, and Run 3 final falls apart.






WarningPitfall: loop over files with a wildcard, over lines with while read



for f in $(ls) and for line in $(cat file) split at every space. Loop over files with a wildcard (for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz), and over the lines of a table with while IFS=$'\t' read -r …; do … done.








CautionMisconception: “for line in $(cat file) goes through a file line by line”



Reality. It goes word by word, split at spaces and tabs, and it matches wildcards. Read lines with while IFS= read -r line.


A loop at the end of a pipe forgets. Bash runs each part of a pipe in its own process (a subshell), including a while loop at the end. Variables set inside the loop disappear with that process. It matters as soon as a loop must remember something, such as “did any row fail?”:


Terminal (laptop)

bad=0
tail -n +2 meta/samples.tsv | while IFS=$'\t' read -r sample folder _; do
  if [[ ! -d "$folder" ]]; then bad=1; fi
done
echo "bad after the loop: $bad"

bad after the loop: 0
Two folders are missing, yet bad is still 0: the bad=1 happened in the subshell. A script that ended with exit "$bad" would report success. (_ is the usual name for “a value I don’t need”; here it takes the rest of the line.) The repair feeds the file to the loop with < instead of a pipe, so the loop runs in the script’s own shell. You will use it, ready-made, in exercise 2:


in a script

bad=0
{
  IFS= read -r _   # skip the header line
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r sample folder rest || [[ -n "$sample$folder$rest" ]]; do
    if [[ ! -d "$folder" ]]; then
      printf '%s: missing folder %s\n' "$sample" "$folder" >&2
      bad=1
    fi
  done
} < "$table"
exit "$bad"

The < "$table" after the closing } feeds the file to everything inside the braces. The first read takes the header line; the while loop gets the rest. Because nothing here is a pipe, bad=1 survives the loop and the script can exit with it. The extra || [[ -n "$sample$folder$rest" ]] handles a last line with no newline at its end: read still fills the variables but reports failure, so a plain while read would skip that row without a word. The test says “or the line was not empty”, so the last row is checked too. (When you only need a total, awk from Chapter 6 is simpler than a loop.)
Limits of read. This way of reading a table is for simple, tidy tables like the practice one, where every field is filled in. A tab counts as “white space” to read, so two tabs in a row do not give an empty field. A row with an empty folder field, sample_C<TAB><TAB>control<TAB>12, gives folder=control, cond=12, and an empty reads, silently shifted. And a plain while read loop skips a last line that has no newline after it (the repair above deals with that one). Real sample sheets are read with R or Python (Chapter 14).
Windows line endings, inside a loop. Section 7.10 showed that a file saved by Excel ends each line in a carriage return, \r. Read the practice CSV with IFS=, and look at the last field:


Terminal (laptop)

tail -n +2 meta/samples_from_excel.csv | head -n 1 | while IFS=, read -r sample folder cond reads; do
  if [[ "$reads" == 12 ]]; then echo "reads is 12"; else echo "reads is not 12"; fi
  (( reads > 10 )) && echo big
done

reads is not 12
bash: ((: 12: arithmetic syntax error: invalid arithmetic operator (error token is "")
The value is really 12\r, so it is never equal to 12, and arithmetic on it fails. (The exact wording of the error differs between bash versions.) The \r sits in the last field: a loop that only used the folder name would never notice it. IFS=, also works only for a simple file like this one, with no commas inside quoted fields; it is not a CSV reader. Look at any table with cat -A before a script relies on it, and fix the line endings first (Section 7.10). Table 8.2 sums up the section.



Table 8.2: Loop patterns.










Task
Pattern
Pitfall it avoids




Every file matching a pattern
for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz; do … "$f" …; done
names with spaces split; stray files matched by a loose pattern


Pattern may match nothing
shopt -s nullglob, a list, and a check that it is not empty
a loop over the literal pattern; a “success” on no files


R1/R2 pairs
r2="${r1/_R1/_R2}", then [[ -e "$r2" ]]
a missing partner noticed only later


A numbered range
for i in {01..03}; do …; done
typing the list by hand


Rows of a TSV
while IFS=$'\t' read -r a b c; do …; done
fields split at spaces


Rows, remembering something
{ …; while read …; done; } < "$table"
a variable lost in a pipe’s subshell


Don’t:
for f in $(ls)
names split at spaces


Don’t:
for line in $(cat file)
lines split into words







Check yourself. A loop for f in data/raw/*.fq.gz; do seqkit stats "$f"; done prints an error for a file called data/raw/*.fq.gz, then stops. The folder holds SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz and SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz. Why, and what would shopt -s nullglob have changed?






TipAnswer





No file matched, so bash passed the pattern unchanged and the loop ran once with f set to data/raw/*.fq.gz. The files end in .fastq.gz, not .fq.gz. With nullglob the loop would have run zero times, so a script should also check that its list is not empty.

title: 8  Shell scripts
text:
8.5 Exit status and conditionals
Every command finishes with an exit status, a number you saw with echo $? in Chapter 4: 0 means success, anything else a kind of failure. grep uses three (Chapter 6): 0 found a match, 1 found none, 2 something went wrong. Check them in the practice folder:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
grep -q sample_E meta/samples.tsv; echo "status $?"
grep -q sample_F meta/samples.tsv; echo "status $?"
grep -q sample_E nope.tsv; echo "status $?"

status 0
status 1
grep: nope.tsv: No such file or directory
status 2
(-q, quiet, makes grep print nothing; only its status matters.) Chapter 7 used one such status to choose what to print. Run it for a sample that is listed and one that is not:


Terminal (laptop)

grep -q sample_E meta/samples.tsv && echo listed || echo "not listed"
grep -q sample_F meta/samples.tsv && echo listed || echo "not listed"

listed
not listed
&& runs the next command only if the one before it succeeded (status 0); || runs the next only if it failed. a && b || c looks like “if a then b else c”, but it is not quite: c also runs when b fails. true && false || echo "c ran anyway" prints c ran anyway. For anything more than a one-liner, use if.
if tests a command’s exit status, and nothing else. The form is:


the form of if

if command; then
  commands to run when it succeeds
elif other_command; then
  commands when the first failed and this one succeeds
else
  commands when all of them failed
fi

elif and else are optional. Any command can follow if:


Terminal (laptop)

if grep -q sample_D meta/samples.tsv; then echo "sample_D is in the table"; else echo "no sample_D"; fi

sample_D is in the table
Tests with [[ … ]]. Most ifs ask a question about a file, a string, or a number. [[ … ]] is a command that does nothing except answer such a question with its exit status:


Terminal (laptop)

f="Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz"
if [[ -f "$f" ]]; then echo "file exists"; fi
if [[ -s "$f" ]]; then echo "and is not empty"; fi
if [[ -d run5 ]]; then echo "run5 found"; else echo "no folder run5"; fi
x=""
if [[ -z "$x" ]]; then echo "x is empty"; fi

file exists
and is not empty
no folder run5
x is empty
The spaces inside [[ and ]] are required: [[-f "$f"]] is an error. Table 8.3 lists the tests you will use most.



Table 8.3: Tests for [[ … ]] and (( … )).










Test
True when
Example




-e path
it exists (file, folder, or other)
[[ -e "$r2" ]]


-f path
it is a regular file
[[ -f "$1" ]]


-d path
it is a folder
[[ -d "$folder" ]]


-s path
it exists and is not empty
[[ -s results/counts.tsv ]]


-r path
you may read it
[[ -r "$table" ]]


a == b, a != b
the strings are the same, or differ
[[ "$ext" == gz ]]


-z s, -n s
the string is empty, or not empty
[[ -z "$x" ]]


a -eq b, -ne, -lt, -le, -gt, -ge
numbers: equal, not equal, less than, …
[[ "$n" -gt 0 ]]


(( a < b )), >, <=, >=, ==, !=
numbers, written as arithmetic
(( n > 0 ))


Trap: [[ 9 < 30 ]]
false: < inside [[ ]] compares text
use (( 9 < 30 )) or -lt


! test
the test is false
[[ ! -d "$folder" ]]






The trap in the table. Inside [[ ]], < and > compare text, in dictionary order, not numbers:


Terminal (laptop)

[[ 9 < 30 ]]; echo "status $?"
(( 9 < 30 )); echo "status $?"
[[ 9 -lt 30 ]]; echo "status $?"

status 1
status 0
status 0
As text, 9 comes after 3, so [[ 9 < 30 ]] is false, the same mistake as sort without -n in Chapter 6. For numbers, use (( )) or the letter tests (-lt, -gt, …).
You will also meet the older single-bracket test, [ … ] (for example [ 9 -lt 30 ], also true). It works in every shell, not only bash, but every variable inside it must be quoted, and it lacks some features. This book uses [[ ]] in bash scripts.
case, for matching patterns. When one value can match several patterns, case is tidier than a chain of elifs. You will see it in other people’s scripts; recognising it is enough here:


Terminal (laptop)

f="Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz"
case "$f" in
  *.fq.gz|*.fastq.gz) echo "FASTQ: $f" ;;
  *)                  echo "skip: $f" ;;
esac

FASTQ: Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
Each pattern ends in ), | means “or”, ;; ends a branch, and *) catches everything else.
A script’s own exit status. A script exits with the status of the last command it ran, unless it calls exit first. exit 0 reports success; any other number, usually exit 1, reports failure. The next program, or you with echo $?, can then tell whether it worked. Scripts that stop early on a problem use exactly this, as the next section shows.

Check yourself. n=9; if [[ $n < 10 ]]; then echo small; else echo big; fi. What prints, and how do you fix it?






TipAnswer





big. Inside [[ ]], < compares text, and 9 sorts after 1. if (( n < 10 )) or if [[ "$n" -lt 10 ]] prints small. The unquoted $n is not the problem: [[ ]] does not split its contents (Section 8.3).

title: 8  Shell scripts
text:
8.6 Script arguments
gtf_types.sh always reads the same file. A useful script works on the files you give it. Chapter 7’s exercise 1 left you a script that does: count_lines.sh. Run it again on the practice table (if you skipped that exercise, the script is the one-line file below; save it as ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/bin/count_lines.sh and chmod u+x it):


~/bioinf-computing-ch07/bin/count_lines.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count_lines.sh: print a file name and its number of lines
printf "%s: %s lines\n" "$(basename "$1")" "$(wc -l < "$1")"



Terminal (laptop)

~/bioinf-computing-ch07/bin/count_lines.sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/meta/samples.tsv

samples.tsv: 7 lines
Now every piece can be read. $1 is the first argument, the first word after the script’s name: here the path to samples.tsv. "$(wc -l < "$1")" runs wc -l on that file and puts its count in place. "$(basename "$1")" puts the file name without its folders. printf fills its two %s with the two values. The quotes inside the $( ) are separate from the ones outside, so both sets are needed.
What a script receives. Save this script in your scratch folder. It prints what it was given, in two ways:


~/bioinf-computing-ch08/args.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# args.sh: show what a script receives as arguments.
1if [[ $# -lt 1 ]]; then
2  echo "usage: args.sh ARG [ARG ...]" >&2
  exit 2
fi
echo "script name (\$0): $0"
echo "number of arguments (\$#): $#"
echo 'with "$@":'
for a in "$@"; do echo "  [$a]"; done
echo 'with $* (unquoted):'
3for a in $*; do echo "  [$a]"; done


1

$# is the number of arguments. Fewer than one: print how to use the script and stop.

2

>&2 sends the message to stderr (below).

3

Deliberately wrong, for comparison; ShellCheck flags it (Section 8.11).


Run it with two arguments, one with spaces in it:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08
chmod u+x args.sh
./args.sh a.fq.gz "Run 3 final/c.fq.gz"

script name ($0): ./args.sh
number of arguments ($#): 2
with "$@":
  [a.fq.gz]
  [Run 3 final/c.fq.gz]
with $* (unquoted):
  [a.fq.gz]
  [Run]
  [3]
  [final/c.fq.gz]
The script received two arguments, and "$@" gives exactly those two, each kept whole. Unquoted $* joins them and splits the result at spaces, giving four. Always pass a script’s arguments on as "$@", in quotes: for f in "$@" loops over the files the user gave, however they are named. Table 8.4 lists these names and the others you will meet.



Table 8.4: Special parameters, with ./args.sh a.fq.gz "Run 3 final/c.fq.gz".










Name
Holds
Example value




$0
the name the script was started as
./args.sh


$1, $2, … $9
the first, second, … ninth argument
$2 is Run 3 final/c.fq.gz


${10}
the tenth argument (braces needed from 10 on)
(empty here)


$#
the number of arguments
2


"$@"
every argument, each as its own word
a.fq.gz, Run 3 final/c.fq.gz


$*
every argument joined into one string; unquoted, split again
four words


$?
the exit status of the last command
0 after a success


$$
the process number of this shell or script
a number such as 48213






A usage check. Run args.sh with no arguments, and then with its output sent to a file:


Terminal (laptop)

./args.sh; echo "exit $?"
./args.sh > out.txt; echo "exit $?"
cat out.txt

usage: args.sh ARG [ARG ...]
exit 2
usage: args.sh ARG [ARG ...]
exit 2
The check at the top caught the mistake before the script did any work, said how to use it, and exited with a nonzero status. Two details make it a good check:

>&2 sends the message to stderr, the error stream from

So even with > out.txt the message still appears on the screen, and out.txt stays empty: a results file never ends up holding an error message. Every message from a script (warnings, progress, usage) goes to stderr; only results go to stdout.

Exit status 2 is the usual convention for “used wrongly”, and 1 for “tried, and something failed”. Any nonzero status tells the caller to stop.

Every script that takes arguments should start with a check like this. A script that needs exactly one file checks if [[ $# -ne 1 ]].
Options. Many tools take options such as --threads 4 or -o out.tsv. Bash can parse them (with a built-in called getopts), but it takes more code than it saves at this stage; Chapter 34 returns to it. When a script’s arguments get complicated, that is a sign it may be better written in R or Python (Chapter 12, Chapter 13).
Arguments, a variable at the top, or a settings file? A script can get its inputs in three ways (Table 8.5). This book uses arguments for the files a script works on, and a variable near the top for settings that rarely change.



Table 8.5: Three ways to give a script its inputs.










Way
Example
Use it for




Arguments
./count_reads.sh run1/*.fastq.gz
the files to work on: they change each run


A variable at the top
threads=4 on line 10
settings that rarely change; easy to find and edit


A settings file
source config.sh
many settings shared by several scripts; later, workflow managers’ parameter files (Chapter 25)







Check yourself. You run ./run.sh "sample A.fq.gz" b.fq.gz. What are $# and $1? And why does the script print its usage message with >&2?






TipAnswer





$# is 2 and $1 is sample A.fq.gz: the quotes on the command line made it one argument. >&2 sends the message to stderr, so with > results.tsv it still appears on the screen and the results file holds only results.




End of sitting A. You can now save commands as a script, quote values, loop over files and table rows, test conditions, and take file names as arguments. That is enough for exercise 1, part A (Section 8.14): fixing a supplied count_reads.sh that gets sample C wrong and counts the stray .tmp file. Part B, and everything else in the second half, is about making scripts dependable: what happens when a command inside them fails.
The first sitting was about writing scripts: saving commands, quoting, loops, tests, and arguments. The second is about making them dependable: stopping when something fails, keeping results and messages apart, reading a real script line by line, chaining steps into a small pipeline, finding bugs, and saving each working version with git. If you are starting a new sitting, go back to your scratch folder first:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08

title: 8  Shell scripts
text:
8.7 Stopping on errors: set -euo pipefail
In Chapter 1, a pitfall said that the shell does not stop on errors unless told to. Here is what that means inside a script. Make a five-line script, count.sh: open it with code count.sh (or nano count.sh), paste, and save.


count.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count.sh: count the reads in one gzipped FASTQ file.
n=$(gunzip -c "$1" | wc -l)
echo "$1: $(( n / 4 )) reads"
echo "done"

Copy one practice file next to it (a copy, so the practice folder stays as it is), make the script executable, and run it three ways: on the copy, on a file that does not exist, and with no argument at all.


Terminal (laptop)

cp ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz .
chmod u+x count.sh
./count.sh sample_A_R1.fastq.gz; echo "exit $?"
./count.sh missing.fastq.gz; echo "exit $?"
./count.sh; echo "exit $?"

sample_A_R1.fastq.gz: 2 reads
done
exit 0
gzip: missing.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
missing.fastq.gz: 0 reads
done
exit 0
gunzip: can't stat:  (.gz): No such file or directory
: 0 reads
done
exit 0
(The error lines come from gzip, and their wording varies: GNU gzip on Linux says gzip: missing.fastq.gz: No such file or directory; Apple’s on a Mac says gunzip: can't stat: …. The last block is from a Mac.)
The first run is right. The other two are wrong in a quiet way. gunzip failed and said so, but bash went on to the next line, wc -l counted the zero lines it was given, and the script printed 0 reads, then done, and finished with exit status 0, which means success. A script that ran later steps on this “result” would never know.
Now add one line after the comment, so that the script reads:


count.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count.sh: count the reads in one gzipped FASTQ file.
set -euo pipefail
n=$(gunzip -c "$1" | wc -l)
echo "$1: $(( n / 4 )) reads"
echo "done"

Run the same three commands again:
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz: 2 reads
done
exit 0
gzip: missing.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
exit 1
./count.sh: line 4: $1: unbound variable
exit 1
The good run is unchanged. The missing file now stops the script at the failed line, with no count and exit status 1. The missing argument stops it before gunzip even starts, with a message that names the line and the problem (Figure 8.3).




  The same script, count.sh, run on a missing file, with and without strict mode.
