Left, without strict mode: gzip prints No such file or directory, then the script prints missing.fastq.gz: 0 reads and done, and ends with exit status 0, a wrong result that looks like success. Right, with set -euo pipefail: the same error line, then the script stops, prints no count, and ends with exit status 1. Below, three cases strict mode still gets wrong. grep -c with no match exits 1, so a strict script stops although nothing is wrong. gunzip piped into head -n 1 on a real FASTQ file ends with status 141, and the script stops although nothing is wrong. seqkit stats on a truncated file prints an error but exits 0, so the script does not stop and a real problem is missed.
  
  
  WITHOUT STRICT MODE
  
    $ ./count.sh missing.fastq.gz
    gzip: missing.fastq.gz:
      No such file or directory
    missing.fastq.gz: 0 reads
    done
    exit status 0
  
  a wrong count, reported as success
  
  
  WITH set -euo pipefail
  
    $ ./count.sh missing.fastq.gz
    gzip: missing.fastq.gz:
      No such file or directory
    exit status 1
  
  
  the script stops here: no count, no "done"
  the failure is visible
  
  WHAT STRICT MODE STILL GETS WRONG
  
    command
    status
    strict mode
  
  
  n=$(grep -c ZZZ file)
  1 (no match)
  stops, though nothing is wrong
  
  gunzip -c SRR…_1.fastq.gz | head -n 1
  141
  stops, though nothing is wrong
  
  seqkit stats -T trunc.fastq.gz
  0 ([ERRO] printed)
  does not stop: real problem missed




Figure 8.3: The same script run on a missing file, without and with set -euo pipefail. Without it, bash goes on past the error and reports a wrong count with exit status 0; with it, the script stops at the failure with exit status 1 and no result. The strips below show what strict mode gets wrong: it stops on a grep that simply found nothing, and on head closing a pipe, and it cannot see a tool that reports success on bad input.



Now name each letter. set changes how bash behaves for the rest of the script. The three settings are independent, and each has its own demonstration (all are small scripts you can make the same way as count.sh).

-e: stop when a command fails. A command “fails” when its exit status is not 0 (Chapter 4). By default bash just moves on to the next line, which is Chapter 1’s pitfall.
-u: an unset variable is an error, not an empty value. This is Section 8.3’s misspelled $outdri, which silently became empty and turned "$outdri/" into /. With set -u:


typo.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
outdir=~/bioinf-computing-ch08/out
echo "would delete: $outdri/"

./typo.sh: line 4: outdri: unbound variable
The script stops (exit status 1) and names the misspelled variable.
-o pipefail: a pipeline fails if any command in it fails. Without it, a pipeline’s exit status is that of its last command. In gunzip -c missing.gz | wc -l, gunzip fails but wc succeeds, so the whole line “succeeds”, and -e alone has nothing to stop on:


pipe.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
lines=$(gunzip -c missing.gz | wc -l)
echo "lines=$lines"
echo "still running"

gzip: missing.gz: No such file or directory
lines=0
still running
Exit status 0. Change the second line to set -eo pipefail and the script stops after the gzip error, with exit status 1. This is the pipefail that Chapter 6 promised. To see each command’s status yourself, bash keeps them in a list, PIPESTATUS, right after a pipeline: gunzip -c missing.gz | wc -l; echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}" prints the count (0) and then 1 0, one status per command.

Then what it does not catch. Strict mode is the book’s rule for every script, but it reacts only to exit statuses, and only in some places. Five things to know, each captured from a real run:
1. A “failure” that is not one. grep exits with 1 when it finds no match (Chapter 6). In a strict script, that stops everything, silently:


grep1.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
n=$(grep -c ZZZ names.txt)
echo "n=$n"

With a names.txt that does not contain ZZZ, this prints nothing and exits with 1. The tempting fix is n=$(grep -c ZZZ names.txt || true): “if it fails, succeed anyway”. It does print n=0. But grep has a second failure status, 2, for a real error such as a missing or unreadable file, and || true swallows that too. With a misspelled file name:
grep: missing.txt: No such file or directory
n=
Exit status 0, and n is empty. The script carries on with no number, which is exactly what strict mode was meant to prevent. Keep the two statuses apart instead:


grep2.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
file=names.txt
1if n=$(grep -c ZZZ "$file"); then
2  :
else
3  status=$?
4  [[ "$status" -eq 1 ]] || exit "$status"
fi
echo "n=$n"


1

A command inside an if does not trigger -e; the if looks at its status instead.

2

: is a command that does nothing and succeeds: here, “a match was found, carry on”.

3

$? is grep’s status; save it before running anything else.

4

Status 1 (no match) is fine; anything else (2, an error) ends the script with that status.


With names.txt it prints n=0 and exits 0. With file=missing.txt it prints grep’s error and exits with 2. When you only need a yes or no, if grep -q ZZZ "$file"; then … is enough, but it treats a missing file as “no”, so check that the file is readable first ([[ -r "$file" ]], Section 8.5).
2. head closing a pipe early. In a strict script, try the Chapter 1 idiom for a first look at a file, on the project’s real reads:


peek.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 1
echo "reached"

It prints the first header line and then stops, without reached, with exit status 141: in all six runs captured on Linux for this book. head read its one line and exited; gunzip, still writing, was stopped by the system (Chapter 6’s 141); and pipefail reported that as a failure. seq 1 1000000 | head -n 1 does the same. On a tiny input, such as the practice folder’s two-read file, the same lines print reached and exit 0, because gunzip finished before head exited. It is a matter of timing, not a guarantee either way, so a script tested on toy data can fail on real data. Keep | head for looking at files in the terminal, not inside strict scripts. (… | head -n 1 || true would also hide a real decompression error, so it is not the fix.)
3. Commands that are being tested. Commands tested by if and while never trigger -e: their status is the test. That includes everything inside a function called from an if:


func.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
f() { false; echo "after false in f"; }
if f; then echo ok; fi

after false in f
ok
In a chain with && or ||, only the commands before the last are exempt. false && echo skipped does not stop a strict script (the false is being tested); true && false does, with exit status 1 (the last false is not tested by anything).
4. Masked statuses. local x=$(false) inside a function, and export x=$(false), succeed: the status that -e sees is that of local or export, which worked, not that of the command inside. Declare and assign on separate lines (local x, then x=$(…)), and the failure stops the script again.
5. Tools that report success despite a problem. This is Chapter 4’s finding, now inside a strict script. Give Chapter 3’s script a truncated read file, with a checksum list made after the truncation (the mistake of making checksums from a damaged copy):
checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: OK
command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz
[ERRO] data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: unexpected EOF
[ERRO]
output:   db1d8098fba21ca3be9934a6cc0dde37  results/read_counts.tsv
finished: 2026-11-22 15:45:39 -0600
seqkit 2.14.0 prints [ERRO] but exits 0, so strict mode sees nothing wrong. The script finishes with exit status 0, and results/read_counts.tsv holds only the header line. In the same way, a gzip file that is valid but holds no reads gives 0 reads and passes both strict mode and gzip -t.
Strict mode only sees exit statuses. The remedy is to check what you expect: a results file with more than a header line, a read count above zero (or equal to the expected one), gzip -t before counting (it catches a damaged stream, not a valid but empty one), and md5sum -c against checksums made from the source (Chapter 3). Section 8.9 adds the first of these to Chapter 3’s script. Table 8.6 sums up the section.



Table 8.6: What set -euo pipefail catches, and what it does not.











Setting or case
Stops the script when
Does not catch
What to do




-e
a command exits nonzero
commands tested by if, while, or before the last &&/\|\|
nothing: by design


-u
an unset variable is used ($outdri)
a variable set to the wrong value
preview with echo


-o pipefail
any command in a pipeline fails
which command failed (see PIPESTATUS)
read the first error message


grep with no match
always (exit 1), although nothing is wrong
—
if n=$(grep …); accept 1, exit on 2; never a blanket \|\| true


… \| head
often on real data (exit 141), rarely on toy data
—
keep head in the terminal


function called from if
—
failures inside the function
do not call work functions from if


local x=$(cmd)
—
cmd failing
local x, then x=$(cmd)


tool reports success on bad input
—
wrong or empty results
check outputs: counts, line numbers, md5sum -c












ImportantKey idea



set -euo pipefail stops a script when a command reports failure. It cannot see a wrong result from a command that reports success, so check the outputs too. Every script in this book starts with it: a seatbelt, not a guarantee.








CautionMisconception: “With set -euo pipefail my script stops on every error”



Reality. It stops on a nonzero exit status, except in conditions, functions called from conditions, all but the last command of an &&/|| chain, and masked assignments such as local x=$(…). It cannot see a tool that reports success on bad input, and it can stop on harmless statuses (grep with no match, head closing a pipe).



Check yourself. Which of these stops a script that starts with set -euo pipefail? (a) grep -c XYZ file with no match; (b) seqkit stats (2.14.0) on a truncated file; (c) gunzip -c missing.gz | wc -l.






TipAnswer






Yes, with exit status 1, although nothing is wrong: put it in an if, accept status 1, and keep status 2 (a real error) fatal, not a blanket || true. (b) No: seqkit prints [ERRO] but exits 0. (c) Yes, thanks to pipefail; with -e alone it would not.





Exercise 1, part B and exercise 2 (Section 8.14) are available from here.

title: 8  Shell scripts
text:
8.8 Logging output and errors
Your finished count_reads.sh from exercise 1 prints one tab-separated line per file. Run it with the two output streams of Chapter 6 sent to two different files: results (stdout) to counts.tsv, messages (stderr) to run.log.


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh */*_R1.f*q.gz > ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/counts.tsv 2> ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/run.log
echo "exit $?"
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/counts.tsv
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/run.log

exit 0
sample_C_R1.fq.gz   4
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz    2
sample_B_R1.fastq.gz    3
The table is clean, and the log is empty. Now give it one good file and one missing one, with the same redirections:


Terminal (laptop)

~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz missing.fastq.gz > ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/counts.tsv 2> ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/run.log
echo "exit $?"
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/counts.tsv
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/run.log

exit 1
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz    2
gzip: missing.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
The error went to the log, not into the table, and the script stopped with exit status 1. Notice the table: it holds the line for the file that worked. A table can look fine and still be incomplete; the exit status and the log are what tell you the run failed.
Now name it. Results go to stdout; messages (progress, warnings, errors, the usage line) go to stderr, in every script you write. Then > results.tsv captures only results, and the messages still reach your screen or a log.
A message to stderr is echo "…" >&2. For a script with several messages, define two short functions once, near the top. A function is a named group of commands (Chapter 7); this is the book’s first use of one:


part of a script

log() { printf '[%s] %s\n' "$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')" "$*" >&2; }
die() { log "ERROR: $*"; exit 1; }

log "counting reads" prints [2026-11-22 14:26:50] counting reads to stderr; die "missing input" logs ERROR: missing input and ends the script with status 1. Inside a function, $* is all its arguments joined into one string: the one place this book joins arguments on purpose. A function must be defined before the line that uses it. Writing your own reusable functions is Chapter 34.
Keeping a log of a whole run. Chapter 3’s script keeps everything it prints in a log file, with this form:


part of a script

log="$(mktemp "logs/01_count_reads_$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M%S)_XXXX.log")"
{
  …the commands…
} 2>&1 | tee "$log"

The { … } group collects the output of all its commands; 2>&1 joins stderr to stdout; tee shows that stream on the screen and writes it to the log. The log name holds the date and time in the ISO form of Chapter 3, and mktemp replaces XXXX with random characters and creates the file, so two runs in the same second never share a log. (This needs GNU mktemp, which fills in X’s that come before a suffix such as .log. The Mac’s own /usr/bin/mktemp only replaces X’s at the very end, so without Chapter 1’s GNU tools the log is literally named …_XXXX.log every run.) Section 8.9 takes this form apart line by line.
Write to a temporary name, then mv. Chapter 6 showed that > empties a file before the command starts, so a failed command can leave a half-written result under the real name. Scripts in this book write each output to name.tmp and move it into place only when the step has succeeded:


part of a script

seqkit stats --quiet -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz > results/read_counts.tsv.tmp
mv results/read_counts.tsv.tmp results/read_counts.tsv

With set -e, a failure stops the script before mv, so a new result is published only after the step succeeds, and a good result from an earlier run is never replaced by a partial one. What this does not do: after a failed rerun, the earlier run’s finished file is still there, and the half-written .tmp may be there too. So the rule is: publish a new result only after the step succeeds; on failure, an older result may still exist, so use the run’s exit status and log to decide whether a result belongs to this run. Section 8.10 shows this on a real rerun. One assumption is built in: a fixed name.tmp is fine while one run at a time writes that output, as in this book’s pipeline. Two runs at once would share the .tmp (unique log names do not help with that), which needs unique temporary names and more care than this chapter covers.
What to log. Chapter 3’s list of what makes a result traceable: start and end time, machine, tool versions, input checksums, the exact command, and the output’s checksum. To see every command as bash runs it, there is bash -x (Section 8.11). Table 8.7 collects the recipes.



Table 8.7: Recipes for output and logs.









Goal
Recipe




Results to a file, messages to a log
script.sh > results.tsv 2> run.log


A message to stderr
echo "…" >&2, or a log function as above


Everything to the screen and a log
{ …; } 2>&1 \| tee "$log" inside a script that has set -o pipefail, as in 01 and run_all.sh


A dated log name that no other run shares
mktemp "logs/name_$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M%S)_XXXX.log" (GNU mktemp)


Publish a result only on success
write name.tmp, then mv name.tmp name (one run at a time)












TipTip



Write each output to name.tmp, then mv it into place, so a new result is published only after the step succeeds. On failure an older result may still exist: the exit status and the log say whether it belongs to this run.



Check yourself. Why does count_reads.sh print its usage message with >&2? And after the run above with the missing file, what should you trust: counts.tsv, or the exit status?






TipAnswer





So the message goes to stderr: with > counts.tsv, it stays on the screen and the file holds only results. And the exit status (1): the table looks fine but lacks the missing file’s line.

title: 8  Shell scripts
section: 8.9 Reading Chapter 3’s script, line by line
text:
8.9 Reading Chapter 3’s script, line by line
Chapter 3 asked you to run src/01_count_reads.sh on trust and promised that this chapter would explain every line. You now know every piece. Look at it again:


Terminal (laptop)

cat ~/bioinf-computing/src/01_count_reads.sh

Before reading on, write in NOTEBOOK.md, in your own words, what each line does. Use Figure 8.1 as the map of its parts. Then compare with the annotations below (click a number to see its note).


src/01_count_reads.sh

1#!/usr/bin/env bash
2# 01_count_reads.sh: check the raw FASTQ files, then count their reads.
# Run from the project folder:  pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh
3set -euo pipefail

4mkdir -p results logs
5log="$(mktemp "logs/01_count_reads_$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M%S)_XXXX.log")"

6{
7  echo "started:  $(date "+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z")"
  echo "host:     $(hostname)"
8  echo "script:   $(md5sum src/01_count_reads.sh)"
9  echo "seqkit:   $(seqkit version)"
  echo "checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:"
10  (cd data/raw && md5sum -c checksums.md5)
11  echo "command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz"
12  seqkit stats --quiet -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz > results/read_counts.tsv.tmp
13  mv results/read_counts.tsv.tmp results/read_counts.tsv
14  echo "output:   $(md5sum results/read_counts.tsv)"
15  echo "finished: $(date "+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z")"
16} 2>&1 | tee "$log"


1

The shebang: run this file with the bash found on PATH (Chapter 7).

2

The header comment: what the script does, and how and from where to run it. Comments start with # and are ignored.

3

Strict mode (Section 8.7): stop on any failure, any unset variable, any failing command in a pipeline.

4

Make the output folders; -p means no error if they already exist.

5

Nested substitutions, run inside out: date makes a time stamp, mktemp turns the name into a new, unique file, and $( ) stores its name in log (Section 8.8).

6

Start of a group: everything up to the closing } sends its output into one pipe (line 16).

7

$( ) puts the current date and time into the line.

8

The script’s own checksum: if anyone edits the script, this line in the log changes.

9

The tool’s version, for the record.

10

A subshell in parentheses: the cd happens in a separate copy of the shell, so the next line still runs from the project folder. && runs md5sum -c only if the cd worked. If a checksum fails, md5sum exits 1 and strict mode stops the script here.

11

The exact command, written to the log.

12

The real work, written to a temporary name.

13

Published under its real name only after the step succeeded.

14

The result’s checksum, for the record.

15

A log with no finished: line means the run did not finish.

16

2>&1 joins error messages to the normal output; tee shows both on the screen and writes them to the log.


Then break it on purpose. Never in data/raw/, which stays read-only (Chapter 3). Copy the inputs, their checksums, and the script to a scratch folder, make the copied reads writable, and append one byte to one of them:


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/proj-copy/data/raw ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/proj-copy/src
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/proj-copy
cp ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/*.fastq.gz ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/checksums.md5 data/raw/
cp ~/bioinf-computing/src/01_count_reads.sh src/
chmod u+w data/raw/*
printf 'x' >> data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
pixi run --manifest-path ~/bioinf-computing/pixi.toml bash src/01_count_reads.sh; echo "exit $?"
ls -A results

(--manifest-path tells pixi to use the project’s environment while you work in another folder.)
started:  2026-11-22 15:45:39 -0600
host:     your-laptop
script:   76fa8eb6a7b90f212042cfbe6d95cfcc  src/01_count_reads.sh
seqkit:   seqkit v2.14.0
checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: FAILED
md5sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match
exit 1
The script stopped at the checksum, exit status 1. results/ is empty: no read_counts.tsv and no .tmp. The log in logs/ keeps the failure. Why does it stop, when the failing command sits inside a group whose output goes through a pipe to tee? The group runs in a subshell that inherits set -e, so the subshell stops and exits 1; pipefail then makes the whole pipeline fail despite tee’s success, and -e stops the script. Remove pipefail (change line 4 to set -eu) and rerun: the same FAILED lines print, but the script exits 0, because without pipefail the pipeline’s status is tee’s.
Run it from the wrong folder. The script uses paths relative to the project folder. Run it from your home folder instead:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~ && pixi run --manifest-path ~/bioinf-computing/pixi.toml bash bioinf-computing/src/01_count_reads.sh; echo "exit $?"

started:  2026-11-22 15:45:49 -0600
host:     your-laptop
md5sum: src/01_count_reads.sh: No such file or directory
script:
seqkit:   seqkit v2.14.0
checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:
bioinf-computing/src/01_count_reads.sh: line 15: cd: data/raw: No such file or directory
exit 1
It failed, but only at line 15, and it has already made empty results/ and logs/ folders, plus a log file, in your home folder. The md5sum failure on the script: line did not stop it either: a command inside echo "…$(…)" is one more case set -e does not see. Look with ls ~/results ~/logs; if they hold only this run’s leftovers, remove them (rmdir ~/results and rm -r ~/logs).
Add a guard. Open the real script, code ~/bioinf-computing/src/01_count_reads.sh, and add one line right after set -euo pipefail:


src/01_count_reads.sh (new line 5)

[[ -f pixi.toml ]] || { echo "run from the project folder" >&2; exit 1; }

From ~, the script now stops at once with run from the project folder and exit status 1, and leaves nothing behind. The guard checks for a file that only the project folder has, so it catches the common mistake of running from the wrong folder; it does not prove that this is the right project. (To repeat the broken-copy test above with the guarded script, copy ~/bioinf-computing/pixi.toml into proj-copy/ first, or it stops at the guard instead of the checksum.)
Add a result check. Section 8.7 showed this very script finishing with exit status 0 and a read_counts.tsv holding only its header line, because seqkit reported a damaged file but exited 0. Strict mode cannot see that; a check of the result can. This project always has two FASTQ files, so a good table has a header and two rows. Add two lines right after the seqkit stats line, before the mv:


src/01_count_reads.sh (after the seqkit line)

  [[ $(wc -l < results/read_counts.tsv.tmp) -eq 3 ]] ||
    { echo "read_counts: expected a header and 2 rows" >&2; exit 1; }

The number 3 belongs to this two-file project; a general script would work out the expected number from its list of inputs. Rerun the damaged-file case from Section 8.7 (a truncated R2 with checksums made after the damage, in a copy) and the script now stops:
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: OK
command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz
[ERRO] data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: unexpected EOF
read_counts: expected a header and 2 rows
The exit status is 1, the mv never runs, and the previous good read_counts.tsv stays as it was (the half-made .tmp is left beside it). On the real files nothing changes: the same table, the same output checksum. Your next run’s log shows a new script checksum (f2857591… instead of 76fa8eb6…): that is exactly what the script: line is for. You commit both changes in Section 8.12.






ImportantKey idea



A failed step should stop the run, leave a log that says why, and publish no new result.



Check yourself. In the script, why is (cd data/raw && md5sum -c checksums.md5) in parentheses?






TipAnswer





The parentheses make a subshell: the cd happens there and ends with it, so the next line still runs from the project folder, where data/raw/*.fastq.gz and results/ are.

title: 8  Shell scripts
section: 8.10 Numbered scripts as a simple pipeline
text:
8.10 Numbered scripts as a simple pipeline
Chapter 3 named scripts by their run order: 01_, 02_, and so on. Now add the second step. It is Section 8.2’s gtf_types.sh, the GTF feature count from Chapter 6, made into a project script. In ~/bioinf-computing, open code src/02_gtf_summary.sh, paste, and save:


src/02_gtf_summary.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# 02_gtf_summary.sh: count the feature types in the reference annotation.
# Run from the project folder:  pixi run bash src/02_gtf_summary.sh
# Input:  data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
# Output: results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv (feature, count; most common first)
set -euo pipefail

1log() { printf '[%s] %s\n' "$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')" "$*" >&2; }
die() { log "ERROR: $*"; exit 1; }

2[[ -f pixi.toml ]] || die "run from the project folder"

gtf="data/ref/genes.gtf.gz"
out="results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv"
3[[ -s "$gtf" ]] || die "missing or empty: $gtf"

mkdir -p results
log "start; input md5: $(md5sum "$gtf")"
{
4  printf 'feature\tcount\n'
  gunzip -c "$gtf" | cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr \
5    | awk -v OFS='\t' '{print $2, $1}'
} > "$out.tmp"
6mv "$out.tmp" "$out"
7log "wrote $out ($(( $(wc -l < "$out") - 1 )) feature types)"
log "output md5: $(md5sum "$out")"


1

The log and die functions from Section 8.8.

2

The guard from Section 8.9, using die.

3

Check the input exists and is not empty (-s) before starting.

4

A header line for the table.

5

Chapter 6’s count, then awk swaps the two columns and separates them with a tab (-v OFS='\t', also Chapter 6).

6

Published only after the step succeeded.

7

Lines in the file minus the header: the number of feature types.


02 is deliberately shorter than 01: its log lines go to the screen (stderr), it keeps no log file of its own, and it records input and output checksums but not tool versions (recording versions properly is Chapter 23). The log file for the whole run comes from the next script, src/run_all.sh, which runs every step in order and keeps one log of all of them, with exactly 01’s form:


src/run_all.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# run_all.sh: run every numbered step in order; stop at the first failure.
# Run from the project folder:  pixi run bash src/run_all.sh
# Log: logs/run_all_<date>_XXXX.log (01 also keeps its own log)
set -euo pipefail
[[ -f pixi.toml ]] || { echo "run from the project folder" >&2; exit 1; }
mkdir -p logs
log="$(mktemp "logs/run_all_$(date +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M%S)_XXXX.log")"
{
  bash src/01_count_reads.sh
  bash src/02_gtf_summary.sh
} 2>&1 | tee "$log"

Because pipefail is set inside the script, a failing step makes run_all.sh fail, despite tee. (A | tee typed in the terminal around run_all.sh would not have pipefail, and would bring back the problem you saw in Section 8.9.) Run the pipeline:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing
pixi run bash src/run_all.sh; echo "exit $?"
cat results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv

started:  2026-11-22 14:26:49 -0600
host:     your-laptop
script:   f28575917774e7916b14362989eeed68  src/01_count_reads.sh
seqkit:   seqkit v2.14.0
checking inputs against data/raw/checksums.md5:
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz: OK
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz: OK
command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz
output:   e1d81de77934f7ab7b44bf72b7520b32  results/read_counts.tsv
finished: 2026-11-22 14:26:50 -0600
[2026-11-22 14:26:50] start; input md5: 504334f6741ee771c665ae845429087f  data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
[2026-11-22 14:26:50] wrote results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv (5 feature types)
[2026-11-22 14:26:50] output md5: 3b9c2b4c499d85a7e70aaf3faaef3c99  results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv
exit 0
feature count
exon    129
transcript  124
CDS 118
start_codon 115
stop_codon  114
The five counts are Chapter 6’s, now as a two-column table that other programs can read. ls logs shows two new logs, one from 01 and one from run_all.sh holding the whole run. Run from ~, 02_gtf_summary.sh stops with ERROR: run from the project folder, exit status 1.
A failed rerun. Section 8.8 promised that a failed step publishes no new result, but that an older one may still be there. See it in the scratch copy: give it 02, the GTF, and the project’s pixi.toml, run 02 once, then swap in a damaged GTF (cut to its first 5,000 bytes, on a copy, as in Chapter 4) and run it again.


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/proj-copy
mkdir -p data/ref
cp ~/bioinf-computing/pixi.toml .
cp ~/bioinf-computing/src/02_gtf_summary.sh src/
cp ~/bioinf-computing/data/ref/genes.gtf.gz data/ref/
bash src/02_gtf_summary.sh; echo "first run exit $?"
md5sum results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv
head -c 5000 ~/bioinf-computing/data/ref/genes.gtf.gz > data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
bash src/02_gtf_summary.sh; echo "rerun exit $?"
md5sum results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv
ls results
cat results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv.tmp

(cp follows the data/ref link of Chapter 3 and copies the file itself.)
[2026-11-22 14:44:15] start; input md5: 504334f6741ee771c665ae845429087f  data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
[2026-11-22 14:44:15] wrote results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv (5 feature types)
[2026-11-22 14:44:15] output md5: 3b9c2b4c499d85a7e70aaf3faaef3c99  results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv
first run exit 0
3b9c2b4c499d85a7e70aaf3faaef3c99  results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv
[2026-11-22 14:44:17] start; input md5: 7e4688760800a9e5632424a6f67a00ae  data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
gunzip: data/ref/genes.gtf.gz: unexpected end of file
gunzip: data/ref/genes.gtf.gz: uncompress failed
rerun exit 1
3b9c2b4c499d85a7e70aaf3faaef3c99  results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv
gtf_feature_counts.tsv  gtf_feature_counts.tsv.tmp
feature count
CDS 39
exon    39
start_codon 39
stop_codon  38
transcript  38
(Captured on a Mac; GNU gzip says gzip: data/ref/genes.gtf.gz: unexpected end of file.) The rerun logged a different input checksum, failed with exit status 1, and wrote no wrote … line. The old result is untouched: same checksum. And the leftover .tmp holds counts that look like a real result. Had the step written straight to the final name, that partial table would now be gtf_feature_counts.tsv. The file on disk is the last good result, not this run’s; the exit status and the log say which run you are looking at.
Now name it. A numbered pipeline is a set of scripts with three habits (Figure 8.4):

Each step reads only raw inputs or earlier steps’ results, and writes only its own outputs.
Each step can be rerun safely: it overwrites its own result, never an input (assuming one run at a time).
The number is the order; the name says what the step does (Chapter 3’s naming rule).

run_all.sh lists the steps by name, not with a pattern such as for s in src/[0-9]*.sh, so a stray 03_old_try.sh never runs by accident. The pattern version is shorter, and some people prefer it; listing by name means you must add each new step to run_all.sh yourself.




  The project's numbered scripts as a small pipeline. run_all.sh, at the top, runs each step in order and stops at the first failure. Step 01_count_reads.sh reads data/raw/*.fastq.gz, checks it with md5sum -c, and writes results/read_counts.tsv. Then step 02_gtf_summary.sh reads the reference annotation data/ref/genes.gtf.gz and writes results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv; if step 01 fails, step 02 never runs. 01 writes its own log into logs/, and run_all.sh writes a log of the whole run there, which also holds 02's messages. On the right, a faint box lists what a workflow manager (Part VI) adds: it skips steps whose inputs have not changed, runs independent steps in parallel, and resumes after a failure.
  
    
      
    
  
  
  
  logs/
  a log for each run
  
  
  run_all.sh
  runs the steps in order
  
  
  
  
  
  data/raw/
  *.fastq.gz
  
  
  01_count_reads.sh
  
  md5sum -c
  
  
  results/
  read_counts.tsv
  
  
  
  
  then
  
  
  stops here if 01 fails
  
  
  data/ref/
  genes.gtf.gz
  
  
  02_gtf_summary.sh
  counts feature types
  
  
  results/
  gtf_feature_counts.tsv
  02's messages go into run_all.sh's log; each step writes only its own result and never changes an input.
  
  
  PART VI
  
    a workflow manager
    also:
    · skips unchanged
    steps
    · runs steps in
    parallel
    · resumes after
    a failure
  




Figure 8.4: The project’s numbered pipeline. run_all.sh calls 01_count_reads.sh (reads in, read counts out, after a checksum check) and then 02_gtf_summary.sh (annotation in, feature counts out), stopping at the first failure; 01 and run_all.sh write logs. On the right, what a workflow manager adds.



Its limits are why Part VI exists. A numbered pipeline reruns every step even when nothing changed; runs one step at a time, even when two steps could run side by side; cannot resume after a failure from where it stopped; and does not know which result came from which version of its inputs. Workflow managers (Chapter 25) solve these, as does the older make (see the GNU make manual); nf-core (Chapter 26) is the one you will use. Running each step as a cluster job is Chapter 10.

Check yourself. You add 03_plot.sh to src/ but forget to list it in run_all.sh. What happens when you run the pipeline?






TipAnswer





It never runs, and nothing warns you. Listing steps by name is deliberate, so check run_all.sh whenever you add a step.

title: 8  Shell scripts
text:
8.11 When a script misbehaves
Two tools find most bugs in short scripts: bash -x, which shows each command as bash runs it, and ShellCheck, which reads a script without running it. Save this script, which has two bugs from earlier sections, as ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/broken.sh:


broken.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# broken.sh: count the reads in each R1 file and save the counts.
outdir=~/bioinf-computing-ch08/out
mkdir -p "$outdir"
for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz; do
  n=$(gunzip -c $f | wc -l)
  echo "$f $(( n / 4 ))" >> "$outdri/counts.txt"
done

Run it from the practice folder with bash -x:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
bash -x ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/broken.sh

+ outdir=/home/you/bioinf-computing-ch08/out
+ mkdir -p /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch08/out
+ for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz
++ gunzip -c Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
++ wc -l
+ n=0
+ echo 'Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz 0'
/home/you/bioinf-computing-ch08/broken.sh: line 7: /counts.txt: Permission denied
+ for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz
++ gunzip -c run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
++ wc -l
+ n=8
+ echo 'run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz 2'
/home/you/bioinf-computing-ch08/broken.sh: line 7: /counts.txt: Permission denied
…
(gunzip’s three error lines after ++ wc -l are left out here.) Each line starting with + is a command after bash has expanded it; ++ marks a command inside $( ). Both bugs are visible. gunzip -c Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz shows the unquoted $f split into three words (Figure 8.2), so sample C counts 0. And "$outdri/counts.txt" became /counts.txt: the misspelled variable is empty, and the write fails only because an ordinary user may not write to /. (On a Mac the message says Read-only file system instead.) set -x at the top of a script does the same as bash -x, from that line on.
Now ask ShellCheck, which is in the book environment:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08
pixi run --manifest-path ~/bioinf-computing/pixi.toml shellcheck broken.sh

In broken.sh line 6:
  n=$(gunzip -c $f | wc -l)
                ^-- SC2086 (info): Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting.

Did you mean:
  n=$(gunzip -c "$f" | wc -l)


In broken.sh line 7:
  echo "$f $(( n / 4 ))" >> "$outdri/counts.txt"
                             ^-----^ SC2154 (warning): outdri is referenced but not assigned.

For more information:
  https://www.shellcheck.net/wiki/SC2154 -- outdri is referenced but not assi...
  https://www.shellcheck.net/wiki/SC2086 -- Double quote to prevent globbing ...
Both bugs are named, with line numbers, before the script ever runs; ShellCheck exits with status 1 when it finds something. Each code (SC2086) has a page on the ShellCheck wiki that explains why.
If pixi says shellcheck is not found, you set up the book environment before ShellCheck joined it. Download the current environment files into the project and install them, as in Chapter 2:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing
curl -fLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/austin-putz/book-bioinf-computing/main/setup/pixi.toml
curl -fLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/austin-putz/book-bioinf-computing/main/setup/pixi.lock
pixi install --locked
pixi run shellcheck --version

The last line should print a version, 0.11.0 or later.
Two more things, one sentence each. The ShellCheck extension for VS Code underlines the same problems as you type: search the Extensions view for its ID, timonwong.shellcheck; it needs no further setup, and hovering over the underlined $f shows the same SC2086 message. And the Mac’s own /bin/bash is version 3.2, which lacks features such as mapfile, declare -A, and ${x,,} (mapfile: command not found): #!/usr/bin/env bash, with Chapter 1’s current bash, avoids it. Debuggers, tests, and linting in depth are Chapter 34.






TipTip



Run ShellCheck on every script before you trust it, and keep the VS Code extension on while you write.



Check yourself. ShellCheck says SC2086: Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting on gunzip -c $f. Which rule of this chapter is it, and what is the fix?






TipAnswer





Quote every expansion (Section 8.3): gunzip -c "$f", so a name with spaces stays one argument.

title: 8  Shell scripts
text:
8.12 Saving scripts with git
Your project now has three scripts that work. Before you change them again, save this working state so you can always get it back. git keeps a history of your files; this section uses a five-command routine, and Chapter 21 teaches git properly, starting from this repository.
One-time setup. Check that git is installed. On a Mac it came with the Xcode Command Line Tools that Homebrew installed in Chapter 1; Ubuntu, WSL, and clusters have it already:


Terminal (laptop)

git --version

git version 2.50.1 (Apple Git-155)
You need git 2.28 or later for the setup shown here (git restore itself needs 2.23, and the init.defaultBranch setting below arrived in 2.28); every system checked for this book had a newer one. Then tell git your name and email (they are stored in each commit) and the name for the first branch, before making a repository:


Terminal (laptop)

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.org"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

Without the last line, git init prints several lines of hint: about the default branch name, worded differently in different git versions. They are harmless; the setting just makes the name main and stops the hint.
Tell git what not to save. In ~/bioinf-computing, make a file .gitignore (code .gitignore), paste, and save:


.gitignore

data/
results/
logs/
.pixi/

Each line is a folder git will ignore: data/ because the raw data are large, read-only, and backed up elsewhere (Chapter 3); results/ and logs/ because the scripts rebuild them; .pixi/ because pixi install --locked rebuilds the environment from pixi.lock. Chapter 21 covers .gitignore rules in full.
The routine. Make the project a repository, look, add, commit, and look at the history:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing
git init
git status --short
git add .gitignore src/ README.md NOTEBOOK.md pixi.toml pixi.lock
git status --short
git commit -m "Add read-count and GTF summary scripts"
git log --oneline

Initialized empty Git repository in /home/you/bioinf-computing/.git/
?? .gitignore
?? NOTEBOOK.md
?? README.md
?? pixi.lock
?? pixi.toml
?? src/
A  .gitignore
A  NOTEBOOK.md
A  README.md
A  pixi.lock
A  pixi.toml
A  src/01_count_reads.sh
A  src/02_gtf_summary.sh
A  src/run_all.sh
[main (root-commit) 447c010] Add read-count and GTF summary scripts
 8 files changed, 4605 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
 …
447c010 Add read-count and GTF summary scripts
(Your commit IDs, such as 447c010, will differ, and git status may list other files you made, such as notes.txt.) ?? means “not yet tracked”; A means “added, ready to commit”. data/, results/, logs/, and .pixi/ never appear: .gitignore works.
Break it. Make a mistake on purpose, comment out the strict-mode line, and see what git shows:


Terminal (laptop)

sed -i 's/^set -euo pipefail$/# set -euo pipefail/' src/01_count_reads.sh
git status --short
git diff

 M src/01_count_reads.sh
diff --git a/src/01_count_reads.sh b/src/01_count_reads.sh
index 5b963b8..05e986d 100644
--- a/src/01_count_reads.sh
+++ b/src/01_count_reads.sh
@@ -1,7 +1,7 @@
 #!/usr/bin/env bash
 # 01_count_reads.sh: check the raw FASTQ files, then count their reads.
 # Run from the project folder:  pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh
-set -euo pipefail
+# set -euo pipefail
 [[ -f pixi.toml ]] || { echo "run from the project folder" >&2; exit 1; }

 mkdir -p results logs
M means “modified since the last commit”. git diff shows the change: - for the old line, + for the new one. Read the diff before you throw anything away. Then bring the file back:


Terminal (laptop)

git restore src/01_count_reads.sh
git status --short

git status --short now prints nothing: the file is as it was. Strictly, git restore file copies the staged version of the file (the one your last git add recorded), which here is the same as the last commit because nothing was staged since; Chapter 21 explains the staging area.
Get back an older version. Make a small second change and commit it, so there are two commits. For example, in src/02_gtf_summary.sh change the # Output: comment to read (two columns: feature, count; most common first), then:


Terminal (laptop)

git add src/02_gtf_summary.sh
git commit -m "Describe the output columns of 02"
git log --oneline
git show --stat HEAD

[main 71bad40] Describe the output columns of 02
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
71bad40 Describe the output columns of 02
447c010 Add read-count and GTF summary scripts
…
 src/02_gtf_summary.sh | 2 +-
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
git log --oneline shows only the messages; git show --stat HEAD shows which files the latest commit (HEAD) changed. Now suppose the older version was better. HEAD~1 means “one commit before the latest”. Look at the old file, bring it back, check it, and save the recovery as a new commit:


Terminal (laptop)

git show HEAD~1:src/02_gtf_summary.sh | head -n 5
git restore --source=HEAD~1 src/02_gtf_summary.sh
git status --short
pixi run bash src/run_all.sh
git commit -am "Restore the shorter output comment in 02"
git log --oneline

…
# Output: results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv (feature, count; most common first)
 M src/02_gtf_summary.sh
…
947b2e9 Restore the shorter output comment in 02
71bad40 Describe the output columns of 02
447c010 Add read-count and GTF summary scripts
Nothing was lost: the history still holds all three versions (Figure 8.5). git commit -am adds every changed tracked file and commits in one step.




  The minimal git routine. Three places: your files in the working folder, the staged copy that the next commit will save, and the history of commits. Before saving, look with git status and git diff. git add copies a change to the staged copy, and git commit saves the staged files as a new commit in the history; the newest commit is HEAD and the one before it is HEAD~1. Two arrows lead back to your files: git restore file copies the staged version back over your edit (normally the same as the last commit here), and git restore --source=HEAD~1 file brings back the version from an older commit.
  
    
      
    
    
      
    
  
  
  
  Your files
  the working folder
  
  02_gtf_summary.sh
  what you edit
  
  
  Staged
  what the next
  commit will save
  
  
  History
  saved commits, with messages
  
  
  
  HEAD~1
  Add the scripts
  HEAD
  Clearer header in 02
  
  look first:
  git status
  git diff
  
  
  git add
  
  git commit
  
  
  git restore file
  from the staged copy; normally the last commit here
  
  
  git restore --source=HEAD~1 file
  from an older commit




Figure 8.5: The minimal git routine. Your files are changed in the working folder, staged with git add, and saved in the history with git commit. git status and git diff look at what changed. git restore file brings back the staged copy (normally the last commit, here), and git restore --source=HEAD~1 file brings back a file from an older commit.



Now name it. A commit is a saved snapshot of the files you added, with a message saying why. Here git does not save data/ or results/, by design. The habit: commit each time a script works, and before you change it. VS Code shows the same information in its Source Control view. Everything else, such as branches, undoing commits, and remotes, is Chapter 21. Table 8.8 lists the routine.



Table 8.8: The minimal git routine.










When
Command
What it does




Once per computer
git config --global user.name …, user.email …, init.defaultBranch main
who you are; name of the first branch


Once per project
git init
make the folder a repository


Every change
git status --short, git diff
what changed, line by line



git add file, git commit -m "why"
stage the change, save a snapshot


Look back
git log --oneline, git show --stat HEAD, git show HEAD~1:file
the history; files in a commit; an old version


Undo an edit
git restore file
back to the staged copy (normally the last commit)


Bring back an old version
git restore --source=HEAD~1 file
the file as it was one commit ago


Everything else
branches, undoing commits, remotes
Chapter 21












NoteBackground



git stores the files you add, as they were at each commit. It does not store what .gitignore excludes: here, data and results, by design. And a repository on the same disk is not an off-machine backup: if the disk fails, the .git/ folder goes with it. Pushing to another machine is one way to make an independent copy (Chapter 22).



Check yourself. You edited 02_gtf_summary.sh, it broke, and you have not committed or staged the change. How do you get the last working version back?






TipAnswer





Look at the change first with git diff, then git restore src/02_gtf_summary.sh, and check with git status --short. It brings back the staged copy, which is the last commit when nothing was staged.

title: 8  Shell scripts
text:
8.13 Summary

A script is commands saved in a file and run, top to bottom, by a new bash process. Start it with #!/usr/bin/env bash and a header comment that says what it does, how to run it, and what it reads and writes. Relative paths are read from where it is run, so project scripts are run from the project folder.
$name is replaced by its value; unquoted, that value is split at spaces and matched as a wildcard. Put double quotes around every expansion: "$f", "$@", "${sample}_R1.fastq.gz". $( ) captures a command’s output and $(( )) does whole-number arithmetic.
Loop over a glob, never over ls or $(cat file); read table rows with while IFS=$'\t' read -r. Preview a loop with echo before it changes anything, and check that a list of files is not empty.
if tests an exit status; [[ ]] tests files, text, and numbers (< compares text, -lt and (( )) compare numbers). Take file names as arguments with "$@", and stop with a usage message (exit 2) when they are missing. set -euo pipefail stops on a reported failure, an unset variable, or a failed pipe stage; it cannot see a tool that reports success on bad input, so check results too.
Send results to stdout and messages to stderr, and keep a log of each run. Write each output to name.tmp and mv it into place only after the step succeeds. Numbered scripts run in order by run_all.sh make a small pipeline. Commit each script once it works, look with git status and git diff, and bring back an old version with git restore.

A template to start every script from. Delete the lines you do not need; keep set -euo pipefail.


template.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# NAME.sh: what this script does, in one line.
# Run:    bash NAME.sh FILE [MORE ...]   (from the project folder)
# Input:  what it reads
# Output: what it writes (results on stdout or in results/, messages on stderr)
set -euo pipefail
shopt -s nullglob     # only if the script loops over a glob

log() { printf '[%s] %s\n' "$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')" "$*" >&2; }
die() { log "ERROR: $*"; exit 1; }

if [[ $# -lt 1 ]]; then
  echo "usage: NAME.sh FILE [MORE ...]" >&2
  exit 2
fi

out="results/NAME.tsv"
mkdir -p results
log "start"
for f in "$@"; do
  [[ -s "$f" ]] || die "missing or empty: $f"
  printf '%s\t%s\n' "$(basename "$f")" "something about $f"
done > "$out.tmp"
mv "$out.tmp" "$out"
log "wrote $out"

Table 8.9 collects the chapter’s commands.



Table 8.9: The chapter’s commands on one page.









Task
Command




Run a script
bash script.sh, or chmod u+x script.sh then ./script.sh


Variables
name=value (no spaces), "$name", "${name}_R1.fastq.gz"


Capture output, do arithmetic
n=$(wc -l < "$f"), $(( n / 4 ))


Trim a value
${f##*/} (drop folders), ${f%.gz} (drop an ending), basename "$f"


Lists
files=(*.fastq.gz), "${files[@]}", ${#files[@]}


Loops
for f in */*_R1.f*q.gz; do …; done, for i in {01..03}, while IFS=$'\t' read -r a b c; do …; done < table.tsv


Tests
if [[ -s "$f" ]]; then …; fi, [[ "$a" == "$b" ]], (( n > 0 ))


Arguments
"$1", "$@", $#, $0; usage message with >&2 and exit 2


Stop on errors
set -euo pipefail; inspect a pipe with "${PIPESTATUS[@]}"


Logging
> results.tsv 2> run.log, { …; } 2>&1 \| tee "$log", mktemp


Safe output
cmd > "$out.tmp" then mv "$out.tmp" "$out"


Find bugs
bash -x script.sh, pixi run shellcheck script.sh


git routine
git status, git diff, git add, git commit -m "…", git log --oneline, git show --stat HEAD, git restore file, git restore --source=HEAD~1 file

title: 8  Shell scripts
text:
8.14 Exercises
Do exercises 1–3 in ~/bioinf-computing-ch08, reading the practice folder ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/ without changing it. Exercises 4 and 5 change your project, ~/bioinf-computing.

Exercise 1. Finish count_reads.sh. Part A after Section 8.6; part B after Section 8.7.
A labmate’s script counts the reads in each FASTQ file it is given. Save it as ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh (code ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh, paste, save) and make it executable with chmod u+x ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh:


~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count_reads.sh: print each FASTQ file's name and its number of reads.
# Usage: count_reads.sh FILE.fastq.gz [MORE.fastq.gz ...]
for f in $@; do
  n=$(gunzip -c $f | wc -l)
  echo "$f $((n / 4))"
done

Run it from the practice folder on every R1 file, and on a file that does not exist:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh */*_R1*; echo "exit $?"
~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh missing.fastq.gz; echo "exit $?"

Write down what is wrong. Then fix it one change at a time, rerunning after each, and record each change in NOTEBOOK.md.

Part A. Quote "$@" and "$f". Add a usage check that prints usage: count_reads.sh FILE.fastq.gz [MORE.fastq.gz ...] to stderr and exits 2 when there are no arguments. Print the file’s base name and its count separated by a tab. Run it with the tighter pattern */*_R1.f*q.gz.
Part B. Add set -euo pipefail and run the missing file again. What changed, and why?

The goal, from ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share:
$ ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh */*_R1.f*q.gz
sample_C_R1.fq.gz   4
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz    2
sample_B_R1.fastq.gz    3
and two runs that stop with a message and a nonzero status, printing no count: no arguments (exit 2) and a missing file (exit 1).






TipAnswer





The script as supplied (captured on macOS; on Linux, GNU gzip words each error as gzip: Run.gz: No such file or directory):
$ ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh */*_R1*; echo "exit $?"
gunzip: can't stat: Run (Run.gz): No such file or directory
Run 0
gunzip: can't stat: 3 (3.gz): No such file or directory
3 0
gunzip: can't stat: final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz (final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz.gz): No such file or directory
final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz 0
run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz 2
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz 3
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp 3
exit 0
Three faults, and the status says 0 through all of them. The unquoted $@ and $f split Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz into three names (Section 8.3), so sample C counts as 0 three times. The pattern *_R1* also matched the stray .tmp copy, counted as a fourth sample (Section 8.4). The missing file prints an error, then missing.fastq.gz 0, and still exits 0.
The finished script:


~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count_reads.sh: print each FASTQ file's name and its number of reads.
# Usage: count_reads.sh FILE.fastq.gz [MORE.fastq.gz ...]
set -euo pipefail

if [[ $# -lt 1 ]]; then
  echo "usage: count_reads.sh FILE.fastq.gz [MORE.fastq.gz ...]" >&2
  exit 2
fi

for f in "$@"; do
  n=$(gunzip -c "$f" | wc -l)
  printf '%s\t%s\n' "$(basename "$f")" "$((n / 4))"
done

$ ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh */*_R1.f*q.gz; echo "exit $?"
sample_C_R1.fq.gz   4
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz    2
sample_B_R1.fastq.gz    3
exit 0
$ ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh; echo "exit $?"
usage: count_reads.sh FILE.fastq.gz [MORE.fastq.gz ...]
exit 2
$ ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/count_reads.sh missing.fastq.gz; echo "exit $?"
gzip: missing.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
exit 1
After part A alone the missing file still printed missing.fastq.gz, a tab, and 0, with exit 0: quoting and the usage check do not stop a failed gunzip. Part B’s set -euo pipefail does. pipefail makes the gunzip | wc -l pipeline fail when gunzip fails, and -e stops the script at that line, before it prints a count. (On a Mac, Apple gzip words the error gunzip: can't stat: missing.fastq.gz ….)
The order of the three lines comes from bash’s sort of the matched names, which depends on your locale: here Run 3 final sorts first, but on many Linux clusters it comes last. The counts are what matter. pixi run shellcheck count_reads.sh on the supplied version flags the unquoted $@ (SC2068) and $f (SC2086); on the finished one it prints nothing.





Exercise 2. Check a sample table against the disk. After Section 8.7.
The sample table meta/samples.tsv lists a run folder for each sample. Save this script as ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/check_samples.sh. It is the loop from Section 8.4 that reads the table with < instead of a pipe, so the bad flag survives the loop:


~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/check_samples.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# check_samples.sh: check that each sample in a table has its run folder.
# Usage:  check_samples.sh TABLE
#   TABLE: tab-separated, header line first, columns sample, run_folder, ...
#   Run it from the folder that the run_folder paths are relative to.
# Problems go to stderr; exit 1 if any row has a problem.
set -euo pipefail

if [[ $# -ne 1 ]]; then
  echo "usage: check_samples.sh TABLE" >&2
  exit 2
fi
table="$1"
[[ -r "$table" ]] || { echo "cannot read: $table" >&2; exit 1; }

bad=0
{
  IFS= read -r _   # skip the header line
  while IFS=$'\t' read -r sample folder rest || [[ -n "$sample$folder$rest" ]]; do
    if [[ ! -d "$folder" ]]; then
      printf '%s: missing folder %s\n' "$sample" "$folder" >&2
      bad=1
    fi
    # Your turn: when the folder exists, check that it holds an R1 file
    # for this sample (sample_X_R1.fastq.gz or .fq.gz), and report it if not.
  done
} < "$table"
exit "$bad"

Run it from ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share with bash ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/check_samples.sh meta/samples.tsv; echo "exit $?". It already reports missing folders on stderr, keeps going after a bad row, and exits 1 if any row failed. Add the R1 check: when the folder exists, look for that sample’s R1 file, report it the same way if there is none, and print the sample and its R1 file, separated by a tab, on stdout when there is one.
Then a prediction. Make a copy, check_samples_csv.sh, that reads meta/samples_from_excel.csv with IFS=,, keeps the last column (read -r sample folder _ reads || [[ -n "$sample$folder$reads" ]]), and also checks that reads is a positive number with if ! (( reads > 0 )). Before running it: which checks will pass, and which will fail? Run it and explain the result from Section 7.10.






TipAnswer





Add shopt -s nullglob under set -euo pipefail, so a pattern that matches nothing gives an empty list, and replace the fi and the comment with an else branch:


~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/check_samples.sh (the loop)

    if [[ ! -d "$folder" ]]; then
      printf '%s: missing folder %s\n' "$sample" "$folder" >&2
      bad=1
    else
      r1=("$folder/${sample}"_R1.f*q.gz)
      if (( ${#r1[@]} == 0 )); then
        printf '%s: no R1 file in %s\n' "$sample" "$folder" >&2
        bad=1
      else
        printf '%s\t%s\n' "$sample" "${r1[0]}"
      fi
    fi

$ bash ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/check_samples.sh meta/samples.tsv; echo "exit $?"
sample_C    Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
sample_A    run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
sample_B    run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
sample_E: missing folder run5
sample_B    run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
sample_D: missing folder run4
exit 1
With 2>/dev/null only the four found rows remain: results and problems go to different streams (Section 8.8). Every bad row is reported, not just the first. To see the R1 check fire, copy the table to ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/, add a row sample_Z, tab, run1, and run on the copy: the output gains sample_Z: no R1 file in run1. The supplied version printed only the two missing folder lines. A follow-up worth thinking about: sample_B is listed twice. The table has a duplicate row, which this script does not look for.
The CSV copy (captured with bash 5.3):
$ bash ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/bin/check_samples_csv.sh meta/samples_from_excel.csv
…check_samples_csv.sh: line 22: ((: 12: arithmetic syntax error: invalid arithmetic operator (error token is "")
sample_C: reads is not a positive number: 12
sample_C    Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
…
Every row fails the number test, and the message even says 12 is not a positive number. The folder and R1 checks give the same result as the TSV. The file has Windows line endings, so each line’s last field, reads, ends in an invisible \r: 12\r is not a number, but the \r does not show on screen. The folder name is not the last field, so those checks never notice. After tr -d '\r' < meta/samples_from_excel.csv > samples_lf.csv, the copy run on samples_lf.csv gives the TSV’s result. The error does not stop the script, because it sits in an if. Older bash versions, such as 5.1 on many clusters, word the message differently. IFS=, works for this simple file only; a real CSV reader handles quoted commas (Chapter 14).





Exercise 3. What strict mode misses. After Section 8.7.
Save this script as ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/ex3/count_ok.sh:


~/bioinf-computing-ch08/ex3/count_ok.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count_ok.sh: count the reads in one FASTQ file, then report OK.
# Usage: count_ok.sh FILE.fastq.gz
n=$(gunzip -c "$1" | wc -l)
echo "$(basename "$1"): $((n / 4)) reads"
echo "OK"

Make a good input and three bad ones next to it: a truncated copy, and a gzip file that is valid but holds nothing (missing.fastq.gz you do not make at all):


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch08/ex3
cp ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz good.fastq.gz
head -c 30 good.fastq.gz > trunc.fastq.gz
gzip < /dev/null > empty.fastq.gz
for f in good missing trunc empty; do bash count_ok.sh "$f.fastq.gz"; echo "exit $?"; done

All four end with OK and exit 0. Add set -euo pipefail and predict which inputs it stops before you rerun. Then add one explicit check so that the remaining bad input stops the script with a message on stderr and exit 1, while good.fastq.gz still prints 3 reads and OK.






TipAnswer





With set -euo pipefail (GNU gzip wording):
$ for f in good missing trunc empty; do bash count_ok.sh "$f.fastq.gz"; echo "exit $?"; done
good.fastq.gz: 3 reads
OK
exit 0
gzip: missing.fastq.gz: No such file or directory
exit 1
gzip: trunc.fastq.gz: unexpected end of file
exit 1
empty.fastq.gz: 0 reads
OK
exit 0
Strict mode catches the missing and the truncated file, because gunzip reports both as failures and pipefail passes that on. (Apple gzip words them gunzip: can't stat: … and gunzip: trunc.fastq.gz: unexpected end of file.) The empty file is a valid gzip stream with no content: gunzip succeeds, wc -l prints 0, and nothing has reported a failure. Only a check of the result catches it:


~/bioinf-computing-ch08/ex3/count_ok.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# count_ok.sh: count the reads in one FASTQ file, then report OK.
# Usage: count_ok.sh FILE.fastq.gz
set -euo pipefail
if [[ $# -ne 1 ]]; then echo "usage: count_ok.sh FILE.fastq.gz" >&2; exit 2; fi

n=$(gunzip -c "$1" | wc -l)
reads=$((n / 4))
if (( reads == 0 )); then
  echo "$(basename "$1"): no reads" >&2
  exit 1
fi
echo "$(basename "$1"): $reads reads"
echo "OK"

$ bash count_ok.sh empty.fastq.gz; echo "exit $?"
empty.fastq.gz: no reads
exit 1
$ bash count_ok.sh good.fastq.gz; echo "exit $?"
good.fastq.gz: 3 reads
OK
exit 0
The other checks you might reach for do not work here. gzip -t empty.fastq.gz exits 0, because the stream is valid, and [[ -s empty.fastq.gz ]] is true, because the file holds 20 bytes of gzip header. Do not confuse it with a zero-byte file named .gz, which gunzip and gzip -t both reject. Dividing lines by 4 is right only for these plain four-line toy records; it does not check that a file is valid FASTQ. Tools that read the format properly come in Chapter 15.





Exercise 4. Add a third step to the project. After Section 8.10.
Add src/03_transcript_biotypes.sh, which counts the transcripts of each biotype (protein-coding, tRNA, and so on) in the reference annotation and writes results/transcript_biotypes.tsv. Follow 02_gtf_summary.sh: header comment, set -euo pipefail, the project-folder guard, log and die, an input check, the .tmp and mv, and the two MD5 log lines. One line is new to you (grep -o prints only the part of each line that matches), so here it is:


the extraction line for src/03_transcript_biotypes.sh

gunzip -c "$gtf" | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "transcript"' \
  | grep -o 'transcript_biotype "[^"]*"' | cut -d'"' -f2 \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr | awk -v OFS='\t' '{print $2, $1}'

Add the step to run_all.sh, run the whole pipeline with pixi run bash src/run_all.sh, and check that the counts add up to the 124 transcripts of Chapter 6. Commit the new script and the changed run_all.sh with a message that says what the step does, and check the commit with git show --stat HEAD.






TipAnswer







src/03_transcript_biotypes.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# 03_transcript_biotypes.sh: count transcripts of each biotype in the reference annotation.
# Run from the project folder:  pixi run bash src/03_transcript_biotypes.sh
# Input:  data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
# Output: results/transcript_biotypes.tsv (biotype, count; most common first)
set -euo pipefail

log() { printf '[%s] %s\n' "$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')" "$*" >&2; }
die() { log "ERROR: $*"; exit 1; }

[[ -f pixi.toml ]] || die "run from the project folder"

gtf="data/ref/genes.gtf.gz"
out="results/transcript_biotypes.tsv"
[[ -s "$gtf" ]] || die "missing or empty: $gtf"

mkdir -p results
log "start; input md5: $(md5sum "$gtf")"
{
  printf 'biotype\tcount\n'
  gunzip -c "$gtf" | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "transcript"' \
    | grep -o 'transcript_biotype "[^"]*"' | cut -d'"' -f2 \
    | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr | awk -v OFS='\t' '{print $2, $1}'
} > "$out.tmp"
mv "$out.tmp" "$out"
log "wrote $out ($(( $(wc -l < "$out") - 1 )) biotypes)"
log "output md5: $(md5sum "$out")"

In run_all.sh, add bash src/03_transcript_biotypes.sh after the 02 line, inside the { … } group. The new step’s log lines and result:
[2026-11-22 15:08:39] start; input md5: 504334f6741ee771c665ae845429087f  data/ref/genes.gtf.gz
[2026-11-22 15:08:39] wrote results/transcript_biotypes.tsv (5 biotypes)
[2026-11-22 15:08:40] output md5: 06f05e65e07083ae63267ee916dedccc  results/transcript_biotypes.tsv
$ cat results/transcript_biotypes.tsv
biotype count
protein_coding  116
tRNA    4
pseudogene  2
ncRNA   1
snoRNA  1
116 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 124, the transcript count from gtf_feature_counts.tsv. Your MD5 should match: the tied ncRNA and snoRNA rows come out in the same order whatever your locale. Then:


Terminal (laptop)

git add src/03_transcript_biotypes.sh src/run_all.sh
git commit -m "Add step 03: count transcripts by biotype"
git show --stat HEAD

git show --stat HEAD lists both files. One more thing to notice: 02 and 03 both read only the GTF and write different files, so they could run at the same time. run_all.sh runs them one after the other, one of the limits in Section 8.10 that workflow managers remove.





Exercise 5. Break, see, recover. After Section 8.12.
In ~/bioinf-computing, delete the line that prints the header in src/02_gtf_summary.sh (printf 'feature\tcount\n'), run the script, and commit the change as if you had not noticed. Then find what changed, bring back the working version from the commit before, check that it works, and commit the recovery. Record each command and what it showed in NOTEBOOK.md.






TipAnswer





The broken script still runs and exits 0, but its log says wrote results/gtf_feature_counts.tsv (4 feature types), and the file starts with exon  129: the header is gone, and the count of “feature types” is now one short because the script subtracts a header line that is not there. Nothing failed; only reading the result shows the problem.
$ git commit -am "Drop header line from GTF summary"
$ git log --oneline -- src/02_gtf_summary.sh
<hash> Drop header line from GTF summary
<hash> Add read-count and GTF summary scripts
$ git diff HEAD~1
diff --git a/src/02_gtf_summary.sh b/src/02_gtf_summary.sh
…
 {
-  printf 'feature\tcount\n'
   gunzip -c "$gtf" | cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr \
     | awk -v OFS='\t' '{print $2, $1}'
 } > "$out.tmp"
$ git restore --source=HEAD~1 src/02_gtf_summary.sh
$ git status --short
 M src/02_gtf_summary.sh
$ pixi run bash src/run_all.sh
$ git commit -am "Restore header line in GTF summary"
Your commit hashes (shown as <hash>) and messages will differ, and your history may have more commits. git log -- file lists only the commits that changed that file. git diff HEAD~1 compares your files with the commit before the last one, so the removed line shows with a -. git restore --source=HEAD~1 copies the file as it was in that commit into your folder; git status shows it as modified, because it now differs from the last commit. Rerunning run_all.sh should give five feature types again, and the new commit records the repair without erasing the mistake from history. (If you had not committed the bad change, git restore src/02_gtf_summary.sh alone would have been enough.)

text:

Shotts (2025), The Linux Command Line, Part 4 “Writing Shell Scripts” — variables, if, loops, and positional parameters, one chapter each, in the same order as this chapter; free online.
Wilson et al. (2019), The Unix Shell, episodes “Loops” and “Shell Scripts” — a second, shorter walk through the same ideas, with exercises and a different dataset.
Buffalo (2015), Bioinformatics Data Skills, chapter 12 “Bioinformatics Shell Scripting, Writing Pipelines, and Parallelizing Tasks” — written for the same readers: set -euo pipefail, loops over samples, and make for pipelines.
Wilson et al. (2017), “Good enough practices in scientific computing” — the sections on software and project organisation give the reasons behind numbered scripts, one command to rerun everything, and version control.
Ramey and Fox (2025), the Bash Reference Manual, sections Shell Expansions and The Set Builtin — the exact rules for word splitting and for when set -e does and does not stop a script. Short, precise, and the place to settle an argument.

title: 9  Working remotely
text:
9.1 What this chapter does
Core. Work through it, with the exercises.
In Section 2.4 you logged in to a cluster once, typed hostname, and logged out. Daily work is different: many logins a day, commands that run longer than your connection lasts, and files moving both ways. This chapter makes those three things routine. Everything before it ran on your laptop (Chapter 1); from here on, the main path assumes a cluster account. If you do not have one yet, every section says which steps work on the laptop alone, and the cluster steps are shown as captured sessions you can read.
Three machines matter from now on (Figure 9.1):
The login node and the DTN sit on the same shared storage, so a file copied to the DTN appears in the same /work or /project folder you see from the login node. We start every transfer from the laptop, in both directions: a laptop behind a home or campus firewall usually cannot accept an incoming SSH connection, so the cluster cannot start a copy to it. Who starts the connection is separate from which way the data flows. A “pull” typed on the laptop still moves files from the cluster to the laptop.
Practice happens in a scratch folder on the laptop. Make it now:
The cluster steps use your own cluster folder: /work/<group>/<netid> on Nova, /project/<project>/<you> on SCINet. What those storage areas are, and why this is the right place, comes in Chapter 10. Two things outside the scratch folder change: your ~/.ssh folder (keys and config, in Section 9.3 and Section 9.4) and, at the end, a copy of your project on the cluster.
Two laptop tools. This chapter needs a current rsync and tmux on the laptop. A Mac’s own /usr/bin/rsync is an older replacement (openrsync, “rsync version 2.6.9 compatible”) that lacks options used here, and macOS has no tmux. Install both with Homebrew, then check that Homebrew’s rsync comes first on your PATH (Section 7.4):
(On an Apple-silicon Mac the first path is /opt/homebrew/bin/rsync.) Ubuntu, including Ubuntu under WSL, already has both: Ubuntu 26.04 ships rsync 3.4.1, tmux 3.6, screen, and OpenSSH 10.2. If type -a rsync or type -a tmux finds nothing on your Linux machine, sudo apt install rsync tmux adds them.
Without a cluster, these parts work on the laptop alone: the broken-transfer demonstration in Section 9.2, making a key in Section 9.3, checking a config file with ssh -G in Section 9.4, all of tmux on the laptop in Section 9.5, and the local rsync and checksum steps in Section 9.6 and Section 9.7.
The outputs shown were captured in November 2026: on a Mac (macOS 15, Homebrew bash, rsync 3.5.0, OpenSSH 9.9, tmux 3.7), on Windows 11 with Ubuntu 26.04 under WSL (OpenSSH 10.2), and by logging in to Nova, Atlas, and Ceres. User names, groups, and addresses are replaced by placeholders such as <netid>, <group>, and <project>.
