Figure 10.6: A job array. One sbatch --array=1-4 makes four tasks; task n reads line n + 1 of reads.tsv (line 1 is the header) and writes its own stats_<run>.tsv and log. A fifth task would find no row and stop. Chapter 8’s for loop, below, does the same work one run after another, in one process.



Managing an array:

--array=1-40%5 runs at most 5 tasks at once: be kind to the queue with large arrays.
scancel 17720815_3 cancels one task; scancel 17720815 all of them.
sacct -j 17720815 lists three lines per task (_N, _N.batch, _N.extern), which is why the JobID column needs %20.
Logs use %A (the array’s ID) and %a (the task number) in --output.
Each site caps the array size (scontrol show config | grep -i MaxArraySize): 10001 on Ceres and Atlas, 1001 on Nova. The largest task number is one less, so Nova allows --array=1-1000.







WarningPitfall: the header row and the task past the end



With the header on line 1, task n must read line n + 1, and four data rows mean --array=1-4. A task past the last row gets nothing from awk, which exits 0, so set -e alone would not stop it: without the [ -n "$row" ] check, task 5 would run seqkit on nothing. Dry-run every task number first.



Check yourself. With the awk line as written and four data rows, what do tasks 0, 1, and 5 read?






TipAnswer





Task 0 reads line 1, the header (its “file” would be fastq_1, which the readable-file check stops); task 1 reads the first run; task 5 reads nothing, and the empty-row check stops it. So the array is --array=1-4.

title: 10  HPC and SLURM
text:
10.11 Chains of jobs (overview)
Overview. Section 8.10 ran numbered scripts one after another with src/run_all.sh and promised a cluster version. The simplest one is a single job that runs run_all.sh: its order and its stop-at-the-first-failure behaviour stay exactly as they are. Make a copy of jobs/01_count_reads.sbatch that runs pixi run bash src/run_all.sh instead, and that is it.
Separate jobs earn their keep when steps need different resources (a big-memory step, a many-CPU step) or can run side by side. SLURM can start one job only after another succeeds:


Terminal (login node)

jid=$(sbatch --parsable jobs/01_count_reads.sbatch)
sbatch --dependency="afterok:$jid" jobs/02_gtf_summary.sbatch
squeue -u $USER

--parsable makes sbatch print only the job ID, which $( ) saves in jid. (jobs/02_gtf_summary.sbatch is a copy of the first job script that runs src/02_gtf_summary.sh; making it is exercise 5.) While the first job waits or runs, squeue shows the second as (Dependency). afterok imposes the order you chose; it passes no data. Here the two steps do not even need each other’s output, so afterok only says “not before”. If you did Chapter 8’s exercise 4, src/03_transcript_biotypes.sh can be submitted with no dependency at all, beside 02, and you can watch both run at once.
When the first job fails, afterok never starts the second. What happens to it then depends on the site (captured 2026-11-23, with a first job that failed):

Ceres and Nova leave it pending for ever, as (DependencyNeverSatisfied). Cancel it yourself with scancel, or submit it with --kill-on-invalid-dep=yes so SLURM cancels it.
Atlas cancels it automatically (its configuration has kill_invalid_depend): the second job went from PD (Dependency) to CANCELLED with no scancel.

So after a failed chain, check squeue: on some sites the job waits forever, on others it is gone. This is also where hand-made chains stop being fun. A workflow manager (Chapter 25) tracks which steps are done, reruns only what changed, and submits each step as a job for you; nf-core pipelines do exactly this on SLURM (Chapter 26).

Check yourself. The first job of a chain fails. What happens to the second?






TipAnswer





It never starts. Depending on the site it stays pending as DependencyNeverSatisfied (Ceres, Nova: scancel it) or is cancelled automatically (Atlas).

title: 10  HPC and SLURM
text:
10.12 GPU partitions (overview)
Overview. A GPU is asked for like any other resource, with --gres (generic resources), and usually in a GPU partition:


jobs/gpu_test.sbatch (the request)

#SBATCH --partition=<gpu partition>
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1

Inside the job, nvidia-smi shows the card you got. Only tools built for GPUs use one: deep-learning tools, NVIDIA’s Parabricks, some basecallers. An ordinary tool on a GPU node leaves the GPU idle while someone who needs it waits.
The exact form is site-specific (observed 2026-11-23):

Atlas has four GPU partitions, gpu-v100, gpu-a100, gpu-a100-mig7, and gpu-l40s, with QOS limits of 2 days (7 for a100). sinfo -o "%P %G" names the cards, for example gpu:nvidia_a100_1g.10gb:56 on the MIG partition (an A100 split into slices). Use the name sinfo shows, or plain gpu:1: the OnDemand form’s gpu:a100_1g.10gb:1 was refused with Requested node configuration is not available.
Nova has no separate GPU partition: GPU nodes sit in the default nova partition (and interactive, scavenger), and the card type goes in --gres, for example --gres=gpu:a100:1.
Ceres has no GPUs.

Check a request without submitting it with sbatch --test-only, which says when and where the job would start, or refuses it. GPUs in depth are Chapter 37.

title: 10  HPC and SLURM
text:
10.13 Etiquette and a checklist
Start with a quick audit, on the login node: what are you running here, what do you have queued, and how full is your storage?


Terminal (login node)

ps -u "$USER"
squeue -u $USER
my_quotas                                  # SCINet; Nova: cat /work/<group>/group_storage_usage

ps (Section 7.7) should show your shell, perhaps tmux and an editor, and nothing heavy.




Table 10.13: Sharing a cluster.










Do
Don’t
Why




edit, sbatch, small file moves, module spider on login nodes
align, sort big files, install large environments, or loop over samples on login nodes
the login node is shared by everyone logged in


measure a test run, then request a margin over it
request whole nodes or days “to be safe”
idle reservations block others and can wait longer


one array for many inputs, throttled (%5)
thousands of separate tiny jobs
each job costs the scheduler work


pass the CPU count to the tool
reserve CPUs the tool never uses
idle CPUs are wasted for everyone


delete your own temporary folders and scratch copies
leave data in scratch to be purged
purges lose data you forgot; quotas fill


scancel jobs and sessions you no longer need
leave a held node or OnDemand session idle
it keeps charging and blocking


use GPU partitions only for GPU tools
run CPU-only work on GPU nodes
GPUs are scarce







scancel -u $USER cancels all your jobs at once; use it with care.






CautionMisconception: “I can run my analysis on the login node”



Reality. The login node is the front desk: shared by everyone, for editing, submitting, and small moves. Analyses run as jobs on compute nodes, interactive for trying things, batch for everything longer than a few minutes.

title: 10  HPC and SLURM
text:
10.14 Summary

A cluster is many computers behind a queue. The login node is for editing and submitting; work runs as jobs on compute nodes, started by SLURM when resources are free. Inside a job, the allocation (SLURM_*, scontrol show job), not free, says what you may use.
A request names a partition, an account, and sometimes a QOS, and each layer can set limits. sinfo is not always the real limit: check scontrol show partition and sacctmgr show qos.
Home is small; projects hold your work; scratch is big but purged; node-local $TMPDIR lasts one job. Count files as well as bytes. Stage work in a temporary folder of your own and copy results back.
Load modules by named version inside job scripts, never in ~/.bashrc; use pixi run for what the book environment has, and never both for one tool.
srun --pty bash -l and salloc are interactive jobs; check hostname after salloc, and give back what you hold. To SSH to a compute node: hold it, find it in squeue, connect with ProxyJump, scancel it.
A job script is a bash script with #SBATCH lines first. Submit from the project folder with mkdir -p logs done; the job starts there with a copy of your environment and no terminal. Check sacct, the log, and the result: COMPLETED only means exit 0.
Ask for CPUs × memory × time on one node, always setting --time and --mem; pass the CPU count to the tool; check AllocCPUS. Smaller, accurate requests can start sooner.
Failures read as OUT_OF_MEMORY 0:125, TIMEOUT (with .batch CANCELLED 0:15), or FAILED 127:0 for a missing command; read the allocation line, the step lines, and the log together. Priority and Resources are normal waiting.
Size the next run from the last: peak memory plus about 25%, time scaled to the input, recorded in NOTEBOOK.md.
A job array runs one script over many inputs; dry-run every task number, guard the row past the end, and give each task its own output. afterok chains jobs; a failed chain waits forever on some sites.

Table 10.14 collects the chapter’s commands.




Table 10.14: The chapter’s commands on one page.









Task
Command




Partitions and their limits
sinfo -s, scontrol show partition <name>


Your accounts and QOS
sacctmgr -n -P show assoc user=$USER format=account,partition,qos,defaultqos, sacctmgr show qos


Node sizes
sinfo -N -o "%N %c %m %G"


Interactive shell
srun --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=4G --time=00:30:00 --pty bash -l (SCINet: -A <project>)


Hold a node
salloc -N1 -n1 --time=00:20:00 --mem=2G sleep infinity, then scancel <jobid>


Submit
sbatch jobs/script.sbatch; sbatch --array=1-4 …; jid=$(sbatch --parsable …)


Your jobs
squeue -u $USER; squeue --start -u $USER


Everything about one job
scontrol show job <jobid>


What a job used
sacct -j <jobid> --format=JobID%20,State%15,ExitCode,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,TotalCPU,ReqMem,MaxRSS; seff <jobid>


Cancel
scancel <jobid>, scancel <jobid>_3, scancel -u $USER (all)


Check a request
sbatch --test-only …


Modules
module spider <name>, module load <name>/<version>, module list, module purge


Site settings
scontrol show config \| grep -i -E 'MaxArraySize\|NamespaceType'

title: 10  HPC and SLURM
text:
10.15 Exercises
Exercises 1–4 are core; 5 and 6 are optional. Each has a route without a cluster. Record what you did and saw in NOTEBOOK.md, in the project for the cluster parts and in ~/bioinf-computing-ch10 for the rest.

Exercise 1. Know your cluster. After Section 10.2 and Section 10.3.
Fill a five-row card in NOTEBOOK.md for your site: the default partition and its real time limit (and where that limit comes from); your accounts; the interactive partition, if any; the quota command and your current use; whether seff exists.
No cluster? Fill the card for this fictional site from its outputs and one sentence of its user guide (“Interactive sessions: use the short partition.”):
$ sinfo -s
PARTITION AVAIL  TIMELIMIT   NODES(A/I/O/T) NODELIST
main*        up 30-00:00:0       40/10/2/52 n[001-052]
short        up    4:00:00         2/6/0/8 s[01-08]
$ scontrol show partition main | grep -o -E '(DefaultTime|MaxTime|QoS)=[^ ]+'
QoS=main
DefaultTime=01:00:00
MaxTime=30-00:00:00
$ sacctmgr -n show qos format=Name%10,MaxWall | grep main
      main  7-00:00:00
$ sacctmgr -n show assoc user=$USER format=account%20
            lab-smith
$ command -v seff || echo "no seff"
no seff
$ site_quota
Path                      Used (GB)   Quota (GB)   Files     File quota
/home/<user>                    4.1         20      31,207     200,000
/proj/lab-smith              1840.0       5000   2,914,330   5,000,000






TipAnswer





For the fictional site: default partition main, whose real limit is 7 days, from the main QOS the partition attaches (sinfo says 30); account lab-smith; interactive partition short (4 hours; it is the user guide that says so, not the time limit); quota command site_quota: home 4.1 of 20 GB, the project 1,840 of 5,000 GB, and this site also counts files (2.9 of 5 million in the project); no seff, so measure with sacct. (df -h would show the file system’s free space, not your quota.) On a real site, compare with Table 10.1.





Exercise 2. Adapt the first job. After Section 10.6.
Copy jobs/01_count_reads.sbatch to jobs/count_small.sbatch. Give it the job name count_small, 1 GB of memory, and 5 minutes. Before submitting, write down the log file’s name. Submit it, and confirm with sacct, the log, and results/read_counts.tsv. Then give a log a date in its name. #SBATCH lines are not expanded, so do it on the command line, where your shell fills in the date before sbatch runs:


Terminal (login node)

sbatch --output="logs/%x_%j_$(date +%F).out" jobs/count_small.sbatch

No cluster? Run the copy with bash on the laptop, and write down what the log would have been called.






TipAnswer





logs/count_small_<jobid>.out. sacct shows COMPLETED 0:0 with ReqMem 1G; the log has the start line, Chapter 8’s lines, and the finish line; the result file has one 50,000-read row per FASTQ file (eight after the array’s data step). The dated version wrote, on Nova, logs/01_count_reads_17720578_2026-11-23.out for the original script: %x and %j are SLURM’s, the date was the shell’s. With bash, there is no log file at all: everything goes to your terminal.





Exercise 3. Diagnose three failures. After Section 10.8.
Submit ok.sbatch, then the three broken scripts. For each, record State, ExitCode, and the one log line that explains it. Then fix one of them, resubmit, and confirm it completes: give oom more memory than it takes (--mem=3G), or timeout more time than it sleeps (--time=00:10:00). If you choose typo, fix the spelling first and submit it: it fails again, for a different reason. Find that reason in the log, and fix it too.
No cluster? Use the captured sacct table and logs in Section 10.8, and answer from these three lines of another user’s jobs as well:
               JobID           State ExitCode    Elapsed     ReqMem     MaxRSS
            31337001   OUT_OF_MEMORY    0:125   00:42:10        16G
      31337001.batch   OUT_OF_MEMORY    0:125   00:42:10                 16.4G
            31337002         TIMEOUT      0:0   12:00:16         64G
      31337002.batch       CANCELLED     0:15   12:00:18                  3.1G
            31337003       COMPLETED      0:0   00:03:05        120G
      31337003.batch       COMPLETED      0:0   00:03:05                  2.2G
Which ran out of memory, which hit its time limit, and which asked for far more memory than it used?






TipAnswer





ok: COMPLETED 0:0, log ok. oom: OUT_OF_MEMORY 0:125, log … Killed … and Detected 1 oom_kill event. timeout: TIMEOUT 0:0 (.batch CANCELLED 0:15), log CANCELLED AT … DUE TO TIME LIMIT. typo: FAILED 127:0, log No such file or directory. With the spelling fixed, typo fails with run from the project folder: the job starts in the scratch folder, and Chapter 8’s guard stops the script there, as it should. A path to the script finds the script; it does not change the folder the script runs in, nor start the book environment that seqkit needs. The full fix replaces the bash line with cd "$project" and pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh. In the extra table: 31337001 ran out of memory (its peak passed 16 GB); 31337002 hit its 12-hour limit (and used only 3.1 of 64 GB, so the next request needs more time but far less memory); 31337003 used 2.2 of 120 GB, so about 3 GB would do.





Exercise 4. Right-size a request. After Section 10.9 and Section 10.10.
Run jobs/02_stats_array.sbatch as an array over the four runs with a generous request (8 CPUs, 16 GB, 1 hour, given on the command line: sbatch --array=1-4 --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=16G --time=01:00:00 …). Use sacct or seff to choose a smaller memory and time request, and resubmit with it. For both runs, record peak memory, elapsed time, and queue wait (sacct -j <id> --format=JobID%20,Submit,Start) in NOTEBOOK.md. Wait times depend on the queue at that moment, so record them; do not expect a “right” answer. These tasks last a second or less, too short for CPU efficiency to mean anything (it will likely read 0%, as for the first job). For the CPU part, use the two 2-minute jobs in Table 10.8 instead: compute each one’s efficiency by hand from TotalCPU, Elapsed, and AllocCPUS, and say how many CPUs you would ask for to run the second one again.
No cluster? Choose the smaller request from the four captured tasks in Section 10.10 (2 CPUs, 2 GB, at most 1 second each), and do the CPU part as above.






TipAnswer





Each task peaked at 72–88 MB and ran a second or less, so about 256–512 MB (the peak plus a margin, rounded up generously for such a small number) and a few minutes is plenty; keep 1–2 CPUs, since a second-long task gains nothing from more. The smaller request often waits less, but not always. CPU part: 478.9 s / (126 s × 4) = 95.0% and 120.0 s / (125 s × 4) = 24.0%; the second job kept one CPU busy, so it needs 1 CPU (or its tool told to use 4).





Exercise 5 (optional). Chain two steps. After Section 10.11.
Make jobs/02_gtf_summary.sbatch by copying the first job script and changing the job name and the pixi run line to src/02_gtf_summary.sh. Submit it with --dependency="afterok:$jid" after the first job, and watch squeue. Then make the first job fail (submit typo.sbatch, or point the first script at a missing file), chain the second after it, and record what your site does with the second.
No cluster? From Section 10.11, write down what you would expect on Ceres and on Atlas, and the command that cleans up on Ceres.






TipAnswer





With a successful first job, the second shows (Dependency), then runs. After a failed first job, Ceres and Nova leave the second pending as (DependencyNeverSatisfied), and scancel <jobid> removes it; Atlas cancels it by itself.





Exercise 6 (optional). Use temporary space in the array. After Section 10.3 and Section 10.10.
Copy the array script to jobs/02_stats_staged.sbatch and add the staging pattern from jobs/ch10_staging.sbatch: each task makes its own folder under $TMPDIR (with ${SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID}_${task} in its name), copies its FASTQ file there, runs seqkit on the copy, copies stats_<run>.tsv back to results/, and removes its folder. Confirm the four results match the unstaged ones (diff) and that each log shows its folder gone. With tiny files the time will not change; the habit is the point.
No cluster? Run it on the laptop with SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID=1 bash jobs/02_stats_staged.sbatch.






TipAnswer





One possible core, after the checks:
project=$PWD
work=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:?}/stats_${SLURM_ARRAY_JOB_ID:-local}_${task}_XXXX")
cp "$fq" "$work/"
pixi run seqkit stats -j "$threads" -T "$work/$(basename "$fq")" > "$work/stats.tsv"
[[ $(wc -l < "$work/stats.tsv") -eq 2 ]] || { echo "expected one stats row for $run" >&2; exit 1; }
cp "$work/stats.tsv" "$project/results/stats_${run}.tsv.tmp"
mv "$project/results/stats_${run}.tsv.tmp" "$project/results/stats_${run}.tsv"
rm -rf "$work"
The table’s first column now shows the temporary path instead of data/raw/…, so diff reports that column; compare the other columns with cut -f 2- results/stats_SRR6357070.tsv.

title: 10  HPC and SLURM
text:
10.16 Further reading

HPC Carpentry (2026), Introduction to High-Performance Computing — a hands-on lesson on the same ground (logging in, the scheduler, job scripts, modules, transferring files), with exercises; good for a second explanation of anything here.
SchedMD (2026), the SLURM Quick Start User Guide — the official short tour of every command in this chapter, with links to each command’s manual page; read the sbatch and sacct pages for the options and fields in Table 10.7 and Table 10.12.
Yoo et al. (2003), “SLURM: Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management” — the original paper by SLURM’s designers: why a scheduler is built around partitions, jobs, and job steps.
McLay (2026), the Lmod user guide — module spider, defaults, and hidden modules, for when your site’s module trees surprise you.
Your site’s own pages: SCINet’s SLURM guide and Ceres and Atlas differences, MSU’s Atlas documentation, and ISU’s SLURM page — the authority for limits, partitions, and storage rules; Appendix A collects the details.




HPC Carpentry. 2026. Introduction to High-Performance Computing. https://www.hpc-carpentry.org/hpc-intro/.

SchedMD. 2026. Quick Start User Guide. Slurm Workload Manager documentation. https://slurm.schedmd.com/quickstart.html.

title: Report an Issue
text:
Which route for what
Quick links: report an error · something doesn’t run · ask a question · suggest an idea · open issues
A computing book goes wrong in more ways than most: a command that worked last year fails with a new tool version, a cluster behaves differently from the one the book was tested on, a download link moves, an install breaks on one operating system. The fastest way to find these is readers. Every report is read, and the fix goes onto the website as soon as it is made.
There is no errata list. When something is wrong it is corrected in the book itself.
Issues and Discussions are kept separate on purpose. The issue tracker holds only things with a fix, so it reads as a to-do list and you can search it to see whether your problem is already reported. Questions go to Discussions because a question is not a defect, but a run of questions on the same section is a sign the explanation failed, and that does become an issue.

title: Report an Issue
text:
You have found
Use




A wrong command, output, or claim
An issue, using the Error in the book form


A command or install that fails for you (pixi, VS Code, a tool, a cluster step)
An issue, using the Something doesn’t run form


A broken link, moved download, or outdated tool version
An issue, using the Error in the book form


A typo or awkward sentence you are willing to fix
A pull request (see below)


A typo you would rather just report
The Error in the book form


A section you did not follow, or are not sure is right
A question in Discussions › Q&A


A suggestion: a better example, a missing topic or tool
An idea in Discussions › Ideas


Something that should not be public
Email the author (the address on the GitHub profile)

title: Report an Issue
text:
Before you report
Note the page. Copy the URL of the page and the section heading. The book changes often while it is being written, so say roughly when you read it.
Search the open issues. If someone has already reported it, add a comment there rather than opening a second one. A second report on the same problem is still useful: it says how many readers it affects.

title: Report an Issue
text:
Reporting an error
You need a free GitHub account. The Error in the book form asks for:

Chapter and section, with the command, code chunk, table, or figure if there is one.
What is wrong (quote it as it appears) and what it should be.
How you know. Optional, and the most useful field: the command you ran and its output, or a link to the tool’s documentation.

title: Report an Issue
text:
Reporting something that doesn’t run
Problems with installs and commands are the most common reports, and the hardest to fix without details. The Something doesn’t run form asks for:

Where you ran it: laptop, cluster login node, or compute node; the operating system (macOS, Windows with WSL2, or Linux); the cluster name if there is one (e.g., SCINet Ceres, ISU Nova).
The exact command, copied, not retyped.
The complete error message, copied as text, not a screenshot, and not shortened. The useful line is often the first error, not the last.
Your environment: the output of pixi info run in the book’s folder. On a cluster, also any module load lines you ran first.

Three more fields are optional but often save a round of questions:

What you expected, for example the output the book shows.
What you have tried: anything you checked or changed, and what happened.
The version of the failing tool, for example the output of pixi run seqkit version. pixi info describes the environment but does not list the versions of the tools in it.







WarningPitfall



Never paste passwords, SSH private keys, access tokens, or private data into an issue. Issues are public and stay public. Replace usernames, paths, and hostnames you would rather not share with placeholders such as <user>.

title: Report an Issue
text:
Fixing it yourself
For a typo or a wording fix, the fastest route is to make the change and propose it on GitHub:

Open the page’s source file in the repository. Chapters live in chapters/, one .qmd file each (Markdown with code), named by number: chapter 5 is chapters/05-shell-basics.qmd.
Click the pencil icon. GitHub offers to fork the repository into your own account; accept.
Make the change, write one line saying what it is, and choose Propose changes, then Create pull request.

The author reviews it, and merges it or asks for a change. Some things to know before you edit:

Edit the .qmd only. _book/ is generated output.
One fix per pull request. A three-line change is reviewed in a minute; a change that touches four chapters waits.
Do not add to references.bib unless you have checked the DOI. Every entry in it has been verified.
Your contribution is offered under the book’s licenses: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for text and figures, MIT for code.
Larger changes (a rewritten section, a new example) should start as a discussion in Ideas, so the shape is agreed before the work is done.

title: Report an Issue
section: Asking a question or suggesting something
text:
Asking a question or suggesting something
Discussions › Q&A is for “I did not follow this step” or “is this right?”. Other readers can answer as well as the author, and an answered question stays there for the next person.
Discussions › Ideas is for a different example, a tool the book should cover, or a better way to explain something. Scope is the author’s call: this book aims for awareness, not depth, and full algorithms belong to the other books in the series. The discussion is where the case is made.

title: Report an Issue
text:
What happens next
A report is labelled with its chapter and its type (error, typo, doesnt-run, link). The fix is made on the main branch and the website updates from it. If a problem only affects one operating system or cluster, the fix may be a note in the chapter rather than a change to the command.

text:
A.2 Accounts
Checked 2026-11-21 against SCINet’s signup page and ISU’s Nova page and FAQ.
SCINet (Ceres and Atlas):

ARS employees fill in the online form on the signup page (sign in with eAuthentication; be signed in to USDA Office 365 first). Contractors name their contracting officer’s representative as supervisor.
A non-ARS collaborator needs an ARS employee sponsor, who submits the form on their behalf, with the collaborator’s details and the agreement that links them to ARS.
The supervisor (the sponsor’s supervisor, for non-ARS users) approves. “It may take up to five business days to create an account after the request is approved.”
You sign in through eAuthentication: with a LincPass, or, for non-USDA users, with Login.gov using the same e-mail address as the SCINet account (alternative logins).
A new account has no project: your Slurm account is sandbox, for jobs of up to 2 hours (Atlas lists sandbox jobs as 2 hours; on Ceres, observed). A project is requested by its principal investigator, who must be a full-time ARS employee; its managers add members (project management). Membership can take a while to reach every system.
On Atlas, your home folder may appear only a day after the welcome e-mail (accessing SCINet).

Nova:

Your user name is your ISU NetID.
Community access: anyone affiliated with Iowa State can ask for lower-priority access with no hardware purchase, through the HPC Cluster Access Request form linked from the Nova page. A community group gets 1 TB of group working space.
Sponsored access: groups that bought nodes get higher priority and larger limits; the group’s owner adds members.
Instructional access: an instructor requests it for a class, with the same request form.
How long approval takes: not stated. Access for collaborators outside Iowa State: not stated.

title: Appendix A — Cluster sites: SCINet and Nova
text:
A.6 Interactive sessions
Checked 2026-11-21 against the pages linked below and by starting a session on each cluster. Chapter 1’s first session uses srun --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=4G --time=01:00:00 --pty bash -l; each site adds its own options. Full SLURM teaching is Chapter 10.

Ceres: salloc -A <project> gives one core, about 6 GB, and a shell for 2 hours (SLURM guide). Partition ceres (default 2 hours, at most 3 weeks); scavenger runs longer but can be stopped. sinfo -s (observed) lists only these two, with partition limits of 60 and 21 days; the 3-week limit on ceres comes from its QOS, not the partition.
Observed: srun -A <project> --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=4G --time=00:30:00 --pty bash -l works and gives a shell on a compute node. sacctmgr -n show assoc user=$USER format=account%30 lists the accounts you may use. On arrival the node prints its settings: TMPDIR and Apptainer’s cache are set to the node’s /tmp, and TMOUT=5400 logs an idle shell out after 90 minutes.
Atlas: -A <project> is required. salloc -A <project> only reserves the node; srun --pty --preserve-env bash then puts you on it, or use srun -A <project> --pty --preserve-env bash in one step (Ceres and Atlas differences). Default partition atlas; others for large memory and GPUs, listed in MSU’s Atlas specifications. sinfo -s (observed) shows atlas, bigmem, four GPU partitions, development, and service, all with no time limit, so the limits come from the QOS.
Observed: the same srun -A <project> ... --pty bash -l line as on Ceres works in one step, and nothing is printed on arrival.
Nova: ISU’s examples have no account option, e.g. salloc -N 1 -n 8 -t 4:00:00 (SLURM page); default partition nova. ISU’s pages say jobs run up to two weeks; the OnDemand form showed a 31-day limit for nova (observed).
Observed: srun --cpus-per-task=1 --mem=4G --time=00:30:00 --pty bash -l works with no -A; SLURM charges your default account (list yours with the sacctmgr line above). On arrival the node prints its settings, as Ceres does: TMPDIR and Apptainer’s cache on the node’s /tmp, TMOUT=5400 (90 idle minutes), and Apptainer set to make /work, /ptmp, and the other shared file systems visible inside containers. sinfo -s (observed) shows nova (31 days), interactive (8 hours; the one ISU’s VS Code page says to pick), instruction (2 days), scavenger, reserved, nova-arm, and a one-minute allnodes.
End the session with exit. After srun ... --pty, exit ends the job too (squeue -u $USER showed nothing left on all three, observed); a reservation from salloc may need scancel <jobid> as well.
Internet from compute nodes: not stated by any of the three. Observed on Ceres: yes (curl -sI https://pixi.sh answered). On Atlas: yes, through a web proxy (the reply begins HTTP/1.1 200 Connection established, which is the proxy speaking). Tools that read the standard https_proxy setting, as curl does, work without changes. The node sets https_proxy, http_proxy, and no_proxy for you (observed). On Nova: yes, directly (observed). So on all three, downloads work inside an interactive session. On Atlas both the pixi installer and pixi install --locked worked through the proxy with no changes (observed 2026-11-22). The book environment took 29 seconds to install on Atlas, 54 on Ceres, and 10 on Nova; it used about 1.3 GB on SCINet and 0.8 GB on Nova’s compressed /work, with the cache’s files shared rather than copied on all three.

text:
A.8 Software on the site
Checked 2026-11-21 against SCINet’s modules and Apptainer guides and ISU’s modules page.

Modules on all three: module avail (or module spider), module load <name>, module list. On Atlas some modules appear only after a gcc module is loaded.
Containers: Apptainer on SCINet (on Atlas, module load apptainer first; run it on a compute node). Nova: not documented on the pages read, but module avail apptainer lists versions 1.1.5 to 1.4.0 (observed), from three dated software trees.
Asking for software: SCINet’s software request form; new system-wide software needs a security review that “takes a few weeks”. Nova: ISU Research IT (Section A.10).
The book’s way: the book environment with pixi in your project storage, for everything it covers; site modules only for what it does not.

title: Appendix A — Cluster sites: SCINet and Nova
text:
A.9 Shared reference data

Ceres has a shared /reference area, including ready-made containers in /reference/containers. Its main folders (observed): data, containers, llms, workshops, and workbook, plus site-admin folders.
Atlas has /reference, copied from Ceres’s /reference/data every night. Observed: data, containers, llms, models, workshops, workbook, and a README that says the folder is “for reference datasets”, “read only on atlas”, and “sync’d nightly from” Ceres’s /reference/data.
Nova: not stated, and none seen: the top-level /shared folder holds the site’s own configuration (SLURM, OnDemand, module files), not reference data (observed).

What /reference/data holds (observed; the same on Ceres and Atlas): mostly the large databases that annotation and classification tools need, one folder per tool, e.g. alphafold, BUSCO, eggnogdb, gtdbtk, kaiju, humann, and Dfam, plus a Genome folder. Before downloading a tool’s database, look here first; some of these databases are very large.
If your site has none, keep references once in a lab-shared folder (Section 3.5).
